# PREFACE.

<term>Philosophy</term><note>In this context, the author uses "Philosophy" to mean the natural human impulse toward wisdom and understanding, rather than just an academic discipline.</note>, considered in general, was born with the world, because at all times men have thought, reflected, and meditated; at all times the great spectacle of the Universe must have struck them with admiration and piqued their natural curiosity. Born for <term>society</term><note>The author reflects Enlightenment values here, suggesting that human beings are naturally social creatures rather than isolated individuals.</note>, man sought the means to live within it with pleasure and satisfaction; good sense, humanity, modesty, the politeness of <term>manners</term><note>The original French term "mœurs" encompasses both social etiquette and moral character.</note>, and the love of this society must therefore have been the objects of his attention.

But however admirable, however striking the spectacle of the Universe may have been for him, and whatever advantage he believed he could draw from society, all these things were not *himself*. Must he not have felt, upon withdrawing into himself, that the <term>preservation</term><note>Refers to "conservation de son être propre," the fundamental instinct of self-care and survival.</note> of his own being was no less interesting an object of study? And would one think that he forgot himself, only to occupy himself with what was around him? Subject to so many <term>vicissitudes</term><note>The unpredictable changes of fortune and the physical instabilities of life.</note>, a target for so many evils—yet made, moreover, to enjoy everything that surrounds him—he undoubtedly...

<summary>This preface introduces philosophy as a natural human instinct, arguing that while humans are naturally curious about the universe and society, the study of self-preservation and one's own nature is equally essential.</summary>
<keywords>philosophy, human nature, society, self-reflection, Enlightenment, manners, self-preservation</keywords>

<margin>1</margin>
...[he] sought the means to prevent or to cure these illnesses, in order to preserve for a longer time a life that is always ready to escape him. He did not need to meditate long to conceive and convince himself that the <term>principle</term><note>The fundamental "spark" or essence that gives life to physical matter.</note> which constitutes his body and sustains it was also the one which ought to preserve him in his state of being. The natural appetite for <term>nourishment</term><note>The original French "alimens" refers to anything that feeds the body, implying a physical and potentially spiritual intake.</note> indicated this to him clearly enough: but he soon perceived that these foods, as perishable as himself because of the mixture of <term>heterogeneous parts</term><note>Elements of a different or "other" nature that do not naturally belong together, causing instability and decay.</note> that constitute them, carried within his interior a principle of death along with the principle of life. It was therefore necessary to reason about the beings of the Universe and to meditate for a long time to discover this <term>fruit of life</term><note>In alchemical and Hermetic traditions, this refers to a universal medicine or "panacea" believed to prolong life indefinitely.</note>, capable of leading man almost to immortality.

It was not enough to have perceived this treasure through the envelope that covers it and hides it from the eyes of the common people. To make the intended use of this fruit, it was indispensable to strip it of its husk and to have it in all its <term>primitive purity</term><note>The original, uncorrupted state of a substance before it was mixed with earthly impurities.</note>. Nature was followed closely; the processes she employs in the formation of individuals and in their destruction were carefully observed. Non

<summary>The author explains that while food sustains life, its impurities also bring death, leading ancient seekers to search for a "fruit of life" or a purified essence of nature to achieve health and near-immortality.</summary>
<keywords>medicine, principle of life, principle of death, fruit of life, immortality, alchemy, nature, purity</keywords>

...not only was it recognized that this <term>fruit of life</term><note>In alchemical traditions, this refers to a universal medicine or "panacea" believed to restore health and prolong life indefinitely.</note> was the basis of all its generations, but that everything finally resolved itself into its own principles.

One therefore took it upon oneself to imitate <term>Nature</term><note>Nature is often personified in these texts as a divine teacher whose processes the alchemist must mimic in the laboratory.</note>; and under such a guide, how could one fail to succeed? To what extent of knowledge did this discovery not lead? What wonders was one not in a position to perform, when one saw Nature as if in a mirror, and had her at one's command!

Can one doubt that the desire to find a remedy for all the evils that afflict humanity, and to extend, if possible, the boundaries prescribed for the duration of life, was the first object of men's ardent searches, and formed the first <term>Philosophers</term><note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to "natural philosophers" or "Philosophers by Fire"—early scientists and alchemists studying the secrets of the physical and spiritual world.</note>? Its discovery must have infinitely flattered its inventor, and made him offer great thanksgivings to the <term>Divinity</term><note>The Divine or God; the text emphasizes that such profound scientific or spiritual breakthroughs were seen as gifts from the Creator.</note> for such a marked favor. But he must have thought at the same time that since God had not given this <term>knowledge</term><note>Original: "connoissance." In 18th-century French, this implies both intellectual understanding and practical skill.</note> to all men, He undoubtedly did not wish it to be disclosed. It was therefore necessary to share it with only a few friends; likewise <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term><note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest," who was believed to be the founder of alchemy and the hermetic sciences.</note>, or "thrice great," the first of all...

Imperfect metals were <term>transmuted</term><note>The alchemical process of transforming one substance into another, typically base metals into gold or silver.</note> into gold and silver; precious stones were manufactured, and the secret of these transmutations was kept with the same scrupulousness as that of the <term>universal panacea</term><note>Also known as the Elixir of Life, a legendary substance capable of curing all diseases and indefinitely prolonging life.</note>, both because one could not unveil the one without making the other known, and because it was perfectly understood that infinite disadvantages for society would result from its disclosure.

To do so by oral tradition would have been to risk abolishing even the memory of them; memory is far too fragile a vessel to be relied upon. Traditions of this kind become obscured as they move away from their source, to the point that it is impossible to untangle the dark chaos in which the object and subject matter of these traditions find themselves buried. I did not intend to write fables, but to explain those that are known. In the Preliminary Discourse, one will see the reasons that led me to place at the beginning general principles of <term>Physics</term> <note>In the 18th century, "Physics" referred broadly to the study of the natural world and the laws of nature, rather than the modern specialized field.</note>, and a Treatise on <term>Hermetic Philosophy</term> <note>The tradition of alchemy and esoteric wisdom based on the writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>. [however well-concerted] they may be, at least in appearance, the systems they have formed, one sees their lack of solidity at every step taken, when one does not allow oneself to be blinded by prejudice. Some believe they find the real history of those distant times, which they nevertheless call the fabulous times <note>original: "tems fabuleux"; a historiographical term used in the 18th century to categorize the era of myth and legend that preceded recorded history.</note>. Others perceive in them only principles of Morality; and one need only open one's eyes to see everywhere examples capable of corrupting morals. Finally, others, little satisfied with these explanations, have drawn theirs from Physics <note>In this period, "Physics" referred to the study of the natural world and the laws of nature.</note>. I ask the Natural Philosophers of our day if they have reason to be more content with them.

Since neither one nor the other has succeeded, it is natural to think that the general principle upon which they established their systems was never the true principle of these fictions. One was needed, by means of which everything could be explained, even to the smallest circumstances of the reported facts, however bizarre, however incredible, and however contradictory they may appear. This system is not new, and I am very far from wishing to take credit for it; I found it in scattered fragments in various Authors, both ancient and modern; their works are little known or little read, because the science <note>Pernety is referring here to the "Hermetic Science" or Alchemy, which he argues is the hidden truth behind Greek and Egyptian myths.</note> they treat therein is the victim of ignorance and prejudice. The greatest grace that one thinks should be granted to those who cultivate it, or who take up its defense, is to regard them as fools, at most worthy of the <term>Petites-maisons: a well-known hospital in Paris during the 17th and 18th centuries used to confine those deemed insane; the name became a common euphemism for a madhouse.</term>. ### EGYPTIAN AND GREEK.

<header>EGYPTIAN AND GREEK.</header>

Authors nevertheless warn that a science such as this one does not wish to be treated as clearly as others, because of the fatal consequences that could result from it for civil life. They make a mystery of it, and a mystery that they study more to obscure than to develop. Therefore, they constantly recommend not taking them literally, to study the laws and processes of nature, to compare the operations of which they speak with nature's own, and to admit only those that the reader finds to be in conformity with them.

To metaphors, the <term>Hermetic Philosophers</term> <note>Thinkers following the tradition of Hermes Trismegistus, encompassing alchemy, astrology, and theurgy.</note> have added Emblems, Hieroglyphs, Fables, and Allegories, and by this means have made themselves almost unintelligible to those whom long study and stubborn work have not initiated into their mysteries. Those who did not wish to take the trouble to make the necessary efforts to decode them, or who made useless ones, believed they had nothing better to do than to hide their ignorance behind the denial of the reality of this science; they have affected to have only contempt for it; they have treated it as a <term>chimera</term> <note>A mythological monster, used here to mean an impossible or foolish fantasy.</note> and a mere figment of the mind.

Ambition and the love of riches are the only springs that set in motion almost all those who labor to instruct themselves in the processes of this science; it presents them with mountains of gold in perspective, and a long and solid health to enjoy them. What lures for hearts attached to the goods of this world! One hurries, one runs to reach this goal, and as one fears not arriving soon enough, one takes the first path...

<summary>The author explains that Hermetic authors intentionally obscure their work with symbols and allegories to prevent misuse, leading many frustrated seekers to dismiss the entire science as a fantasy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Preliminary Discourse" regarding the skepticism surrounding Hermetic science. The previous page ended by discussing how ambition and the love of riches drive people to seek shortcuts in this study without proper instruction.</meta>

-># FABLES<-

which seems to lead there more promptly, without wanting to take the trouble to sufficiently instruct oneself in the true path by which one arrives there. Thus one walks, one advances, and one believes oneself to be at the end; but as one has walked blindly, one finds a precipice there, and falls into it. One then thinks to hide the shame of one's fall by saying that this alleged goal is nothing but a shadow that cannot be embraced; one treats one's guides as treacherous, and finally comes to deny even the very possibility of an effect, because one is ignorant of the causes. What! Because the greatest <term>Naturalists</term> <note>Early scientists who studied the physical world, including biology and geology.</note> have wasted their sleepless nights and their labors wanting to discover what processes Nature employs to form and organize the <term>fetus</term> <note>Original: "fétus".</note> in its mother's womb, to make a plant germinate and grow, or to form metals in the earth, would one have the audacity to deny the fact? Would one regard as sensible a man whose ignorance formed the basis of his denial? One would not even deign to go to the expense of the slightest proof to convince him of it.

But learned people, enlightened and skillful <term>Artists</term> <note>In this context, "Artists" refers to practitioners of the "Great Art" or alchemy.</note> have studied their whole lives, and have worked ceaselessly to achieve it; they died at their task: what is to be concluded? That the thing is not real? No. From about the year 550 of the foundation of Rome until our days, the most skillful people had worked to imitate the famous <term>burning mirror</term> <note>A device using mirrors to focus sunlight and create intense heat; Archimedes famously used this to defend Syracuse against Roman ships.</note> of <term>Archimedes</term> <note>A renowned Greek mathematician and inventor (c. 287–212 BC).</note>, with which he burned the Roman ships in the port of <term>Syracuse</term>; no one had been able to succeed, and the event was treated as a story invented for pleasure; it was called a fable, and the very manufacture of the mirror was deemed impossible.

[...of] Buffon thought to take a simpler path than those who had preceded him, he succeeded; people are surprised, and they finally admit that the thing is possible.

Let us conclude then, with better reason, that these scholars, these skilled <term>Artists</term> <note>In alchemical texts, "Artists" refers to practitioners of alchemy or the "Great Art."</note> relied too heavily on their supposed knowledge. Instead of following the straight, simple, and smooth paths of Nature, they attributed to her subtleties that she never possessed. The <term>Hermetic Art</term> <note>The tradition of alchemy and spiritual transformation attributed to the mythical figure Hermes Trismegistus.</note> is, say the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>Here, "Philosophers" refers specifically to "Philosophers by fire"—alchemists who sought the underlying truths of nature.</note>, a mystery hidden from those who trust too much in their own knowledge: it is a gift from God who casts a favorable and propitious eye upon those who are humble, who fear Him, who place all their trust in Him, and who, like Solomon, ask Him with insistence and perseverance for this wisdom, which holds health *(a)* <note>Original: "santé". While the French text says "health," biblical translations of Proverbs 3:16 usually render this as "length of days" or "long life."</note> in her right hand, and riches in her left; this wisdom that the Philosophers prefer to all honors, to all the kingdoms of the world, because she is the tree of life to those who possess her *(b)*.

All the Hermetic Philosophers say that although the <term>Great Work</term> <note>Original: "grand Œuvre". The process of creating the Philosopher's Stone or achieving the pinnacle of alchemical success.</note> is a natural thing, both in its matter and in its operations, there are nonetheless things that occur within it so surprising that they infinitely elevate the spirit of man toward the Author of his being, that they manifest His wisdom and His glory, that they are far above human intelligence, and that those alone understand them to whom God deigns to open...

[...before] their eyes. The proof is evident enough by the blunders and the lack of success of all those famous <term>Artists</term> <note>Practitioners of chemistry and alchemy.</note> in common chemistry, who, despite all their skill in manual work, despite all their so-called knowledge of Nature, have wasted their efforts, their money, and often their health in the search for this inestimable treasure.

<margin>(a) The New Chemical Light <note>Original: "Novum lumen Chemicum." A classic alchemical text by Michael Sendivogius.</note>, Treatise 1.
(b) The Secret Work of Hermetic Philosophy <note>Original: "Arcan. Herm. Philosophiæ opus." Written by Jean d'Espagnet in 1623.</note>, Canon 6.</margin>
How many like Becher, Homberg, Boerhaave, Geoffroy, and so many other learned chemists have, through their tireless work, forced Nature to reveal some of her secrets? Despite all their attention in watching her processes, in analyzing her productions to catch her in the act, they have almost always failed because they were the tyrants of nature, and not her true imitators. Sufficiently enlightened in common chemistry and well-instructed in its procedures, but blind in <term>Hermetic Chemistry</term> <note>Alchemy, which seeks to work with the "vital spirit" of matter rather than just its external form.</note> and carried away by custom, they have built furnaces for sublimation (a), calcination, and distillation; they have employed an infinity of vessels and crucibles unknown to simple Nature; they have called to their aid the <term>fratricide of natural fire</term> <note>A metaphorical term for the violent heat of a furnace, which alchemists believed "killed" the living essence or "natural fire" within matter.</note>. How could they have succeeded with such violent procedures? They are absolutely removed from those methods followed by the Hermetic Philosophers, if we are to believe President d’Espagnet (b):

"Common chemists have gradually become accustomed to distancing themselves from the simple way of Nature by their sublimations, their distillations..."

[exis]tence, and have left behind through enigmatic and allegorical writings the manner of performing it, that it is hardly possible to doubt it, when one knows how to adapt these writings to the principles of Nature.

The <term>Hermetic Philosophers</term> <note>Followers of the "Hermetic" tradition, named after Hermes Trismegistus, who sought to understand the hidden laws of nature and the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> differ absolutely from ordinary Philosophers or <term>Physicists</term> <note>In the 18th century, "physicists" referred to natural scientists who studied the physical world through observation and theory, often lacking the spiritual or "alchemical" focus of the Hermeticists.</note>. These latter have no certain system. They invent new ones every day, and the latest seems imagined only to contradict and destroy those that preceded it. Finally, if one rises and establishes itself, it is only upon the ruins of its predecessor, and it only lasts until a new one comes to topple it and take its place.

The Hermetic Philosophers, on the contrary, are all in agreement with one another: not one contradicts the principles of the other. He who wrote thirty years ago speaks like he who lived two thousand years ago. What is even singular is that they never tire of repeating this <term>axiom</term> <note>A self-evident truth or established rule.</note> that the Church <margin>Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitory* <note>A 5th-century work by Saint Vincent of Lérins outlining how to distinguish the true faith from heresy.</note></margin> adopts as the most infallible mark of truth in what it proposes for us to believe: 

> What has been believed everywhere, by everyone, and at all times, that you must believe most firmly. <note>original Latin: "Quod ubique, quod ab omnibus, & quod semper creditum est, id firmissimè credendum puta."</note>

See, they say, read, meditate on the things that have been taught in all times, and by all the Philosophers; the truth is contained in those places where they are all in agreement.

What likelihood is there, indeed, that people who lived in such distant centuries, and in countries so different in language, and I dare [to say it]...

...there, a sort of sect was formed, which, having misunderstood and poorly explained the writings of the Philosophers <note>In alchemical literature, "the Philosophers" refers specifically to the ancient masters of the Hermetic Art, such as Hermes Trismegistus or Geber.</note>, introduced a new Chemistry <note>original: "Chymie"</note> and imagined that no other was real but their own. **Hermetic Chemistry**? <note>original: "Chymie Hermétique"</note> Here it is. The first is properly the art of destroying the compounds that Nature has made; and the second is the art of working with Nature to perfect them. The first makes use of the *furious tyrant*, and destroyer of Nature <note>A reference to the violent, high-heat fires used in common chemical assaying and metallurgy.</note>: the second employs its *gentle and benign agent*. **Hermetic Philosophy** takes for the material of its work the secondary principles or the "principled" elements of things, in order to lead them to the perfection of which they are capable, by ways and processes conforming to those of Nature. **Vulgar Chemistry** <term>Vulgar Chemistry: Ordinary or common chemistry, focused on the practical decomposition of substances rather than the pursuit of the "Great Work."</term> takes mixtures already arrived at the point of their perfection, decomposes them, and destroys them. Those who are curious to see a more extensive parallel of these two Arts may have recourse to the work composed by one of the great antagonists of **Hermetic Philosophy**, the Jesuit Father Kirker <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a renowned Jesuit scholar who was skeptical of the physical transmutation of metals.</note>, which Manget <note>Jean-Jacques Manget (1652–1742), author of the *Bibliotheca Chemica Curiosa*, a famous collection of alchemical texts.</note> has included in the first volume of his *Library of Curious Chemistry*.

The **Hermetic Philosophers** hardly ever fail to mark the difference between these two Arts in their works. But the most infallible mark by which one can distinguish an **Adept** <term>Adept: An alchemist who has successfully discovered the secret of the Philosopher's Stone.</term> from a **Chemist** is that the Adept, according to what all the Philosophers say, takes only a single thing, or at most two of the same nature, a single vessel or two at most, and a single furnace to lead the work to its perfection; the Chemist, on the contrary, works on all sorts of materials indifferently. This is also the touchstone by which one must test those roguish **blowers** <term>Blower (Souffleur): A derogatory term for amateur or fraudulent alchemists who focused on the physical bellows and intense heat rather than the philosophical principles of the Art.</term>, who are after your purse, who...

**Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to "Philosophers by fire"—adepts who have successfully created the Philosopher's Stone—rather than academic scholars.</note> are not as common as **Physicians**. They are very few in number. They possess the secret to cure all diseases; they do not lack the goodwill to do good to everyone; but this world is so perverse that it is dangerous for them to do so. They cannot do it without risking their lives. Should they cure someone as if by a miracle? A murmur will be heard rising among the Physicians and the People; and even those who most doubted the existence of the **philosophical remedy** <note>The Elixir of Life or the Universal Medicine, believed to be a byproduct of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> will then suspect it exists. This man will be followed; his movements will be observed; rumors will spread; the greedy and the ambitious will pursue him to obtain his secret. What then can he hope for but persecutions, or voluntary exile from his homeland?

The examples of the **Cosmopolite** <note>A pseudonym for the famous alchemist Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), or his master Alexander Sethon, who was reportedly imprisoned and tortured for his secret.</note> and **Philalethes** <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, a 17th-century alchemist whose identity remains a subject of debate; his works were highly influential on Isaac Newton.</note> are a very convincing proof of this. The world is so wicked and perverse today, and self-interest and ambition so dominate men, that all their actions have no other goal. If we wish, like the Apostles, to perform works of mercy, evil is returned to us..."

It is therefore beyond doubt that the Chemical Art of Hermes was known among the Egyptians. It is no less certain that the Greeks who traveled to Egypt learned it there—or at least some of them did—and that having learned it through hieroglyphs, they later taught it under the veil of fables. Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and archbishop known for his extensive commentaries on Homer.</note> gives us to understand as much in his commentary on the *Iliad*.

Albert the Great <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and bishop who became one of the most influential medieval scientists.</note>, Archbishop of Ratisbonne <note>The city now known as Regensburg, Germany.</note>, is one of the first known since the Arabs. Among his other works full of science and erudition on Dialectic, Mathematics, Physics, Metaphysics, Theology, and Medicine, one finds several on Chemistry, one of which bears the title *Alchemy* <note>original Latin: *Alchymia*</note>; it was subsequently stuffed with an infinity of additions and sophistications <note>In this context, "sophistications" refers to fraudulent or adulterated passages added by later scribes.</note>. The second is entitled: *On the Agreement of the Philosophers* <note>original Latin: *De concordantia Philosophorum*</note>. The third, *On the Composition of the Composite* <note>original Latin: *de compositione compositi*</note>. remarks, which clearly prove either that they have not meditated upon them at all, or that they have done so in a way that adapts the expressions of the Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemical adepts or "Philosophers by Fire."</note> to the false ideas that prejudice had placed in their minds regarding operations and matter, rather than seeking to rectify their own ideas based on those of the Authors they were reading.

These works by false Philosophers are numerous; everyone has wanted to try their hand at writing, and most of them, no doubt, to find in the Bookseller’s <note>original: "Libraire"</note> purse a resource they otherwise lacked, or at least to make a name for themselves that they certainly do not deserve. An Author once wished that some true Philosopher would have enough charity toward the Public to publish a list of the good Authors in this branch of science, in order to strip away from a great number of persons the confidence with which they read the bad ones who lead them into error.

Consequently, toward the end of the last century, Olaus Borrichius the Dane <note>Oluf Borch (1626–1690), a Danish physician and polymath known for his history of chemistry.</note> had a work printed titled: *A Survey of the Most Famous Chemists* <note>original: "*Conspectus Chymicorum celebriorum*"</note>. He provides separate entries for each person and says quite prudently what he thinks of them. He excludes a large number of Authors from the class of true Philosophers; but are all those whom he presents as true actually so? Furthermore, the number of them is so great that one does not know which to choose in preference to others. Consequently, one must be quite bewildered when wishing to devote oneself to this study. # GENERAL PRINCIPES

### *According to Hermetic Philosophy.*

It is not granted to everyone to penetrate into the sanctuary of the secrets of **Nature** <term>Nature: In this context, "Nature" refers to the hidden, vital forces of the universe that the alchemist seeks to understand and direct.</term>: very few people know the path that leads there. Errors have their source in prejudice, as well as in the lack of light and solid instruction. The true route can only be very simple, since there is nothing simpler...

### *On the First Matter.*

Air, being closest to the principle of rarefaction, is the most subtle; water comes next, and then the earth.

As the objective I propose in providing these abbreviated principles of Physics <term>Physics: In this context, "Physique" refers to Natural Philosophy, or the study of how the physical world operates according to divine and natural laws.</term> is only to instruct on what may enlighten the amateurs <note>In the 18th century, an "amateur" was a "lover of the arts," someone who studied a subject deeply for the love of it, rather than a mere hobbyist.</note> of Hermetic Philosophy <term>Hermetic Philosophy: A tradition of knowledge based on the works attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, focusing on the relationship between the divine, the human, and the natural world, often through alchemy.</term>, I shall not enter at all into the details of the formation of the stars and their movements.

## *On light, and its effects.*

Light, after having acted upon the parts of the dark mass that were closest to it, and having rarefied them more or less in proportion to their distance, finally penetrated even to the center, to animate it in its entirety, to fertilize it, and to make it produce everything that the Universe presents to our eyes. It then pleased God to fix its natural source in the Sun, without, however, gathering it all there entirely. It seems that God wished to establish the Sun as the sole dispenser, so that the light created by the one God—Himself being the uncreated light—might be communicated to creatures by a single source, as if to indicate to us its primary origin.

[ani]mals, whenever the opportunity arises, if this spirit were not subordinate to another substance far superior to its own. The soul, which is purely spiritual, holds the reins: it guides and leads the spirit in all deliberate actions. Sometimes, the spirit does not leave the soul time to give its orders and exercise its authority. It acts on its own; it sets the body’s <term>springs</term> <note>The author uses mechanical metaphors common in the 17th and 18th centuries, viewing the body's movements as a system of springs and levers put in motion by "animal spirits."</note> in motion, and man then performs purely animal actions. Such are those we call "first impulses," and those performed without reflection—such as coming, going, or eating—when the mind is entirely preoccupied with some serious matter.

Animals always and unfailingly obey their natural inclinations, because they strive solely for the preservation of their mortal and fleeting existence, which is the source of all their happiness and bliss. But man does not always follow this path; for while he is inclined to preserve his mortal self, he also feels another inclination that leads him to work for the happiness of his immortal soul, to which he is deeply convinced he must give priority.

### *Of the Elements.*

Nature therefore employed from the beginning only two simple principles, from which everything that exists was formed: namely, the passive <term>prime matter</term> <note>The fundamental, formless substance of the universe.</note> and the luminous agent which gave it form. As for the fire of Nature, it is impossible for <term>art</term> <note>Here "art" refers to human skill or experimental science (like alchemy), contrasted with "nature."</note> to manifest it otherwise than by its effects.

## *Of the Earth.*

The earth is cold by its nature, because it partakes more of the first matter, which is opaque and dark. This coldness makes it the heaviest body, as well as the densest; and this density renders it less penetrable to light, which is the principle of heat. It was created in the midst of the waters, with which it is always mixed; and the Creator seems to have made its surface dry only to make it suitable for the dwelling of plants and animals.

The Creator made the earth spongy, so that air, water, and fire might have freer access to it, and so that the <term>internal fire</term> <note>A central concept in early modern science and alchemy, referring to a vital heat or "central sun" within the earth that drives growth and geological change.</note>, which was infused into it by the Spirit of God before the formation of the Sun (*a*), could push the virtues of the <term>elements</term> from the center to the surface through its pores. This process allows it to exhale those moist vapors which corrupt the seeds of things through a slight <term>putrefaction</term> <note>In this context, "corruption" and "putrefaction" are not merely decay, but the necessary chemical breakdown of a substance that allows new life to begin.</note>, and prepares them for <term>generation</term>. These seeds, once so disposed, then receive celestial and life-giving heat, attracting it even by a "magnetic love"; the germ develops, and the seed produces its fruit.

The heat proper to the womb of the earth is suited only for corruption. Its humidity weakens it, and it could produce nothing if it were not aided by celestial heat—pure and without mixture—which leads to generation by exciting the action of the internal fire, developing it, and expanding it—

(*a*) <note>original: "Cosmop. Tract. 4." refers to the fourth treatise of *The New Chemical Light* by Michael Sendivogius (the "Cosmopolite"), a highly influential alchemical text.</note>

The Author of Nature, wishing the earth to be the womb of all mixtures, consequently warms it continually by the heat of the celestial and central fires, and joins to it the moist nature of water; so that, aided by the two principles of generation—the hot and the moist—it might not be sterile, and might become the vessel in which all generations occur (a). Pure earth is animated by a fire that gives life to mixtures, and preserves them in their state of being for as long as the cold of the impure earth does not dominate it, or as long as it is not over-excited and tyrannized by artificial and elemental fire—its fratricide <note>Literally "brother-killer"; the author suggests that external or "artificial" fire can destroy the subtle, life-giving "internal" fire of the earth.</note>. ### *On Water*

Water possesses a density that occupies the middle ground between that of air and that of earth. It is the <term>menstruum</term> <note>In early chemistry and alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent—a substance used to dissolve or extract components from a solid.</note> of Nature and the vehicle of seeds. It is a volatile body that seems to flee the attacks of fire and evaporates into vapors at the slightest heat. It is susceptible to all shapes and is more changeable than Proteus <note>A Greek sea god known for his ability to transform into many different shapes.</note>. Water is a <term>mercury</term> <note>Likening water to "mercury" refers to the alchemical principle of fluidity and volatility, rather than just the metal itself.</note> which, taking at times the nature of a terra-aqueous body and at times that of an aqua-aerial body, attracts and seeks out the virtues of both superior and inferior things. By this means, it becomes the messenger of the Gods and their mediator; it is through water that commerce is maintained between heaven and earth.

<margin>(a) Memoirs of the Academy of Berlin.</margin>
An oily phlegm is spread throughout water. (a) Mr. Eller <note>Johann Theodor Eller (1689–1760), a prominent physician and chemist who served the Prussian kings and published extensively in the Memoirs of the Berlin Academy.</note> recognized this quite well in his observations. Water, he says, when highly purified and freed of all heterogeneous parts (after the manner of the common Chemists), can suffice for vegetation. It provides the earth—the base of the solidity of plants—and even spreads within it that inflammable, oily, or resinous part found therein.

At the slightest thinning, it seems to abandon the earth to take on the nature of air; should it be condensed by the slightest cold, it leaves the air and goes to reunite with the earth.

The nature of water is moist rather than cold, because it is more porous and open to light than the earth is. Water has preserved the humidity of the primary matter and of chaos; the earth has retained its coldness.

From this come the changes we experience in the lower region, as much from cold as from heat.

### *Of the Operations of Nature.*

Sublimation, descension, and coction are three instruments or ways of operating that *Nature* employs to perfect her works. Through the first, she evacuates superfluous moisture, which would suffocate the fire and prevent its action within the earth, its matrix <term>matrix</term> <note>In early science and alchemy, the 'matrix' refers to a womb-like environment or the fundamental substance in which something is formed.</note>.

Through descension, she restores to the earth the moisture of which plants or heat have deprived it. Sublimation occurs through the rising of vapors into the air, where they condense into clouds. The second <note>descension</note> occurs through rain and dew. Fair weather follows rain, and rain follows fair weather in alternation; continual rain would flood everything, while perpetual fair weather would wither everything. Rain falls drop by drop, because if poured too abundantly it would destroy everything, like a *Gardener* watering his seeds with full buckets. Thus does *Nature* distribute her blessings with weight, measure, and proportion.

Coction is a digestion of the raw humor <term>humor</term> <note>Referring here to a vital fluid or moisture necessary for life and growth.</note> instilled into the womb of the earth—a ripening and a conversion of this moisture into nourishment by means of its secret fire.

These three operations are so closely linked together that the end of one is the begin-

No sooner are these vapors sublimated than they condense into rain; from being spiritual and invisible, they become, a moment later, a dense and aqueous body, falling back upon the earth to soak it with celestial nectar, with which they were impregnated during their stay in the air. As soon as the earth has received it, *Nature* works to digest and "cook" it <note>The process of "coction," where heat matures or ripens a substance.</note>.

Every animal, even the vilest worm, is a small world <term>microcosm</term> <note>The philosophical idea that the human body or small organisms contain the same patterns and processes as the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note> where all these things take place. If man seeks the world outside of himself, he will find it everywhere. The *Creator* has fashioned an infinity of them from the same matter; only the form is different. Humility, therefore, perfectly suits man, and glory belongs to **God** alone.

Water contains a ferment, a vivifying spirit, which flows from superior natures onto inferior ones, with which it became impregnated while wandering through the air, and which it then deposits into the womb of the earth. This ferment is a seed of life, without which man, animals, and vegetables would neither live nor reproduce. Everything in *Nature* breathes; and man does not live by bread alone, but by this aerial spirit that he breathes in incessantly.

God alone, and Nature his minister, know how to make themselves obeyed by the material elements, which are the principles of bodies. Art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to human skill, specifically the practice of alchemy or chemistry.</note> cannot reach this level. But the three that result from them become sensible <note>perceptible to the senses</note> in the breakdown <term>resolution</term> of mixed bodies. Chemists call them sulfur, salt, and mercury. These are the primary elements <term>principiate elements</term> <note>These are not the four base elements (earth, air, fire, water), but the three "essences" that alchemists believed made up all physical matter.</note>. Mercury is formed by the mixing of water and earth; sulfur, from earth and air; and salt, from condensed air and water. The fire of Nature joins them as the formal principle. Mercury is composed of a greasy, viscous earth and a clear water. Sulfur is composed of a very dry, very subtle earth, mixed with the moisture of the air. Salt, finally, is composed of a thick, pungent <note>original: *pontique*; refers to a sharp, astringent, or bitter quality</note> water and a crude air that is found trapped within it. See the *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: *Physique ſouterraine*; a reference to "Physica Subterranea" (1669) by Johann Joachim Becher, a foundational text in early chemistry.</note> of Becher.

Democritus said that all mixtures were composed of atoms; this sentiment does not seem at all far from the truth when one pays attention to what reason dictates and what experience demonstrates. This Philosopher, like the others, veiled the true mixing of elements under this obscure manner of explaining himself; for to be in conformity with the operations of Nature, this mixing must be done intimately, or as they say, *through the smallest parts* <note>original Latin: *per minima*</note> and *actually indivisible little bodies* <note>original Latin: *actu indivifibilia corpuſcula*</note>. Without this, the parts would not form a continuous whole. Mixtures are resolved into a very subtle vapor by artificial distillation; and is Nature not a much more skillful worker than even the most experienced man? This is all Democritus meant to say.

## On the general ways of being of *Mixed Bodies.*

One notices three ways of being (a), which constitute three genres, or three classes called *kingdoms*: the animal, the vegetable, and the mineral. Minerals are generated in the earth alone; vegetables have their roots in the earth and rise into the water and the air; animals take birth in the air, the water, and the earth; and air is for all of them a principle of life.

Whatever difference mixed bodies <term>mixtes</term> <note>In early modern natural philosophy, a "mixed body" refers to any substance formed by the chemical combination of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water), resulting in a new, distinct substance.</note> seem to have regarding their external forms, they do not differ in their principles (b); earth and water serve as a base for all of them, and air enters into their composition almost only as an instrument, much like fire. Light acts upon the air, air upon the water, water upon the earth. Water often becomes the instrument of mixing in the works of art <note>In this context, "art" refers to human industry or craft—the manual labor of people—rather than fine art.</note>, but this mixing is only superficial, as we see in bread, brick, etc. There is another intimate mixing that Becher <note>Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), a German chemist and scholar previously mentioned on page 97.</note> calls *central* (c). It is that by which water is so mixed with earth that one cannot separate them without destroying the form of the mixed body. We shall not enter into the detail of the different degrees of this cohesion, in order to be brief. One may see all of this in the work we have just cited.

<margin>(a) Cosmopolite, *New Light of Chemistry*, Treatise 7. <note>Original: *Cosmop. Nov. lum. Chem.* This refers to Michael Sendivogius, a famous alchemist who wrote under the name "The Cosmopolite."</note></margin>
<margin>(b) Cosmopolite, Treatise 2.</margin>
<margin>(c) *Subterranean Physics*, section 1, chapter 4. <note>Original: *Phys. sub.* referring to Becher's *Physica Subterranea*.</note></margin>

# *On the difference found between these three Kingdoms.*

## *The Mineral.*

It is commonly said of minerals that they exist, and not that they live, as is said of animals and vegetables; although one could say that metals derive their life in some way from minerals, either because in their generation there is a sort of joining of the male and the female under the names of sulfur and mercury <note>In alchemical theory, all metals were believed to be born from the union of two principles: Sulfur (the active, masculine principle) and Mercury (the passive, feminine principle).</note>, which through a fermentation, a circulation, and a continued cooking <term>cuisson</term> <note>In alchemy, 'cooking' or 'decoction' refers to the prolonged application of steady heat to mature and purify a substance over time.</note>, purify themselves with the help of the salt of nature, cook, and finally form into a mass that we call metal; or because perfect metals contain a principle of life, or innate fire, which—having become languid and seemingly without movement under the hard bark that encloses it—is hidden there like a treasure, until, being set free by a philosophical solution <note>A "philosophical" solution refers to a chemical process that dissolves a solid back into a liquid state without destroying its internal "seed" or vital energy, unlike common corrosive acids.</note> of this bark, it develops and exhales through a vegetative movement to the highest degree of perfection that art <note>The "Art" refers specifically to the practice of Alchemy (the Hermetic Art).</note> can give it.

## *The Vegetable.*

A vegetative soul or spirit animates plants; it is through this that they grow and multiply. However, they are deprived of the sensation and movement of animals. Their seeds are her- <note>The text likely continues as "hermaphrodite," referring to the self-contained reproductive nature of plants.</note>

## *On the Soul of Mixts.*

All perfect <term>mixts</term> <note>In alchemy and early natural philosophy, a "mixt" (or composite) refers to any substance created by the combination of the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> that possess life have a soul, or spirit, and a body. The body is composed of <term>silt</term> <note>Original: "limon." This refers to the primordial "slime" or fertile earth from which life was thought to be molded.</note>, or of earth and water; the soul, which gives form to the mixt, is a spark of the fire of Nature, or an imperceptible ray of light, which acts within these composites according to the current disposition of matter and the perfection of the organs specified in each of them. If beasts have a soul, it differs little from their spirit except by degree.

The specific forms of mixts—or if one prefers, their souls—retain a certain indefinable knowledge of their origin. The soul of man often reflects upon divine light through contemplation. It seems to desire to penetrate into that sanctuary accessible to God alone: it strives toward it incessantly, and finally returns there. The souls of animals, having emerged from the secrets of the Heavens and the treasures of the Sun, seem to have a sympathy with that Star, shown by the different omens of its rising, its setting, the very movement of the heavens, and the changes in air temperature, all of which the movements of animals announce to us.

Supplied by the air, and almost entirely aerial, the souls of plants push the heads of their stems upward as much as they can, as if eager to return to their homeland.

## *On the Generation and Corruption of Mixtures.*
<note>In early natural philosophy, "Mixtures" or "Mixed bodies" (mixtes) refers to any substance or living being composed of a combination of the four elements—earth, air, fire, and water.</note>

Everything returns to its principle. Every individual exists in potentiality within the material world before appearing in the light under its individual form, and will return in its own time and in its own rank to the same point from which it emerged, like rivers into the sea, to be reborn in their turn (a). It was perhaps in this way that Pythagoras understood his metempsychosis <note>The philosophical term for the transmigration of the soul, or reincarnation</note>, which has not been understood.

When the mixture dissolves, through the defect of the corruptible elements that compose it, the Ethereal part <note>The "Ethereal part" refers to the celestial or spiritual essence that gives life to the material body</note> abandons it and returns to its homeland.

(a) Ecclesiastes 1:7. <note>original: "Eccles. 1. 7." This biblical verse reads: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again."</note>

### *Of Light.*

   The origin of light proves to us its spiritual nature. Before matter began to receive its form, God created light; it immediately spread through matter, which served it as a wick for its maintenance. The manifestation of light was thus the first act that God exercised upon matter; the first marriage of the creator with the creature, and that of the spirit with the body.

...luminous worms, calcined and rubbed clay, etc., [Pott] says that the matter of light in its purity, or separated from all other bodies, does not allow itself to be perceived; that we only deal with it when it is surrounded by an envelope, and that we only know of its presence by induction <note>In this context, "induction" refers to the logical process of inferring the existence of a cause (pure light) by observing its effects (visibility or heat).</note>. This properly distinguishes light from the clarity <note>The author uses "light" (*lumière*) to refer to the invisible physical substance or "principle," and "clarity" (*clarté*) to describe the visible brightness we see with our eyes.</note> which is its effect. With this distinction, it is easy to account for an infinity of phenomena that would otherwise be very difficult to explain.

Heat, although an effect of movement, is essentially identified with it. Since light is the principle of fire, it is also the principle of movement and of heat—the latter being merely a lower degree of fire, or the movement produced by a more moderate fire, or one further removed from the body being affected. It is to this movement that water owes its fluidity, since without this cause it becomes ice.

We must not, therefore, confuse **<term>elementary fire</term>** <note>Elementary fire was considered a universal, subtle substance that exists everywhere in nature, distinct from the common fire we use for cooking.</note> with the fire of our kitchens; and we must observe that the former only becomes an actual burning fire when it is combined with combustible substances; on its own, it yields neither flame nor light. Thus, **<term>phlogiston</term>** <note>Before the discovery of oxygen, scientists believed a substance called "phlogiston" was the essence of fire contained within all combustible materials, which was released during burning.</note>—or oily, sulfurous, and resinous substances—is not the principle of fire, but rather the matter suitable for maintaining, nourishing, and manifesting it.

The reasonings of Mr. Pott prove that the opinions of d'Espagnet <note>Jean d'Espagnet (1564–1637) was a French jurist and alchemist; the author is attempting to show that "modern" chemistry of the 1700s actually supports older alchemical ideas.</note> and other <term>Hermetic Philosophers</term> <note>Thinkers following the tradition of alchemy and the "Hermetic" arts, which sought to understand the hidden laws of nature and the transformation of matter.</note> regarding fire and light are reasoned opinions, and very much in conformity with the most exact **<term>Physico-Chemical</term>** observations, since they agree with this learned Professor.

## On the Radical Moisture.

Life and the preservation of individuals consist in the close union of form and matter. The knot, the bond that forms this union, consists in that of the <term>innate fire</term> <note>original: "feu inné." In ancient and alchemical medicine, this refers to the vital heat or "spark" that sustains life.</note> with the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "l'humide radical." This was believed to be a fundamental, life-sustaining fluid or "oil" found within all living things, acting as the fuel for the innate fire.</note>. This moisture is the purest, most refined portion of matter, like an oil extremely rectified by the <term>alembics</term> <note>Apparatus used for distillation; here used metaphorically to describe Nature's internal processes.</note> of Nature. The seeds of things contain much of this radical moisture, in which a spark of celestial fire is nourished; and placed in a suitable matrix, it operates—when constantly aided—everything necessary for <term>generation</term> <note>The process of creation or biological birth.</note>.

One finds something immortal in this radical moisture; the death of <term>composites</term> <note>original: "mixtes." In alchemy, this refers to any substance or body formed by the combination of the four elements.</note> does not make it vanish or disappear. It even resists the most violent fire, since it is still found in the ashes of burned corpses.

Each composite contains two moistures: the one we just spoke of, and an **elementary moisture**, which is partly watery and partly airy. The latter yields to the violence of fire; it flies away in smoke and vapors, and when it is entirely evaporated, the body is nothing more than ashes, or parts separated from one another.

It is not so with the radical moisture; as it constitutes the basis of composites, it braves the tyranny of fire, suffers martyrdom with insurmountable courage, and remains stubbornly attached to the ashes of the composite; which clearly indicates its great purity.

### *On the harmony of the Universe.*

The superior and inferior bodies of the world, having the same source and the same matter as their principle, have preserved among themselves a **sympathy**<note>A core concept in Hermetic philosophy suggesting that all parts of the universe are interconnected and resonate with one another ("as above, so below").</note> which ensures that the purest, the noblest, and the strongest communicate to those that are less so all the perfection of which they are capable. But when the organs of the composites find themselves poorly disposed, whether naturally or by accident, this communication is disturbed or hindered: the order established for this commerce is deranged; the weak, receiving less aid, weakens further, succumbs, and becomes the principle of its own ruin; **it collapses under its own weight.**<note>original Latin: "mole ruit suâ." A quote from the Roman poet Horace, suggesting that something too large or poorly balanced will eventually be destroyed by its own bulk or inherent flaws.</note>

### *On Movement.*

There is no real rest, properly speaking, in Nature (b) <margin>Ibid. Treatise 4.</margin>. She cannot remain idle; and if she allowed real rest to succeed movement for even a single instant, the whole machine of the Universe would fall into ruin. Movement has, as it were, drawn it out of nothingness; rest would plunge it back into it. That to which we give the name of rest is only a movement that is less accelerated, less perceptible. Movement is therefore continual in every part as in the whole. Nature always acts within the interior of composites: even corpses are not at rest, since they <term>decay</term><note>original: "se corrompent." In the context of alchemy, corruption or putrefaction is seen as a necessary stage of movement and transformation, not a state of static death.</note>, and decay cannot occur without movement.

# TREATISE
### ON
## THE HERMETIC WORK.

The source of health and wealth, the two foundations upon which the happiness of this life rests, are the object of this art. It was always a mystery; and those who have treated it have spoken of it at all times as a science whose practice has something surprising about it, and whose result borders on the miraculous, both in itself and in its effects. God, the author of Nature, whom the <term>Philosopher</term><note>original: "le Philofophe." In Hermetic texts, a "Philosopher" is not just a thinker, but specifically an alchemist—one who studies the hidden laws of nature to achieve transformation.</note> proposes to imitate, can alone enlighten and guide the human spirit in the search for this inestimable treasure, and in the labyrinth of the operations of this art. Thus, all these authors recommend turning to the Creator and asking him for this grace with great fervor and perseverance.

Should one be surprised that the possessors of such a beautiful secret have veiled it with the shadows of hieroglyphs, fables, allegories, metaphors, and enigmas to withhold knowledge of it from the common man? They wrote only for those to whom God would deign to grant the intelligence to understand it. To decry them, to declaim loudly against the science itself because one has made useless efforts to obtain it, is a base vengeance; it is a harm to one’s own reputation, an advertisement of one’s ignorance, and of the impotence one feels in attempting to achieve it. 

By all means, let one raise their voice against the <term>puffers</term><note>original: "souffleurs." Who among them can flatter themselves with knowing the operations and procedures of this art? Monsieur de <term>Maupertuis</term><note>Pierre Louis Maupertuis (1698–1759) was a renowned French mathematician and philosopher who famously headed the expedition to Lapland to measure the shape of the Earth.</note> thinks quite otherwise (in his letters); under whatever aspect one considers the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term><note>original: "pierre Philofophale." Mr. de <term>Justi</term><note>Johann Heinrich Gottlob von Justi (1717–1771), a leading German political economist and mineralogist.</note>, Director General of the mines of the <term>Empress Queen of Hungary</term><note>Referring to Maria Theresa (1717–1780), who held these titles.</note>, proves not only its possibility, but its actual existence, in a discourse he gave to the public, and whose arguments are based on his own experience.

### *Philosophical Advice.*

Adore God alone; love Him with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself. Always propose the glory of God as the end of all your actions; invoke Him, and He will hear you; glorify Him, and He will exalt you.

Be slow in your words and in your actions. Do not rely on your own prudence, on your knowledge, nor on the word and riches of men, especially the Great. Put your trust only in God. Make use of the talent He has entrusted to you. Be stingy <note>The text likely continues "with your time" or "of your secrets," as was common in these moral treatises.</note>

# APHORISM

## ON THE TRUTH OF THE SCIENCES.

There are two kinds of sciences, and no more: Religion and <term>Physics</term><note>In this historical context, "Physics" (Physique) refers to "Natural Philosophy"—the study of the physical world and its laws, which often included what we now call biology, chemistry, and even alchemy.</note>; that is to say, the science of God and the science of Nature. All the rest are but branches of these. There are even bastard sciences; but these are errors rather than true sciences.

God gives the first in its perfection to the Saints and the children of Heaven. He enlightens the mind of man to acquire the second, and the Devil casts clouds upon it to insinuate the bastard ones.

Religion comes from Heaven; it is the true science, because God, the source of all truth, is its author. Physics is the knowledge of Nature; with it, man performs surprising things. *The human mind is the worker of wonders.*<note>original: "Mens humana mirabilium effectrix." This Latin maxim reflects the Renaissance and Enlightenment belief in the nearly limitless potential of human reason and scientific discovery.</note>

The power of man is greater than one could imagine. He can do everything through God, and nothing without Him, except for evil.

## The Key to the Sciences.

The first step to wisdom is the fear of God; the second is the knowledge of Nature. Through nature, one ascends to the knowledge of its Author (a). Nature teaches the clear-sighted <term>Hermetic Physics</term><note>A branch of natural philosophy based on the teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, focusing on the hidden laws of the universe and the relationship between the macrocosm and microcosm.</note>. The "long work" is always that of Nature; she operates simply, successively, and always by the same means to produce the same results. The work of art <note>In the context of this period, "Art" refers to human skill, artifice, or technology—specifically the alchemical "Art" that assists or accelerates natural processes.</note> is shorter; it greatly accelerates the steps of Nature. The work of God is done in an instant. Alchemy, properly so-called, is an operation of Nature aided by art. It places in our hands the key to natural magic or Physics, and makes us admirable to men by raising us above the common crowd.

## On the Secret.

The statue of <term>Harpocrates</term><note>The Greek interpretation of the Egyptian god Horus the Child. Because he was depicted with his finger to his lips, he was adopted by the Greeks and Romans as the god of silence and secrecy.</note>, who had a hand over his mouth, was among the ancient Sages the emblem of the secret, which is strengthened by silence and is weakened or vanishes through revelation. Jesus Christ our Savior revealed our mysteries only to His Disciples, and always spoke to the people through allegories and parables. *To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven... without parables He did not speak to them* (b) <note>original: "Vobis datum est noscere mysteria regni cælorum... sine parabolis non loquebatur eis"</note>.

The Priests among the Egyptians, the Magi among the Persians, the <term>Mekubalim</term><note>original: "Mécubales," from the Hebrew "Mekubalim," meaning "those who have received" the tradition; it refers to the practitioners of the Kabbalah.</note> and the Kabbalists

### *The means to attain the Secret.*

The necessary preparations to reach the secret are the knowledge of Nature and of oneself. One can only perfectly possess the first, and even the second, through the aid of Alchemy, the love of wisdom, a horror of crime and lies, the avoidance of <term>Cacochymists</term><note>A derogatory term for false alchemists or "puffers" who worked with impure materials and lacked philosophical understanding; literally "those who work with bad juices."</note>, the company of the wise, and the invocation of the Holy Spirit. One must not pile secret upon secret, but rather focus on a single thing, because God and Nature delight in unity and simplicity.

Since man is the summary of all Nature, he must learn to know himself as her condensation and shortcut. Through his spiritual part, he participates in all immortal creatures, and through his material part, in all that is perishable in the Universe.

The salt of tartar is this same nitre, more fully cooked and digested by the heat of the womb where it had been deposited, because this womb serves as Nature’s furnace. Thus, from nitre and tartar, plants are formed. This salt is found wherever nitre has been deposited, but particularly on the surface of the earth, where dew and rain provide it in abundance.

Vitriol is the same salt-nitre which, having passed through the nature of tartar, becomes a mineral salt through a longer "cooking" and in more intense furnaces. It is found in abundance...

### *Of Metallic Principles.*

From the salts we have just discussed, and from their vapors, <term>mercury</term><note>The alchemical "Mercury" was not just the liquid metal, but a philosophical principle of fluidity and connectivity.</note> is produced, which the Ancients called the <term>mineral seed</term>. From this mercury and from <term>sulfur</term><note>Representing the principle of combustion and "soul," sulfur was thought to combine with mercury to create all metallic matter.</note>—whether pure or impure—all metals are formed within the bowels of the earth and upon its surface.

When the elements, embodied through their union, take the form of <term>saltpeter</term>, <term>tartar</term>, and <term>vitriol</term>, the fire of Nature—stirred by solar heat—<term>digests</term><note>In alchemical terms, "digestion" refers to the slow, steady maturation of a substance through heat, mimicking the way the body processes food or the earth ripens minerals.</note> the moisture that the dryness of these salts attracts. By separating the pure from the impure, the salt from the earth, and the homogeneous from the heterogeneous parts, it thickens it into <term>quicksilver</term><note>A common historical name for liquid mercury.</note>, then into pure or impure metal, depending on the mixture and the quality of the <term>matrix</term><note>The "womb" or surrounding geological environment in which a mineral grows.</note>.

The variety of sulfur and mercury—being more or less pure, and more or less digested—their union and their various combinations form the vast family of the <term>mineral kingdom</term>. Stones, <term>marcasites</term><note>A term often applied to various sulfide minerals like iron pyrite; they were seen as "half-formed" metals.</note>, and minerals differ further from one another according to the difference of their matrices and the degree of their <term>cooking</term><note>Alchemists believed that metals naturally "cooked" or ripened toward perfection (gold) over long periods of time under the earth's natural heat.</note>.

### *Matter is one and all things.*

The Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists or seekers of the Hermetic secrets.</note>, always careful to hide both their matter and their processes, give the name of "matter" indifferently to this same substance in all the various states it assumes during the course of the operations. To this end, they give it many specific names that only apply to it in a general sense, and never has any compound possessed so many names. It is one and all things, they say, because it is the radical principle <note>The "radical principle" refers to the fundamental root or essence of a substance.</note> of all compounds. It is in everything and similar to everything, because it is capable of taking on all forms, but only before it has been specified into any particular species among the individuals of the three kingdoms of Nature <note>The three kingdoms are the Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral.</note>. When it is specified into the mineral genus, they say it is similar to gold, because it is its base, its principle, and its mother. This is why they call it raw gold, volatile gold, immature <note>original: "immeur"; meaning unripe or not yet perfected.</note> gold, or leprous gold. It is analogous to the metals, being the mercury <note>The "mercury of the philosophers" is not the common quicksilver found in thermometers, but a theoretical metallic soul or solvent.</note> of which they are composed. The spirit of this mercury is so "congealing" that it is named the father of all stones, both precious and common. It is the mother who conceives them, the moisture that nourishes them, and the matter that makes them. Minerals are also formed from it; and as

Antimony is the Proteus <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea-god capable of changing his shape at will; alchemists used this name for antimony because of its many different forms and chemical behaviors.</note> of Chemistry, & the mineral which has the most properties & virtues. Artephius <note>Artephius (c. 1150) was a legendary alchemical author to whom several important medieval texts were attributed.</note> named the matter of the great work *Antimony of the parts of Saturn*. But although it gives a true mercury, one must not imagine that this mercury is drawn from vulgar <note>In alchemy, "vulgar" means common or commercial-grade materials found in a shop, as opposed to the "philosophical" or purified substances prepared by the alchemist.</note> antimony, nor that it is common mercury. Philalethes <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes was the pseudonym of a 17th-century alchemist, likely George Starkey, author of the famous "Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King."</note> assures us (a) that in whatever way one treats vulgar mercury, one will never make of it the Philosophical mercury. The Cosmopolite <note>The Cosmopolite was the pseudonym of Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist.</note> says that this one is the true mercury, & that common mercury is but its bastard brother (b). When the mercury of the wise is mixed with silver & gold, it is called the electrum <note>Electrum is naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver, but here refers to a specific alchemical stage.</note> of the Philosophers, their brass, their latten <term>latten: a yellow alloy resembling brass, often used as a metaphor for the matter during the "yellowing" stage of the work</term>, their copper, their steel; and in the operations, their venom, their arsenic, their orpiment, their lead, their latten which must be whitened; Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, the Moon & the Sun.

This mercury is a fiery water, which has the power to dissolve all mixtures, minerals, stones, & everything that other solvents or strong waters <note>The original term is "menstrues" or "eaux fortes," referring to corrosive acids like nitric acid.</note> cannot do; the scythe of the old man Saturn overcomes them; which has caused it to be given the name of universal solvent <term>universal solvent: also known as the Alkahest, a mythical substance capable of dissolving any other substance into its primary essence</term>.

### The Key to the Work.

Basile Valentin (*a*) <note>Basil Valentine, a legendary 15th-century alchemist and author of the "Twelve Keys," often depicted as a Benedictine monk.</note> says that he who has flour will soon have dough, and he who has dough will soon find an oven to bake it. One must first begin by preparing the agents; and it is of this preparation that the Philosophers have not spoken at all, because everything depends upon it, and because the second work is, according to their saying, but child's play and women’s amusement. <note>The phrase "child's play" (ludus puerorum) is a common alchemical trope suggesting that once the primary "mercury" is prepared, the rest of the process is governed by nature and requires little effort.</note> One must not, therefore, confuse the operations of the second work with those of the first, although *Morien* (a) <note>Morienus Romanus was a legendary 7th-century hermit-alchemist said to have taught the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid (King Calid).</note> assures us that the second work, which he calls *disposition*, is but a repetition of the first. ...matter cannot be reduced to water except by **dissolution**, when one does not employ the distillation of <term>common chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chymie vulgaire"; this refers to the laboratory practices of ordinary chemists or apothecaries, which the alchemists viewed as purely physical and lacking the "philosophical" or "vital" component of their Great Work.</note>, which is excluded from the work.

It is helpful to note here that all the terms of common chemistry that the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>In alchemical literature, "Philosophers" is the standard term for the true masters of alchemy (the Hermetic Philosophy).</note> employ in their books must not be taken in the ordinary sense, but in the **Philosophical sense**. This is why *Philalethes* <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes was the pseudonym of a highly influential 17th-century alchemist, likely George Starkey, famous for his "Introitus Apertus" and his commentaries on earlier masters.</note> warns us (a) that the terms **distillation**, **sublimation**, **calcination**, **roasting**, **reverberation**, **dissolution**, **descension**, and **coagulation** are but one and the same operation, performed in one and the same vessel—that is to say, a cooking of the matter; we will show the differences between them later, when we speak of each one in particular.

It must further be noted that the demonstrative signs of the work, which the Philosophers mention, particularly concern the **second work**. One will also observe that the majority of <term>Hermetic Authors</term> <note>Writers within the tradition of Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> begin their treatises at this second operation, and they assume their **mercury** and their **sulfur** are already made; the descriptions they give in their enigmas, their allegories, their fables, etc., are almost all drawn from what occurs in this second disposition of *Morien* <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit who was said to have passed the secrets of the stone to the Arab world.</note>; and from this arise the apparent contradictions found in their works, where one says that two matters are required, another only one, another three, another four, etc. Thus, to express oneself in accordance with the ideas of the Philosophers,

### *Definitions & properties of this Mercury.*

Mercury is a substance that dissolves metals through a natural dissolution, and which leads their spirits from potentiality into actuality. <note>original: "puissance en acte." This is an Aristotelian concept often used in alchemy to describe how the hidden "spirit" or potential of a metal is brought into its final, perfected state.</note>

Mercury is that substance which makes the matter of metals lucid, clear, and without shadow—that is to say, which cleanses them of their impurities, and draws out from the interior of perfect metals <note>In alchemy, "perfect metals" usually refers to gold and silver, which were believed to be free of the "leprosies" or impurities found in base metals.</note> their nature and seed which is hidden there.

The dissolving mercury is a dry vapor, <note>The "dry vapor" (vapeur séche) is a classic alchemical paradox; it refers to a substance that behaves like a gas or spirit but originates from a solid or metallic base.</note> in no way viscous, possessing much acidity, very subtle, very volatile in fire, and having a great property of penetrating and dissolving metals while preparing them; and in performing this dissolution, beyond the length of the labor, one runs a very great danger, says Philalethe. <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes (1628–1665) was a highly influential and mysterious alchemist, likely the American George Starkey, whose writings were studied by Isaac Newton.</note> He consequently recommends protecting one's eyes, ears, and nose.

The preparation of this mercury, adds the same Author, is the greatest of Nature's secrets; it can hardly be learned except by the revelation of God, or from a friend; for one does not...

## Of the vessel of Art & of that of Nature.

Three kinds of <term>matrices</term> <note>From the Latin "matrix" meaning "womb"; the environment where a substance is conceived and grown.</note>: the first is the earth, the universal matrix of the world, the receptacle of the elements, the great vessel of Nature, the place where the <term>corruption of seeds</term> <note>Alchemists believed that for a seed to grow, it must first "die" or rot (corrupt) in the earth to release its life force.</note> occurs, the sepulcher and the living tomb of all creatures. It is, in particular, the matrix of the vegetable and the mineral.

The second matrix is that of the uterus in the animal; that of birds is the egg, and the rock alone is that of gold and silver.

The third, that of metal, is known to few people. The matrix being, along with the <term>sperm</term> <note>In this context, "sperm" refers to the active metallic seed or essence, rather than a biological fluid.</note>, the cause of the specification of the metal.

<header>FABLES</header>

Knowledge of this precious vessel, and of the fixed and stone-making spirit <note>original: "saxifique"; a technical term describing the ability to transform a substance into stone or a solid state.</note> implanted within it, was one of the greatest secrets of the Egyptian <term>Cabala</term> <note>In this context, "Cabala" refers to a secret, mystical tradition of knowledge passed down through generations, often applied to the "sacred art" of alchemy.</note>. It was therefore necessary to find a vessel analogous to the one Nature employs for the formation of metals; a vessel that would become the matrix of the Philosophers' "Golden Tree"—and none was found better than glass. They added the method of sealing it, in imitation of Nature, so that none of its principles might escape. For as Raymond Lully <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath whose name was frequently attached to alchemical treatises.</note> says, the composition formed from the substance of exhaled vapors, which are then beaten back down upon the decaying matter to moisten and dissolve it, is called <term>putrefaction</term> <note>In alchemy, putrefaction is the essential first stage where the "matter" breaks down, often turning black, to allow for new life to emerge.</note>. This vessel must therefore have a shape suitable for facilitating the circulation of spirits, and must be of a thickness and consistency capable of resisting their impetuous force.

## *Names given to this vessel by the Ancients.*

The Philosophers took care to weave this vessel into their allegories in such a way that no one would have the slightest suspicion of their true meaning. Sometimes it was a tower, sometimes a ship, here a chest, there a basket. Such was the tower of Danaë; the chest of Deucalion, and the tomb of Osiris; the basket, the wineskin of Bacchus, and his bottle; the golden amphora or vessel of Vulcan; the cup that Juno presented to Thetis; the ship of Jason; the marsh of Lerna, which was thus named from the Greek word *larnax* <note>original: "λάρναξ"; meaning a chest, coffer, or ark.</note>, or *chest* <note>original Latin: "capsa"</note>, or *small compartment* <note>original Latin: "loculus"</note>; the basket of Erichthonius; the casket in which

» …in addition, there is a fire that is hot, dry, moist, and cold. If the fire went out, it was seen as a catastrophic omen for the state.</note> to whom the care of its maintenance was entrusted were punished by death if, through negligence or otherwise, they allowed it to be extinguished.
