<meta>This page continues the discussion of alchemical theory, shifting from the specific types of philosophical fire mentioned on the previous page to the overarching "Operating Principles" of the Great Work. <header>EGYPTIAN AND GREEK [FABLES].</header>

### Operating Principles.

The preparation is composed of four parts. The first is the solution of the matter into mercurial water <note>Mercurial water: Not common mercury (quicksilver), but the "universal solvent" or "First Matter" in a liquid state, believed to be the starting point of the Work.</note>; the second is the preparation of the Mercury of the Philosophers; the third is corruption <note>Corruption: Also known as "putrefaction," this is the stage where the matter turns black (the *nigredo*), signifying the death of the old forms before a new life can emerge.</note>; the fourth is the generation and creation of Philosophical Sulfur <note>Philosophical Sulfur: In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and fiery principle of matter, whereas mercury represents the passive, feminine, and fluid principle.</note>. The first part is accomplished by the mineral seed of the earth; the second volatilizes and spermatizes <note>spermatizes: To infuse with "seed" or life-giving, generative potential.</note> the bodies; the third brings about the separation of substances and their rectification <note>rectification: The process of purifying a liquid by repeated distillation.</note>; the fourth unites and fixes them, which constitutes the creation of the stone <note>the stone: The Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate goal of alchemy, capable of transmuting metals and perfecting human health.</note>. The Philosophers have compared this preparation to the creation of the world, which was at first a mass, a chaos, a void earth—formless and dark—which was nothing in particular, but everything in general. The second stage is a form of heavy and viscous water, full of the occult spirit of its sulfur; and the third is the figure of the earth which appeared dry after the separation of the waters.

God said, "Let there be light," and light was made; it emerged from its limbo <note>original: "limbe." In this context, it refers to a border or an edge of existence where things remain unmanifested.</note> and placed itself in the highest region. Then the darkness disappeared before it; chaos and confusion gave way to order, night to day, and, so to speak, nothingness to being.

God spoke a second time; the confused elements separated, the lightest lodged themselves above, and the heaviest below; then the earth, freed from its moist abysses, appeared, and appeared capable of producing everything.

<summary>This page defines the four stages of alchemical preparation—solution, preparation of mercury, corruption, and the creation of sulfur—while explicitly framing the alchemist's work as a recreation of the divine Genesis.</summary>

This separation of water from the earth, where air was found and fire spread out, is only a successive change of matter under this double form; this is what led the Philosophers to say that water is the entire foundation of the work, without which the earth could not be dissolved, rotted <note>rotted: This refers to the process of *putrefaction*, where the matter is broken down and blackened to prepare it for a new form.</note>, or prepared, and that the earth is the body where the humid elements end, congeal, and bury themselves in a way, in order to regain a nobler life.

A circulation then takes place, the first movement of which sublimes the matter by thinning it; the second lowers it by congealing it; and the whole finally ends in a kind of rest, or rather an internal movement, an imperceptible cooking <note>cooking: In alchemy, this is known as *coction*, the prolonged application of heat to mature the "philosophical egg."</note> of the matter.

The first wheel of this rotation of elements, as d'Espagnet <note>Jean d'Espagnet (1564–c. 1637): A French magistrate and alchemist whose work *Enchiridion Physicae Restitutae* (1623) was a major influence on 17th-century hermetic thought.</note> calls it, consists in the reduction of matter into water, where generation begins; the eclipse of the Sun and the Moon then occurs <note>eclipse: A symbolic term for the *nigredo* or blackening stage, where the "lights" of the metals are darkened during dissolution.</note>. The second is an evacuation of superfluous moisture, and a coagulation of the matter in the form of a viscous and metallic earth; the third wheel effects the separation and the rectification of substances; the waters are separated from the waters. Everything becomes spiritualized or volatilized; the Sun and the Moon regain their clarity, and light begins to appear on the earth. The fourth is the creation of sulfur <note>sulfur: Here referring to "Philosophical Sulfur," the active, masculine principle that gives the Stone its power to fix and transform.</note>.

## *Operative Principles in Particular.*

### *Calcination.*

Common calcination <note>original: "calcination vulgaire"; in alchemical texts, "vulgar" refers to the ordinary chemical processes used by tradesmen or non-initiates</note> is nothing other than the death and mortification <term>mortification: the process of breaking down a substance, often associated with a change in color to black, symbolizing the "death" of its previous form</term> of the compound, through the separation of the spirit, or the moisture that bound its parts together. It is, properly speaking, a pulverization by fire, and a reduction of the body into lime, ash, earth, flowers <term>flowers: in this context, "flowers" (flores) refers to the fine powder or sublimate that rises when a substance is heated</term>, etc.

Philosophical [calcination] is an extraction of the substance of water, salt, oil, and spirit, leaving the rest as earth; it is a change of accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are the external qualities of a thing (like color or shape) that can change without changing the essential nature of the substance itself</note>, an alteration of quantity, and a corruption of the substance, in such a way, however, that all these separated things may be reunited so that a more perfect body results from them. Common calcination is performed by the action of the fire of our kitchens, or the concentrated rays of the Sun; Philosophical calcination has water for its agent; which led the Philosophers to say: *The Chemists burn with fire, and we burn with water;* from which one must conclude that common Chemistry is as different from Hermetic <term>Hermetic: relating to Hermes Trismegistus and the esoteric tradition of alchemy</term> Chemistry as fire differs from water.

<meta>This page continues the technical definitions of alchemical processes following the discussion of Calcination on the previous page. The author, likely Antoine-Joseph Pernety, is defining "Solution" and "Putrefaction" from both a chemical and a "Philosophical" (alchemical) perspective.</meta>

### *Solution.*

Solution, chemically speaking, is an attenuation <note>the thinning or weakening of a substance</note>, or liquefaction of matter in the form of water, oil, spirit, or humor. But the Philosophical [Solution] is a reduction of the body into its first matter <note>original: "premiere matiere"; the *materia prima* is the primitive, formless base of all substance in alchemical theory</note>, or a natural disunion of the parts of the compound, and a coagulation of the spiritual parts. This is why the Philosophers call it a solution of the body and a congelation of the spirit. Its effect is to liquefy, dissolve, open, re-incrudate <term>re-incrudate: the process of returning a processed or "cooked" substance back to its raw, "crude" state</term>, un-cook, and evacuate the substances of their earthiness, to de-corporify <note>to strip a substance of its physical, solid form</note> the mixture in order to reduce it to seed <term>seed: in alchemy, "sperm" or seed refers to the generative essence from which metals are believed to grow</term>.

### *Putrefaction.*

Putrefaction is, in a way, the key to all operations, although it is not properly the first. It reveals to us the interior of the mixture; it is the tool that breaks the bonds of the parts; it makes, as the Philosophers say, the hidden manifest. It is the principle of the change of forms, the death of accidental qualities <note>the external properties of a thing, like color or smell, which can change while the essence remains</note>, the first step toward generation, the beginning and the end of life; the middle point between non-being and being.

The Philosopher maintains that it occurs when the body, dissolved by a natural resolution, is subjected to the action of putrefactive heat. Distillation and sublimation were only invented in imitation of those processes of Nature regarding the elements, whose inclination, or disposi—

...tion to rarefy and rise, to condense and descend, constitute the entirety of the mixture and the productions of Nature.

Distillation differs from sublimation in that the former is achieved by the elevation of moist things, which then distill drop by drop; whereas sublimation is the elevation of a dry matter that attaches itself to the vessel. Both of these are common <note>original: "vulgaires"; in this context, it refers to standard chemical practices as opposed to the "Philosophical" or secret alchemical ones</note> operations.

Distillation and sublimation, philosophically speaking, are a purgation, subtilization, and rectification of matter.

Coagulation and fixation are the two great instruments of Nature and Art <note>In alchemy, "Art" refers to the human labor and skill used to perfect or accelerate natural processes</note>.

### Fermentation.

The ferment in the work is what leaven <note>or yeast</note> is in the making of bread. One cannot make bread without leaven, and one cannot make gold without gold. Gold is therefore the soul and that which determines the intrinsic form of the Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>. Let us not blush at learning how to make gold and silver just as the baker makes bread, which is but a compound of water and kneaded flour, fermented, and which differs from the other only by the baking. In the same way, the golden medicine is only a composition of earth and water—that is to say, of sulfur and mercury fermented with gold; but with a re-incrudated <term>re-incrudated: the process of returning a processed, "cooked," or solid metal back to its raw, "crude," or liquid state so it can be used in the Work</term> gold. For just as one cannot make leaven from baked bread, one cannot make it with common gold so long as it remains common gold.

Mercury or mercurial water is this water; sulfur is this flour, which through a long fermentation turn sour and are made into leaven <note>original: "levain"; the ferment or yeast used to trigger the transformation of the whole batch</note>, with which gold and silver are made. And just as leaven multiplies eternally and always serves as the material for making bread, the Philosophical medicine <note>Another name for the Philosopher's Stone or its transformative elixir</note> also multiplies and serves eternally as leaven for making gold.

### *Signs or demonstrative principles.*

The colors that appear in the Philosophical matter during the course of the work’s operations are demonstrative signs, which let the Artist <note>In alchemical texts, "the Artist" refers to the practitioner or alchemist performing the labor</note> know that they have proceeded in a way that leads to success. They follow one another immediately and in a specific order; if this order is disturbed, it is proof that the work has been performed incorrectly. There are three principal colors; the first is black, called the **raven’s head** <note>original: "tête de corbeau"; the *nigredo* stage, symbolizing the death of the old form</note>, and many other names that we have reported previously in the article entitled: *Key to the Work*.

The beginning of this blackness indicates that the fire of Nature is beginning to operate and that the matter is in the process of solution <note>the stage where solids are dissolved into liquid</note>; when this black color is perfect, the solution is also complete, and the elements are confounded <note>thoroughly mixed or unified</note>. The grain rots in order to prepare itself for generation. "He who does not turn black will not know how to turn white," says Artéphius <note>A celebrated and semi-mythical alchemical author, often said to have lived for a thousand years</note>; because blackness is the beginning of whiteness, and it is the mark of putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the symbolic and physical decomposition of the alchemical matter, necessary before it can be purified and "reborn"</term> and alteration. Here is how this occurs: In putrefaction...

Artéphius <note>a legendary alchemical author often cited in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, sometimes identified as a 12th-century figure or an ancient philosopher who allegedly lived for a thousand years</note> says that the whiteness comes from the fact that the soul of the body floats above the water like a white cream; and that the spirits then unite so strongly that they can no longer flee, because they have lost their volatility.

The great secret of the work is therefore to whiten the latten <term>latten</term> <note>original: "laiton"; in alchemy, this refers to the base matter or "philosophical brass" that must be purified to reach the silver or white stage</note>, and leave aside all other books, so as not to be burdened by reading them, which could give rise to ideas of some useless and expensive labor. This whiteness is the stone perfected to the white stage; it is a precious body which, when it is fermented and becomes the white elixir, is full of an exuberant tincture that has the property of communicating itself to all other metals. The spirits, previously volatile, are then fixed. The new body is resurrected beautiful, white, immortal, and victorious. This is why it has been called *resurrection, light, day*, and by all the names that can indicate whiteness, fixity, and incorruptibility.

Flamel <note>Nicolas Flamel (c. 1330–1418), a French scribe who posthumously gained a reputation as a master alchemist who discovered the Philosopher's Stone</note> has represented this color in his Hieroglyphical figures by a woman surrounded by a white scroll, to show you, he says, "that the Rebis <term>Rebis</term> <note>from the Latin "res bina," meaning "double thing"; it represents the alchemical hermaphrodite or the union of opposites (spirit and matter, male and female)</note> will begin to whiten in this same way, whitening first at the extremities all around this white circle." The elixir, according to d’Espagnet <note>Jean d'Espagnet (1564–1637), a French magistrate and alchemist whose works were highly influential in the 17th and 18th centuries</note>, is composed of a triple matter: namely, a metallic water (or philosophically sublimated mercury), the <term>white ferment</term> <note>A substance, usually refined silver, used to "leaven" or stabilize the elixir for transmuting metals into silver</note> if one wishes to make the elixir "at the white," or the <term>red ferment</term> <note>Usually refined gold, used to stabilize the elixir for transmuting metals into gold</note> for the elixir "at the red," and finally the second sulfur; all according to the Philosophical weights and proportions. ### *Quintessence.*

The quintessence is an extraction of the most spirituous and radical substance of the matter; it is done by the separation of the elements which end in a celestial and incorruptible essence freed from all heterogeneities <note>Impurities or foreign substances that are not part of the core essence</note>. Aristotle calls it a very pure substance, incorporated into certain matter not mixed with accidents <note>In Aristotelian logic, "accidents" are properties that can change without affecting the essential nature of a substance, such as size or color</note>. Heraclitus calls it a celestial essence which takes the name of the place from which it draws its origin. Paracelsus <note>The famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist known for his "Spagyric" medicinal theories</note> says it is the being of our centric heaven; Pliny calls it a corporeal essence nevertheless separated from all materiality, and freed from the commerce <note>Entanglement or interaction</note> of matter. It has consequently been named a spiritual body, or a corporeal spirit, made of an ethereal substance. All these qualities have caused it to be given the name of quintessence, that is to say, a fifth substance, which results from the union of the purest parts of the elements.

## The Tincture.

When those ignorant of Hermetic Philosophy <note>The esoteric tradition based on the teachings of Hermes Trismegistus, focusing on the transmutation of both matter and the soul</note> read the term "tincture" in works dealing with this science, they imagine it must be understood only as the color of metals, such as orange for gold, and white for silver. And since it is said in these same works that sulfur is the principle of the tincture, they labor to extract this sulfur using nitric acids <note>Original: "eaux fortes"</note>, aqua regia <note>Original: "eaux régales"; a powerful mixture of acids capable of dissolving noble metals like gold</note>, through calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile parts or achieve oxidation</note>, and the other operations of vulgar chemistry <note>Common or laboratory chemistry, which the author distinguishes from the "Sacred Art" of the true alchemists</note>. This is not properly the idea of the Philosophers, not only regarding the operations, but for the tincture considered in itself. The tincture of gold cannot be separated from its body, because it is its soul; and one could not extract it without destroying the body—which is not possible for vulgar chemistry, as all those who have attempted this experiment know very well.

The tincture, in the Philosophical sense, is the elixir itself, rendered fixed, fusible, penetrating, and staining <note>Original: "tingéant"; the power of the elixir to "tinge" or transform the qualities of another substance</note>, through the corruption <note>The alchemical stage of breaking down a substance to its core, often associated with the "Black Work" or Nigredo</note> and the other operations of which we have spoken. This tincture, therefore, does not consist of the external color, but in the very substance which provides the tincture...

### *Multiplication.*

By **Philosophical multiplication**, one understands an increase in quantity and in qualities, and both beyond all that one can imagine. That of quality is a multiplication of the **tincture** <note>In alchemy, the "soul" or coloring principle of a substance capable of transmuting other bodies</note> through a **corruption**, a **volatilization**, and a **fixation** <note>Three stages of alchemical processing: breaking down, turning to vapor, and then solidifying into a stable form</note> repeated as many times as pleases the **Artist** <note>The alchemist performing the work</note>. The second increases only the quantity of the tincture without increasing its virtues.

There are, nevertheless, three ways to perform **multiplication** <note>The stage of the "Great Work" where the alchemist increases the power (virtue) and the quantity of the produced Elixir</note> if we are to believe **d’Espagnet** <note>Jean d'Espagnet (1564–1637), a French alchemist and magistrate known for his influential work *Enchiridion Physicae Restitutae*</note>, who describes them in the following manner. The first is to take one part of the perfect red **elixir** <note>The final medicinal or transmuting agent; the "Red Elixir" was specifically for the transmutation of metals into gold</note>, which is mixed with nine parts of its red water; the vessel is placed in a **bath** <note>A "bain-marie" or water bath, used to provide gentle, consistent heat</note>, to dissolve everything into water. After the solution is formed, this water is cooked until it coagulates into a substance resembling a **ruby**; this substance is then applied in the manner of the elixir; and from this first operation, the medicine acquires ten times more virtue than it previously had. If this same process is repeated a second time, it will increase by a hundred; a third time by a thousand, and so on, always by a factor of ten.

The second way is to mix the desired quantity of elixir with its water, while maintaining the proportions between the two, and after placing everything in a well-sealed **reduction vessel** <note>A specialized glass container designed to withstand the pressures of alchemical "reduction" or refinement</note>, dissolving it in the bath, and following the entire regimen of the second [sulfur] by successively distilling the elements by their own fires, until the whole becomes stone. One then applies it as in the other method, and the virtue of the elixir increases by a hundred from the first time, but this path is longer. It is repeated like the first, to increase its strength more and more.

Finally, the third way is strictly speaking multiplication in quantity. One projects an ounce of the e- <note>The text cuts off here at the beginning of "elixir"</note>

The more the multiplication in quality is reiterated, the more effect it will have in **projection** <note>The final stage of the Great Work, where the Elixir is "projected" or cast onto molten base metals—like lead or mercury—to instantly transform them into gold or silver.</note>; but not in the third manner of multiplying of which we have spoken; for its strength diminishes at each projection. One can only push this reiteration, however, until the fourth or fifth time, because the medicine <note>Alchemists often called the Philosopher's Stone a "medicine" (medicina), viewing it as a substance that "healed" imperfect metals by bringing them to the state of gold.</note> would then be so active and so **fiery** <note>original: *ignée*. This refers to the concentrated "spiritual fire" within the Stone; if too potent, it was believed the substance could become too volatile or "active" to be safely managed in a laboratory.</note> that the operations would become instantaneous; since their duration shortens at each reiteration. Its virtue, moreover, is great enough at the fourth or fifth time to fulfill the desires of the Artist <note>A traditional term for the alchemist, implying that the work was as much a creative craft as a science.</note>, since from the first, one grain can convert a hundred grains of mercury into gold, at the second a thousand, at the third ten thousand, at the fourth a hundred thousand, and so on. One should judge this medicine as one does grain, which multiplies every time it is sown.

### Very instructive general rules.

<meta>This page continues the explanation of the alchemical process, clarifying that the many technical terms used by "Philosophers" (alchemists) actually describe different stages of transformation occurring within a single vessel.</meta>

### EGYPTIAN AND GREEK [FABLES].

...same vessel. The Philosophers <note>In alchemical texts, "the Philosophers" refers to the long lineage of alchemical authorities whose works formed the basis of the "Great Work."</note> gave all these names only to the different things or changes they saw happening within the vessel. When they perceived the matter exhaling as a subtle smoke and rising to the top of the vessel, they named this ascent *sublimation*. Seeing then this vapor descend to the bottom of the vessel, they called it *descension* or *distillation*. Morien <note>Morienus (or Morienus Romanus) was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist, famously credited with teaching the secrets of alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says consequently: "Our entire operation consists of extracting the water from its earth and returning it there until the earth rots and purifies itself." When they saw that this water, mixed with its earth, coagulated or thickened, becoming black and foul-smelling, they said that this was *putrefaction*, the principle of generation. This putrefaction lasts until the matter has become white.

This matter, being black, reduces to powder when it begins to turn gray; this appearance of ash gave rise to the idea of *calcination* <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</term>, *inceration* <term>Inceration: The act of adding liquid to a dry substance until it achieves the consistency of soft wax.</term>, *incineration*, and *dealbation* <term>Dealbation: From the Latin "dealbare," meaning to whiten or bleach; the process of turning the matter white.</term>; and when it has reached a great whiteness, they named it *perfect calcination*. Seeing that the matter took on a solid consistency and no longer flowed, it formed their *congelation* and their *induration* <term>Induration: The process of a substance becoming hard or solid.</term>; this is why they said that the entire **magistery** <term>Magistery: Also known as the "Magisterium," this refers to the completed alchemical process or the mastery of the Great Work.</term> consists of dissolving and coagulating naturally.

This same matter, congealed and hardened so that it no longer resolves back into water, made them say that it must be dried and fixed; they thus gave to this purported operation the names of *desiccation*, *fixation*, and *ceration*, because they explain this term as a perfect union...

It should also be known that all the following expressions signify only the same thing: Distilling in the alembic <term>Alembic: A distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube; used here to describe the rising and falling of vapors within the sealed flask.</term>; separating the soul from the body; burning; liquefying; calcining; waxing; giving to drink <note>A metaphor for adding liquid to dry matter.</note>; adapting together; making eat; assembling; correcting; sifting; cutting with pincers; dividing; uniting the elements; extracting them; exalting them; converting them; changing them into one another; cutting with a knife; striking with a sword, an axe, or a scimitar; piercing with a lance, a javelin, or an arrow; stunning; crushing; binding; unbinding; corrupting; laminating; melting; engendering; conceiving; bringing into the world; drawing water; moistening; watering; imbibing; making a paste; amalgamating; burying; incerating <term>Inceration: Turning a substance into a waxy state.</term>; washing; washing with fire; softening; polishing; filing; beating with a hammer; mortifying; blackening; putrefying; turning on the lathe; circulating; rubefying <term>Rubefying: The act of turning the matter red (the "Rubedo"), representing the final stage of the alchemical work.</term>; dissolving; subliming; leaching; entombing; resurrecting; reverberating; grinding; reducing to powder; pounding in a mortar; pulverizing on marble, and so many other similar expressions. 

All of this means nothing other than cooking by the same regimen <term>Regimen: The precise management of heat and time throughout the alchemical process.</term>, until the matter reaches a deep red. One must therefore take great care not to move the vessel, and not to remove it from the fire; for if the matter were to cool, everything would be lost.

### On the Virtues of the Medicine.

It is, according to the words of all the Philosophers <note>In alchemical literature, "Philosophers" refers to the "Philosophers by Fire" or Alchemists who have attained the secret knowledge.</note>, the source of wealth and health; for with it one can produce gold and silver in abundance, and one can be cured not only of all diseases that are capable of being healed, but through its moderate use, one can even prevent them. ## *Of the Diseases of Metals.*

The first defect of metals arises from the initial mixing of principles with quicksilver <note>original: "argent vif."</note>, and the second is found in the union of sulfurs and mercury. The more the elements are purified, the more they are proportionally mixed and homogeneous, the more they possess weight, malleability, fusion, extension, brilliance <term>fulgidité: from the Latin "fulgidus," meaning a glittering or lightning-like brightness</term>, and permanent incorruptibility.

There are thus two kinds of diseases in metals: the first is called original and incurable; the second arises from the diversity of the sulfur which causes their imperfection and their maladies—namely, the leprosy of Saturn <note>Saturn is the alchemical symbol for Lead; "leprosy" refers to its dull, scaly oxidation.</note>, the jaundice of Venus <note>Venus represents Copper; "jaundice" refers to its yellow-green tarnish.</note>, the congestion <note>original: "enrhusmement." Likely referring to the "dullness" or lack of resonance in the metal.</note> of Jupiter <note>Jupiter represents Tin.</note>, the dropsy <term>hydropisie: an archaic term for edema, or an unhealthy accumulation of fluid</term> of Mercury <note>Mercury represents Quicksilver.</note>, and the mange <note>original: "galle."</note> of Mars <note>Mars represents Iron; "mange" or "scab" refers to rust.</note>.

The dropsy of mercury occurs only due to an excess of wateriness and crudity, which find their cause in the coldness of the matrix <note>The "matrix" was the womb-like cavity within the earth where alchemists believed metals "grew."</note> where it is engendered, and from a lack of time to "ripen" <note>original: "se cuire," literally "to cook." Alchemists believed metals reached perfection (gold) by being "cooked" by the earth's internal heat over centuries.</note>. This defect is an original sin in which all other metals participate. This coldness, this crudity, and this wateriness can only be cured by the heat and fiery nature <note>original: "ignéité."</note> of a very powerful sulfur.

Besides this disease, the other metals also suffer from those caused by their sulfur, both internal and external. The latter, being merely accidental, can be easily separated because it does not belong to the initial mixture of elements. It is black, impure, and foul-smelling; it does not mix with the radical sulfur <note>The "radical" sulfur is the essential, internal soul of the metal, as opposed to surface impurities.</note> because it is heterogeneous to it. It is not

Arnaud de Villeneuve (a) states that its efficacy is infinitely superior to that of all the remedies of Hippocrates, Galen, Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Tralles, a prominent 6th-century Byzantine physician.</note>, Avicenna, and all of ordinary medicine; that it gladdens the heart, provides vigor and strength, preserves youth, and makes old age grow green again. Geber (b), without listing the specific diseases that this medicine cures, contents himself by saying that it overcomes all those which ordinary physicians regard as incurable. It rejuvenates the elderly and maintains them in health for many years, even beyond the ordinary span of life, by taking only a dose the size of a mustard seed two or three times a week on an empty stomach.

Philalethes (c) adds to this that it cleanses the skin of all spots, wrinkles, etc.; that it delivers a woman in labor, even if the child were dead, simply by holding the powder to the mother's nose; and he cites Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy is attributed.</note> as his guarantor. He asserts that he has himself rescued many patients from the arms of death who had been abandoned by their physicians. The manner of using it is found particularly in the works of Raymond Lull and Arnaud de Villeneuve.

## *On the Diseases of Metals.*

The first defect of metals arises from the initial mixture of principles with quicksilver <note>Quicksilver is the traditional name for liquid mercury.</note>, and the second is found in the union of sulfurs and mercury. The more the elements are purified, the more they are proportionately mixed and homogeneous, and the more they possess weight, malleability, fusibility, ductility, brilliance, and permanent incorruptibility.

"Leprosy" refers to its dull, porous, and easily corroded surface.</note>, the <term>jaundice of Venus</term> <note>Venus represents Copper. "Jaundice" likely refers to the yellow-green tarnish or "verdigris" that forms on it.</note>, the <term>head-cold of Jupiter</term> <note>Jupiter represents Tin. This defect is an original sin in which all other metals participate. This coldness, this rawness, and this wateriness can only be cured by the heat and fieriness of a most powerful sulfur.

Besides this disease, the other metals also have those which come to them from their sulfur, both internal and external. The latter, being only accidental, can be easily separated, because it is not part of the first mixture of elements. It is black, impure, and stinking; it does not mix at all with the radical sulfur <note>The "radical sulfur" is the essential, pure combustible principle of the metal.</note>, because it is heterogeneous to it. Other metals must be in a molten state and purified. The crucible is left in the fire until after the <term>detonation</term> <note>A sudden chemical reaction or "crack" indicating the transformation is taking place.</note>, and then it is removed, or left to cool in the fire.

## *Conclusion.*

This entire treatise is drawn from Authors; I have almost always used their own expressions. I have cited some of them from time to time, in order to better persuade [the reader] that I only speak according to them. When I have not cited their works, it is because I did not have them at hand at the time. One must have noticed a perfect agreement among them, although they speak only through riddles and allegories. I had at first intended to report many features drawn from the **Twelve Keys** <note>A famous alchemical text attributed to Basil Valentine, illustrating the stages of the Great Work through twelve symbolic images.</note> of **Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, often depicted as a Benedictine monk; his works are foundational to later European alchemy.</note>, because he has more often than the others employed the allegories of the Gods of **Fable** <note>Refers to classical Greek and Egyptian mythology, which the author interprets as coded chemical instructions.</note>; and because they would have had, consequently, a more immediate relationship with the following treatise; but riddles do not explain riddles; moreover, this work is quite common; it is not the same with the others.

<margin>(a) Eusebius <note>original: "Euseb. l. 1. c. 7." This refers to the *Praeparatio Evangelica* (Preparation for the Gospel) by the historian Eusebius of Caesarea, who quoted ancient sources on Phoenician and Egyptian theology.</note>, Book 1, Chapter 7.</margin>
*Phthath* <note>The author uses a variant of Ptah, the Egyptian creator god often associated with craftsmanship and the arts.</note> by his compatriots, *Taut* <note>Also spelled Taaut or Thoth.</note> by the Phoenicians (a), and *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>Greek for "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest."</note> by the Greeks. Nature seemed to have chosen him as her favorite, and consequently had lavished upon him all the qualities necessary to study and know her perfectly; God had, so to speak, infused him with the arts and sciences, so that he might instruct the entire world.
   Seeing that superstition had been introduced into Egypt, and that it had obscured the ideas that their ancestors had given them of God, he thought seriously about preventing the idolatry that threatened to creep imperceptibly into Divine worship. However, he felt clearly that it was not appropriate to reveal the overly sublime mysteries of Nature and its Author to a people as little capable of being struck by their grandeur as they were unlikely to understand them. Persuaded that sooner or later the common people would turn these truths into abuses, he decided to invent symbols so subtle and so difficult to understand that wise men, or those with the most penetrating minds, would be the only ones who could see clearly through them; meanwhile, the common man would find in them only a subject of admiration. Having, however, the intention of transmitting his clear and pure ideas to posterity, he did not wish to leave them to be guessed at without determining their meaning, and without communicating them to certain persons. To this end, he chose a certain number of men whom he recognized as the most fit to be the guardians of his secret, and only—

The great secrecy maintained by the **Priests**, and the high sciences they practiced, caused them to be regarded and respected throughout all of Egypt—both during the long years when they had no communication with foreigners, and after they had granted freedom of trade. ### EGYPTIAN AND GREEK. 223

Persia <note>Likely referring to the conquest of Egypt by Cambyses II in 525 BC, which led to the displacement of the priestly class.</note> scattered many **Priests** into neighboring countries and into Greece. They brought their **sciences** <term>sciences: in this context, the word refers to specialized or occult knowledge and religious doctrines</term> there; but they undoubtedly continued to teach them in the manner customary among them—that is to say, mysteriously. Not wanting to lavish them upon everyone, they enveloped them further in the shadows of fables and **hieroglyphs**, so that the common people, in seeing, would see nothing, and in hearing, would understand nothing. All drew from this source; but some took only the pure and clear water, while they muddied it for others, who found nothing there but mud.

From this arose that source of absurdities which flooded the earth for so many centuries. These mysteries, hidden under so many layers, misunderstood and poorly explained, spread through Greece, and from there throughout the entire earth.

**Solomon** <note>King Solomon, traditionally credited with the biblical books of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, was revered in the Renaissance and Enlightenment as a master of hidden wisdom and natural secrets.</note> regarded <term>hieroglyphs|Sacred carvings or symbols used to encode complex ideas</term>, proverbs, and riddles as an object worthy of a wise man’s study; one can see the praise he gives them in all his works. *The wise man will devote himself (a) to the study of parables; he will apply himself to interpreting expressions, sentences, and the enigmas of the ancient Sages. He will penetrate (b) into the twists and subtleties of parables; he will discuss proverbs to discover what is most hidden there, etc.*

The **Egyptians** did not always express themselves through hieroglyphs or riddles; they only did so when it was a matter of speaking of **God** or of what occurred most secretly in the operations of **Nature**; and the hieroglyphs of one person were not always the hieroglyphs of another. **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure who was believed to have invented writing and magic in Egypt.</note> invented the writing of the **Egyptians**; scholars do not agree on the kind of character he first put into use; but it is known that there were four kinds; the (c) first was the characters of <term>common writing|Also known as Demotic, the script used by the general population for everyday business and letters</term>, known to everyone and employed in commerce.

One must not, therefore, confuse all these different ways the **Egyptians** had of depicting and giving form to their thoughts. This lack of distinction has caused the errors into which many Antiquaries <note>Scholars who studied ancient history and artifacts before the formal development of archaeology.</note> have fallen, who, having only one objective in mind, explained all ancient monuments according to that single objective. From this came the many dissertations written by various authors who do not agree with one another. 

To succeed perfectly, one would need to have models of all these different characters. Whatever was written in an ancient work using a certain type of script would then be explained according to the things expressed by that script. If it were the first [Egyptian script], one could be certain that the matters deduced concerned the business of life, history, etc.; if it were the second, matters of Nature; and the fourth, that which concerns God, His worship, or the fables. One would not then find oneself needing to resort to conjecture, or explaining an ancient monument as one thing when it actually had a completely different purpose. But in truth, nothing certain remains of all this except for the fables, as **Hermes** had foreseen in the *Asclepius* <note>original: "Asclépius d’Apulée". ...to have other objects. **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermès." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the origins of alchemy and Egyptian wisdom were attributed.</note>, in establishing **hieroglyphs** <term>hieroglyphs: used here to mean sacred symbolic images or allegorical writing containing hidden truths.</term>, did not intend to introduce **idolatry**, nor to keep secret the ideas that one ought to hold regarding the **Divinity**; his goal was even to make God known as the unique God, and to prevent the people from worshipping others; he strove to make Him recognized in all individuals, by pointing out in each of them traits of divine wisdom. If he veiled some sublime mysteries under the shadow of **hieroglyphs**, it was not so much to hide them from the people, as because these mysteries were not within their grasp, and because, being unable to contain them within the bounds of a prudent and wise knowledge, they would not fail to abuse the instructions given to them in this regard. The **Priests** were the only ones to whom this knowledge was entrusted after a trial of several years. 

It was necessary, therefore, that this secret have another object. Several Ancients have told us that it consisted in the knowledge of what **Osiris**, **Isis**, **Horus**, and the other so-called **Gods** had been; and that it was forbidden, under pain of death, to say that they had been men. But were these Authors quite certain of what they asserted? Kircher’s idea is not precisely that of the **Philosopher’s Stone**; I do not know in what he believes it consists. One can judge this as much by what we have said thus far, as by what we shall say in the following pages. The object of the ancient or modern **Hermetic Philosophers** was always to extract from a certain subject, by natural ways, that **elixir** or **quintessence** <term>quintessence: literally the "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated form of a substance that remains after the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) are removed</term> of which Father Kircher speaks; and to operate by following the laws of Nature, in such a manner as to separate it from the heterogeneous <note>original: "hétérogènes" — referring to impure or unrelated parts that mask the true essence</note> parts in which it is enveloped. This is done in order to put it in a state to act without obstacles, so as to deliver the **three kingdoms of nature** <note>The three kingdoms are the animal, vegetable, and mineral kingdoms. Alchemists believed the Stone could "cure" or perfect all three—healing human illness, accelerating plant growth, and turning "sick" (base) metals into "healthy" (noble) gold.</note> from their infirmities. One can hardly deny that this is possible, since this **universal spirit**—being the soul of Nature and the base of all compounds—is perfectly analogous to them, just as it is analogous in its effects and properties to the **Sun**. This is why the Philosophers say that the Sun is its father and the Moon its mother. <note>This is a direct reference to the "Emerald Tablet," a foundational Hermetic text which states of the Stone: "The Sun is its father, the moon its mother, the wind hath carried it in its belly, the earth is its nurse."</note>

One must not confuse the **Hermetic Philosophers** or the true **Alchemists** with the **blowers** <note>original: "souffleurs" — a derogatory term for amateur or fraudulent alchemists who focused solely on the literal, chemical attempt to make gold, named for their constant use of bellows to heat their furnaces</note>. The latter seek to make gold immediately with the materials they employ; whereas the former seek to make a **quintessence** which might serve as a **universal panacea** to heal all the infirmities of the human body, and an **elixir** to **transmute** <term>transmute: the alchemical process of changing one substance, particularly a base metal like lead, into another, like gold</term> imperfect metals into gold. <sig>Part I. Q</sig>

**Ceres** <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture, equivalent to the Greek Demeter, often associated with the earth and fertility</note>, does not differ from what concerns **Osiris** and **Isis**; and all that has been invented with such freedom in the widely circulated fables must be understood in the same manner, much like what is observed in the sacred mysteries, which are said to be a crime to reveal to the common people.

Since everything in **Nature** is engendered from heat and moisture, the Egyptians gave the name of **Osiris** to the former and **Isis** to the latter, and said they were brother and sister, husband and wife. They were always taken to represent **Nature** itself, as we shall see in what follows.

When one wishes not to resort to over-subtleties, it will be easy to discover what the Egyptians, the Greeks, etc., understood by their hieroglyphs and their fables. They had so ingeniously imagined them that they hid several things under the same representation, just as they also understood a single thing through various hieroglyphs and different symbols; the names, the figures, and even the stories varied, but the substance and the object were not different.

It is well known—and one need only open the works of the **Hermetic Philosophers** <note>Alchemists who followed the tradition attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note> to see at first glance—that they have at all times not only followed the method of the Egyptians for treating the **Philosopher's Stone**, but that they have also employed the same hieroglyphs and the same fables in whole or in part, according to how they were inclined. The **Arabs** imitated the Egyptians even more closely, because they translated into their language a great number...

Thus, from them all bodies are generated and nourished, and the nature of things is perfected by the Sun and Moon.

*Diodorus, Book 1, Chapter 1.*

(b) <note>original Latin: "Quæ de Gigantibus & Titanibus apud Græcos cantantur..."</note> What is sung among the Greeks concerning the Giants and Titans, the crimes of Saturn, the struggle of Python with Apollo, the exiles of Bacchus, and the wanderings of **Ceres** <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture, equivalent to the Greek Demeter</note>, is not far removed from the fate of Osiris and Isis and other similar things which have been freely invented by men. The same reasoning applies to those things which are performed secretly in the mystic rites, which it is said to be a crime to reveal to the common people or to be seen by them.
*Plutarch, On Isis.*

When one wishes not to resort to subtleties, it will be easy to discover what the **Egyptians**, the **Greeks**, etc., understood by their **hieroglyphs** and their fables. They had so ingeniously imagined them that they hid several things under the same representation, just as they also understood only one and the same thing by various hieroglyphs and various **symbols**; the names, the figures, even the stories were varied, but the substance and the object were not different.

# CHAPTER ONE.

## *On the Hieroglyphs of the Egyptians.*

WHEN one takes the fables of Egypt literally, and explains them as being about the Divinity, nothing is more bizarre, nothing more ridiculous, and nothing more extravagant. <term>Antiquarians: Early scholars who studied ancient artifacts and manuscripts before the formalization of modern archaeology</term> have commonly followed this system in their explanations of the monuments that remain to us. I admit that these are very often marks of the superstition which prevailed among the people in the times after those in which <term>Hermes: Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom many alchemical and philosophical texts are attributed</term> devised the hieroglyphs; but to unveil what is obscure about them, it is necessarily required to go back to their institution, and to become acquainted with the intention of those who invented them. Neither the ideas that the common people attached to them, nor even those held by Greek or Latin Authors—though they were very learned in other matters—should serve as our guide on these occasions. If they only frequented the common people, they could only have had popular ideas in this regard. One must be certain that they had been initiated into the mysteries of *Osiris*, *Isis*, etc., and instructed by the Priests to whom the understanding of these hieroglyphs had been entrusted. Hermes says more than once in his dialogue with <term>Asclepius: A major text in the Hermetic tradition, presented as a dialogue between Hermes and his disciple concerning the nature of God and the universe</term> that God cannot be represented by any figure; that one cannot give him a name, because being alone, he has no

The two principles accepted by the Priests of Egypt should be understood only as the two principles—good and evil—of Nature, which are always found mingled within her *compounds* <note>The author uses the term "mixtes," referring to substances formed by the chemical union of different elements.</note>, and which contribute to their composition; this is why they said that *Osiris* and *Typhon* were brothers, and that the latter was always at war with the former. *Osiris* was the good principle, or the *radical humor* <term>Radical humor: In early natural philosophy, this was the vital fluid or "innate moisture" believed to be the essential fuel for life and the structural integrity of matter.</term>*, the base of the compound, and the pure and homogeneous part*; *Typhon* was the *evil principle, or the heterogeneous and accidental parts, and the principle of destruction and death*, just as *Osiris* was that of *life and preservation*.

The two serpents of the monument in question represent, in truth, two principles, but they are the two principles that Nature employs in the production of individuals: by analogy, they are called *one male and the other female*. Let us bring together all the symbolic parts of this monument: the relationship they have with one another will reveal this particular intention to us.

The person who commissioned this monument is named *Herrennuleius Hermès*, and he wears a long robe like the Philosophers; there is, therefore, a strong appearance that this Herrennuleius was one of those scholars initiated into the Hermetic mysteries (which is designated by his surname of Hermès), who, as I said previously, being instructed in these mysteries, took the name of Adris or Hermès. Indeed, a considerable part of Egypt, the Thebaid <note>The region of Upper Egypt, centered around the ancient city of Thebes.</note>, says Plutarch, recognized no mortal God, but rather a God without beginning and immortal, who in the language of the country was called *Cneph*, and according to Strabo, *Knuphis* <note>Kneph (also Chnuphis or Khnum) was an Egyptian creator deity, often associated with the water and the potter's wheel upon which he fashioned humanity.</note>. Isis and Osiris, around whom almost all Egyptian theology revolves, were—according to the collected opinions of various authors—all the Gods of paganism. Isis, according to them, was Ceres, Juno, the Moon, the Earth, Minerva, Proserpine, Thetis, the Mother of the Gods or Cybele, Venus, Diana, Bellona, Hecate, Rhamnusia, Nature herself: in a word, all the Goddesses. # CHAPTER III.

## *History of Osiris.*

Osiris and Isis, having become husband and wife, devoted all their care to making their subjects happy. As they lived in a perfect union, they worked toward this in concert; they applied themselves to civilizing their people, teaching them agriculture, giving them laws, and instructing them in the arts necessary for life (a). They taught them, among other things, the use of tools and mechanics, the manufacturing of weapons, the cultivation of the vine and the olive tree, and the characters of writing with which **Mercury**, **Hermes**, or **Thoth** <note>Thaut in the original French; the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing.</note> had instructed them. 

Isis built in honor of her parents **Jupiter** and **Juno** a Temple famous for its grandeur and magnificence. She had two other small ones of gold constructed, one in honor of the celestial Jupiter, the other smaller in honor of the terrestrial Jupiter, or the King her father, whom some have called **Ammon** <note>The Greek and Roman authors frequently identified the Egyptian god Amun with Jupiter.</note>. **Vulcan** <note>Likely the Egyptian god Ptah, the divine craftsman, whom the Greeks identified with Hephaestus and the Romans with Vulcan.</note> was too commendable to be forgotten: he also had a superb Temple, and every God, continues **Diodorus**, had his Temple, his cult, his Priests, and his sacrifices. Isis and Osiris also instructed their subjects in the veneration they should have...

In the Thebaid <note>The region of Upper Egypt surrounding the ancient city of Thebes.</note>, one saw craftsmen working in all kinds of metals. Some forged weapons for hunting beasts; others made the instruments and tools suitable for the cultivation of the land and for other arts; Goldsmiths made small Temples of gold and placed statues of the Gods within them made of the same metal. The Egyptians even claim, adds our Author <note>Likely Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian whom the author is summarizing.</note>, that Osiris particularly honored and revered Hermes <note>The Egyptian god Thoth, whom the Greeks identified with Hermes and the Romans with Mercury.</note> as the inventor of many things useful to life. It is Hermes, they say, who first showed men the manner of setting down their thoughts in writing and putting their expressions in order, so that a continuous discourse resulted. He gave suitable names to many things; he instituted the ceremonies that were to be observed in the worship of each God. He observed the course of the stars, invented music, various physical exercises, arithmetic, medicine, the art of metals, and the three-stringed lyre; he regulated the three tones of the voice: the high pitch taken from Summer; the low pitch taken from Winter, and the middle pitch from Spring. This same figure taught the Greeks the manner of interpreting terms, from which they gave him the name Hermes, which means "interpreter" <note>original: "Hermès qui signifie interprete." The author notes the Greek etymology linking the god's name to the word for interpretation, *hermeneia*.</note>. Finally, all those who in the time of Osiris made use of the sacred letters <note>The term for hieroglyphics.</note> learned them from Mercury.

Osiris, having thus arranged everything with wisdom and rendered his states flourishing, conceived the design of making the entire Universe a participant in the same good- <note>The original French text ends on the catchword "bon-", likely completing the word "bonheur" (happiness or prosperity) on the following page.</note>

Osiris then departed, and care is taken to note that he paid particular attention to the maintenance of his hair until his return. He made his way through Ethiopia, where he found Satyrs <note>In historical texts of this era, "Satyrs" often referred to long-haired monkeys or specific forest-dwelling tribes rather than the goat-men of myth.</note> whose hair reached down to their waists. Since he greatly loved music and dance, he took a large number of musicians with him; but one particularly noted nine young girls under the guidance of Apollo, whom the Greeks called the nine Muses, and said that Apollo had been their master, which is why they gave him the name of musician and inventor of music.

At that time, authors say, the Nile—at the rising of the Dog Star Sirius <note>original: "Syrius"</note>, that is to say, at the beginning of the dog days—flooded the greater part of Egypt, and particularly the region over which Prometheus <note>Here, Prometheus is interpreted as a historical governor rather than a Titan stealing fire.</note> presided. This wise Governor, overwhelmed with grief at the sight of the desolation of his country and its inhabitants, wished in despair to take his own life. Hercules fortunately came to the rescue, and did so much through his advice and his labors that he caused the Nile to return to its bed. The rapidity of this river and the depth of its waters caused it to be given the name of *Eagle* <note>The Greek word "Aetos" (Eagle) was an ancient name for the Nile, reflecting its swift, soaring current.</note>.

This great Prince finally left humanity to go enjoy the society of the Gods. Isis and Mercury <note>The author uses the Roman name Mercury for the Egyptian god Thoth, the messenger and scribe of the gods.</note> decreed honors for him, and instituted mysterious ceremonies in the worship to be rendered to him, to give a grand idea of the power of Osiris.

cannot say that by "Vulcan," Diodorus or the 
Egyptians had Cain or Abel in mind. This 
fire, the invention of which is attributed to Vulcan, 
was therefore different from that of our forges, 
even though Vulcan is commonly regarded as the 
God of Blacksmiths. This fire, according to the 
ideas of Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure associated with the origins of alchemy and Egyptian wisdom.</note>...

...was the fire of which the Philosophers make such a great mystery; this fire whose invention, according to **Artephius** <note>A 12th-century writer to whom several influential alchemical treatises are attributed.</note>, requires a man who is skillful, ingenious, and learned in the science of Nature; this fire which must be administered geometrically according to the same **Artephius** and **d'Espagnet** <note>Jean d'Espagnet (1564–1637), a French jurist and alchemist known for his work *Arcanum Hermeticae philosophiae*.</note>; in the manner of a furnace <note>The original term *clibaniquement* refers to the use of a *clibanus*, a small earthen oven or furnace used for controlled heating in alchemy.</note> if we are to believe **Flamel**, and by weight and measure according to the report of **Raymond Lulle** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan polymath; many alchemical texts were attributed to him in the centuries following his death.</note>. One can say of such a fire that it was invented, and not that of our kitchens, which is known to everyone, and which to all appearances has been so since the beginning of the world. The people of Egypt, from whom **Diodorus** had undoubtedly borrowed what he said of **Vulcan**, knew no other fire than the common one; he could therefore only speak of that one. The Priests, the Philosophers instructed by **Hermes** knew this other fire which is the principal agent of the <term>Sacerdotal Art</term> <note>The "Priestly Art," a term used here for alchemy, implying its sacred and secretive nature.</note> or Hermetic Art; but they were very careful to avoid explaining themselves on its subject, because it was part of the secret entrusted to them. **Vulcan** was this very fire personified by them, and was indeed found by this means to be the grandfather of **Osiris**, or of the fire hidden in the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term>, which **d'Espagnet** calls the <term>mine of fire</term>.

Here then is Osiris as the son of Saturn. It is no less easy to explain the opinion of those who make him the son of Jupiter, and here is how: when the black color vanishes, the matter passes through gray before arriving at white; & the Philosophers gave the name of Jupiter to this gray color. If one reflects a little seriously on what I have just said, one will find no embarrassment nor difficulties in conceiving how Osiris & Isis could be brother & sister, husband & wife, children of Saturn, children of Vulcan, or children of Jupiter; or even how Osiris could have been the father of Isis, since Osiris, being the fire...

In two words: the Egyptians understood by Isis and Osiris both the volatile substance and the fixed substance of the matter of the <term>Work</term> <note>The "Work" (or *Magnum Opus*) refers to the multi-stage process of creating the Philosophers' Stone.</note>, as well as the white and red colors that it assumes during the operations <note>In alchemy, these stages are known as the *Albedo* (whiteness) and *Rubedo* (redness), representing the final stages of purification and perfection.</note>.

These explanations, someone might say, do not agree at all with the fable that makes Vulcan the son of Jupiter and Juno, and who, consequently, could not be the father of Saturn. I respond to this that these contradictions are merely apparent; one will be convinced of this once they have read the chapter concerning Vulcan in particular, to which I refer the reader so that I may return to Osiris and his expedition.

At the mere telling of this story, there is no sensible man who would not recognize it as a fiction. To form the plan of going out to conquer the whole earth, assembling for that purpose an army composed of men and women, of satyrs, of musicians, and of female dancers; to take it into one’s head to teach men what they already knew—this is already not very well-conceived. But to suppose that a King with an army of this kind traveled through Africa, Asia, and Europe to their furthest ends; that there was not even a single place where he had not been, according to this inscription:

> *I am the eldest son of Saturn, sprung from an illustrious stem and noble blood; cousin of the day: there is no place where I have not been, and I have liberally spread my benefits over all of humankind (a).*

The fact is not plausible, and one would not understand how the Abbé Banier <margin>(a) Mythology, Vol. I.</margin> <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741) was a French cleric who argued that myths were actually distorted accounts of historical events.</note> could have recounted it with such cold blood, if one did not know that he willingly adopts, without much critique, everything favorable to his "system," and even what is reported by authors of whom he says, in more than one place, that one should not make much account.

It is at least useless to resort to the expedition of Osiris to determine the time when land cultivation began in Attica <note>The historical region surrounding Athens, Greece.</note>, and other countries of Asia and Europe. The Holy Scriptures, the oldest and truest book of all history, teach us that agriculture was known even before the Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note> itself. Without pointing out the falsity and ridicule of such a story when taken literally, it suffices to present it to a man somewhat versed in reading the <term>Hermetic Philosophers</term> <note>Alchemists who followed the tradition of Hermes Trismegistus, seeking the secrets of the transmutation of matter.</note>, for him to decide at the first telling that it is a palpable symbol of their work. This circle must distribute the water onto the ground by weight, by measure, and in geometric proportion (a). It is therefore necessary to raise dikes, either to force the river back into its bed—as Hercules did in the territory of Prometheus—or to prevent it from flooding, as Osiris did in Ethiopia.

The author of the mythic history of Osiris forgot nothing that was necessary to provide a symbolic idea of both the components of the work, the required operations, and the demonstrative signs. He first notes that during Osiris's stay in Ethiopia, the Nile overflowed, and that this Prince had dikes raised to protect the country from the damage that its flooding would have caused. By this, the author intended to signify the <term>resolution</term> <note>The process of dissolving a solid substance into a liquid state.</note> of matter into water, just as by the flooding of the Nile in Egypt, in whose territory Prometheus was King or Governor. The artist of the <term>Great Work</term> <note>The *Magnum Opus*, the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> must note that Ethiopia was not flooded, while the government of Prometheus was. This is because the part of the earthly matter that putrefies and blackens floats upon the dissolution; whereas the <term>fixed</term> <note>In alchemy, "fixed" refers to substances that are stable and do not evaporate when heated.</note> part, which contains the innate fire that Prometheus stole from heaven to make...

this institution belongs to **Hermes** alone, since there is every appearance that he was the inventor both of the history of **Isis** and **Osiris**, and of the mysterious cult that was rendered to them in **Egypt**. But what was the use of this mystery, if it were only a matter of recounting a real history and instituting ceremonies to recall its memory? A simple narrative of facts, festivals, and triumphs would have more than sufficed to immortalize both. It would have been much more natural to recall their memory through representations taken from the core of the thing itself. Since the intention was for all the people to be instructed, everything should have been placed within their reach, rather than inventing **hieroglyphs** to which only the **Priests** would have the key. This mystery, then, must lead one to suspect some secret hidden beneath these hieroglyphs, which was unveiled only to the initiated, or to those whom one wished to initiate into the <term>Sacerdotal Art</term> <note>The "priestly art," a common synonym for alchemy, implying it is a sacred science known only to the elite.</note>.

The two works which are the object of this Art are comprised, the first in the expedition of **Osiris**; the second in his death and his apotheosis. By the first, one makes the **stone**; by the second, one forms the **elixir**. Osiris, in his journey, traversed **Ethiopia**, then the **Indies**, **Europe**, and returned to Egypt by the **Red Sea** <note>Alchemists often used geographical names to represent color stages: Ethiopia for black (*nigredo*), and the Red Sea for the final red stage (*rubedo*).</note>, to enjoy the glory he had acquired; but there he found death. It is as if one were to say: in the first <term>work</term> <note>The primary stage of the alchemical process.</note>, the matter passes first through the color **black**, then through various colors—the **gray** and the **white**—and finally the **red** occurs, which is the perfection of the first work, and that of the stone or of <term>Philosophical sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of matter, which must be purified to reach perfection.</note>.

Many people, adds Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note>, think that the bodies of these Gods are not in the places where the public is told they are; but that they were placed on the mountains of Egypt & Ethiopia, near the island called the *gates of the Nile*, because of the field consecrated to these Gods. Some monuments favor this opinion; in this island one sees a Mausoleum erected in honor of Osiris, and every day the Priests of this place fill three hundred and sixty urns with milk, and recall the mourning for the death of this King and this Queen, by giving them the titles of God and Goddess. This is why no stranger is permitted to land on this island. The inhabitants of Thebes, which is considered the oldest city in Egypt, regard as the greatest oath that which they make by Osiris who dwells in the clouds; claiming to have in their possession all the members of this King's body that Isis had collected. They count more than ten thousand years, some say nearly twenty-three thousand, from the reign of Osiris and Isis until that of Alexander of Macedon <note>Alexander the Great, who conquered Egypt in 332 BCE.</note>, who built a city in Egypt in his name.

Plutarch (a) teaches us in what manner Typhon <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, the brother and murderer of Osiris.</note> caused Osiris to lose his life. Typhon, he says, having invited him to a superb feast, proposed after the meal to the guests to measure themselves in a chest of exquisite workmanship, promising to give it to whoever would be of the same size.

*Isis*, informed of the tragic end of her husband, set out to search for his body; and having learned that it was in Phoenicia <note>A region in the Levant, corresponding to modern-day Lebanon.</note>, hidden under a tamarisk tree where the waves had cast it, she went to the Court of Byblos, where she entered the service of *Astarte* <note>A Phoenician goddess, often identified by the Greeks with Aphrodite or Hera.</note>, to have a better opportunity to discover it. She finally found it, and made such great lamentations that the son of the King of Byblos died of grief; this so deeply moved the King, his father, that he permitted *Isis* to take the body away and return to Egypt. *Typhon* <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, the brother and murderer of Osiris.</note>, informed of the mourning of his sister-in-law, seized the chest, opened it, tore the body of *Osiris* into pieces, and had the limbs carried to different parts of Egypt. *Isis* carefully gathered these scattered members, enclosed them in coffins, and consecrated the representation of the parts she could not find <note>According to tradition, the phallus was lost in the Nile and eaten by fish; Isis created a ritual image of it to complete his body.</note>. Finally, after having shed many tears, she had him buried at Abydos <note>One of the most important archaeological sites of ancient Egypt, considered the gateway to the underworld.</note>, a city located to the west of the Nile. As for the fact that the Ancients place the tomb of *Osiris* in other locations, it is because *Isis* built one for each part of her husband's body, in the very place where she had found it.

I have only reported this according to *Plutarch* <note>Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus (c. 46–119 AD), a Greek philosopher whose work "On Isis and Osiris" is the primary source for this myth.</note>, to show that authors agree on the fundamentals, even if they vary on the details.    Let us honestly admit: even if Holy Scripture and the Historians did not convince us of the falsehood of the Egyptians' chronological calculations, does the rest of this story have any air of plausibility? Is it likely that a Queen as illustrious and well-known as *Isis* would go into service for a neighboring King? That the son of this King should die of grief upon seeing her lament over the body of her lost husband? That she finally finds him under a tamarisk tree, and carries him back to Egypt, and so on? Such stories do not deserve to be refuted; their absurdity is so palpable that it is surprising Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman historian (c. 46 – 119 AD) who wrote the primary surviving account of the Isis and Osiris myth.</note> deigned to preserve it for us, and even more astonishing that learned Authors uphold it.

### FABLES

Since the chronology of the Kings of Egypt is not the focus of this work, I leave it to others to resolve these chronological difficulties. I return instead to Isis, viewed as the general principle of Nature and the material principle of <term>the Hermetic art</term> <note>The "Hermetic art" refers to alchemy, named after the mythical figure Hermes Trismegistus.</note>.

The portrait of Isis that we have provided based on Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), a Roman writer whose work *The Golden Ass* contains a famous description of an initiate's vision of Isis.</note> is an allegory of the "Great Work," <note>The alchemical process of transforming base matter into a perfected state, often called the *Magnum Opus*.</note> clear to those who have carefully read the texts on the subject. Her crown and the colors of her clothing symbolize both general and specific concepts. *Isis* was regarded as the Moon, the Earth, and Nature herself. Her crown, formed by a globe as brilliant as the Moon, announces her to all. The two serpents supporting this globe are the same as those we discussed in the first chapter of this book when explaining the monument of A. Herennuleius Hermes <note>An ancient Roman funerary monument often used by scholars of this era to interpret Egyptian and Greek mysteries.</note>. The globe is also the same thing as the egg from that same monument. The two ears of grain emerging from it signify that the matter used in the Hermetic art is the same as that which Nature employs to make everything in the Universe grow. Are not the colors that appear in this matter during the alchemical operations explicitly named in the description of Isis's garments? A cymar <note>A light, loose-fitting robe or undergarment.</note> or long robe, striking in its deep blackness—<note>original: "palla nigerrima splendescens atrô nitore"</note> *a very black cloak, shining with a dark luster*—covers Isis's body so completely that it only allows a glimpse at the top of another robe made of fine linen, which is first white, then saffron, and finally the color of fire. <note>original: "Multicolor bysso tenui pertexta, nunc albo can-"</note> *Woven of fine linen in many colors, now with a white [glow...]*

One might perhaps object to me that this black robe is the symbol of the night; and that the matter is sufficiently indicated by the crescent of the Moon placed in the middle with the stars with which it is entirely strewn; but the other accompaniments do not suit this interpretation at all. It is not surprising that a crescent was placed on Isis's robe, since she was taken for the Moon; but as night prevents one from distinguishing the color of objects, Apuleius would have spoken quite inappropriately if he had said that the four colors of Isis’s garment were distinguishable, and that each in particular cast such a great brilliance that he was dazzled by it. Isis was usually represented not only holding a **sistrum** <term>sistrum: an ancient Egyptian percussion instrument used in religious ceremonies, consisting of a metal frame with jingling rods</term>, but with a pail, or other vessel in her hand, or beside her, to signify that she could do nothing without the **mercurial water**, or the mercury that had been given to her for counsel. She is the earth or the *laton* <term>laton: an alchemical term for the base, impure "body" of matter before it has been purified into "white" or "gold" stages</term> of the Philosophers; but the *laton* can do nothing by itself, they say, if it is not purified and whitened by the **azoth** <term>azoth: considered the "universal solvent" or essential transformative agent in alchemy, often personified as mercury</term> or the mercurial water. For the same reason, Isis was very often represented with a pitcher on her head. Often also with a **horn of plenty** in her hand, to signify Nature in general, which provides everything abundantly, and in particular the source of happiness, health, and wealth, which is found in the **Hermetic work** <note>The "Hermetic work" or "Great Work" is the alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone, believed to grant both wealth and health.</note>. In Greek monuments (a) she is sometimes seen surrounded by a serpent, or accompanied by this reptile, because the serpent was the symbol of **Asclepius** <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>, the God of Medicine, whose invention the Egyptians attributed to Isis. But we have more reason to regard her as the very matter of **Philosophical or Universal Medicine**, which the Priests of Egypt used to cure all sorts of diseases, without the people knowing how (b).

> “Nature contains within herself **Philosophy**, and the science of the **seven liberal arts**; she contains all geometric forms and their proportions; she concludes all things through arithmetic calculation, by the equality of a certain number, and by a reasoned and rhetorical knowledge, she leads the intellect from **potentiality into act** <note>A concept from Scholastic philosophy referring to the transition from a thing's potential to its actual realization.</note>.”

This is how **Mercury** was the interpreter of everything, and served as counsel to **Isis**. She could do nothing without Mercury, because he is the base of the work, and without him nothing can be done. One cannot reasonably attribute the invention of everything to Mercury or **Hermes** in any other sense, since it is known that the arts were known before the **Deluge** <note>The Great Flood; alchemists often argued that their "Hermetic" knowledge survived from a time before the biblical flood.</note>; and after the Deluge, the **Tower of Babel** is new proof of this.

Isis, according to **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE whose works on Egypt were frequently cited by alchemists.</note>, built temples entirely of gold—**golden shrines** <note>original: *delubra aurea*</note>—in honor of **Jupiter** and the other Gods. In what place in the world, and in what century does history teach us that even a single one of such a kind was ever erected? Never was mined gold so common as it is today, and despite this abundance, what people could provide for such a thing? Was it not intended to be said that these Temples were of the same nature as the Gods they contained? And is it not to be believed that they were none other than **Hermetic Temples** and Gods; that is to say, the **aurific matter** <term>Aurific matter: The gold-making substance or the "philosophical gold" used to achieve the final stage of the transmutation.</term> and the colors of the work that Isis indeed built, since she is the matter itself? For this same reason, it is said that Isis held artists in gold and in other metals in infinite regard. She

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As for the Chronology of the Egyptians, it is equally mysterious. They do not appear to agree among themselves—not because they actually disagree, but because they wished to hide and complicate the matter on purpose; and not, as many ignorant people claim, because they wanted to establish the eternity of the world. It is the same with them as it has been with the Adepts <term>Adepts: Masters of the alchemical secrets who have successfully created the Philosopher's Stone.</term> at all times, because the latter have always followed the paths of the former.
