## CHAPTER V.

### *History of Horus.*

SEVERAL Authors have confused Horus or Orus with Harpocrates <note>Harpocrates was the Greek adaptation of the Egyptian deity "Horus-the-Child." He is often depicted with a finger to his lips, which Greeks interpreted as a symbol of silence and secrets.</note>; but I will not discuss here the reasons which may have led them to do so. The most accepted view is that Horus was the son of Osiris and Isis, and the last of the Gods of Egypt—not that he was last in merit, but in the establishment of his worship, and because he is in fact the last of the chemical Gods <note>original: "Dieux chymiques"</note> being Hermetic gold <term>Hermetic gold: Not literal currency, but the "Philosophical Gold" or the perfected Philosopher's Stone, which represents the successful conclusion of the alchemical process.</term>, or the result of the Work. It is this Horus or Apollo for whom Osiris undertook such a great journey, and endured so many labors and hardships. He is the treasure of the Philosophers, the Priests, and the Kings of Egypt; the Philosophical child born of Isis and Osiris, or if one prefers, Apollo born of Jupiter and Latona <note>Latona is the Latin name for the Greek Leto, mother of the sun-god Apollo.</note>. But some Authors, it will be said, have regarded Apollo, Osiris, and Isis as children of Jupiter and Juno; Apollo cannot, therefore, be the son of Isis and Osiris. Some Authors even say that the Sun was the first King of Egypt, then Vulcan, then Saturn, and finally Osiris and Horus. All this,

I admit, it could cause embarrassment, & present insurmountable difficulties in a historical system; but regarding the Hermetic Work <note>The "Hermetic Work" or "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) refers to the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> there are none. This is new proof that the Work was the object of all these fictions. The agent & the patient <note>In alchemy, the "agent" is the active, masculine force, and the "patient" is the passive, feminine matter it acts upon.</note> in the work being homogeneous <note>original: "homogênes"</note>, they unite to produce a third similar to them, proceeding from both; the Sun & the Moon are its father & mother, says Hermes <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy is attributed.</note>, & the other Philosophers after him. These names of Sun & Moon given to many things cause an ambiguity, which occasions all these difficulties; it is from this source that all the qualities of father, mother, son, daughter, grandparent, brother, sister, uncle, husband & wife have emerged; & so many other similar names, which serve to explain the alleged incests, & the adulteries so often repeated in ancient Fables. To explain these expressions of the <term>Philosophers</term><note>In alchemical texts, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists themselves, practitioners of the "Hermetic Philosophy."</note>; one must marry the *mother* with the *son*. That is to say, after its *first coction* <note>A term for "cooking" or heating a substance to mature it.</note> it must be mixed with the *raw matter* from which it came, and cooked again until they are reunited and become one. During this operation the *raw matter dissolves and putrefies the digested matter*: it is *the mother who kills her child*, and places him in her womb to *be reborn and resurrected*. During this dissolution the *Titans kill Horus*, and his mother then *brings him back from death to life*. The son then, less affectionate toward his mother than she was toward him, say the Philosophers (a), *puts his mother to death and reigns in her place*. That is to say, that the *fixed, or Horus, fixes the volatile, or Isis*, who had *volatilized* him; for *to kill, to bind, to close, to bury, to congeal, to coagulate, or to fix* are synonymous terms in the language of the Philosophers; just as *to give life, to resuscitate, to open, to unbind, to travel* signify the same thing as *to volatilize*.

*Isis & Osiris* are therefore rightly considered the principal Gods of Egypt along with *Horus* who in effect reigns last, since he is the result of the entire *Priestly Art* <note>Another name for alchemy, implying its sacred and secret nature.</note>. This is perhaps what caused some to confuse him with *Harpocrates, God of secrecy*, because the object of this secret was none other than *Horus*, whom one also had reason to call the *Sun or Apollo*, since he is the *Sun or the Apollo of the Philosophers*. If Antiquarians had studied *Hermetic Philosophy*—

His mouth exhaled nothing but flames; his eyes were like glowing coals, and with a voice more terrible than thunder, he would sometimes bellow like a bull, sometimes roar like a lion, and at other times bark like a dog. Such was this Typhon, formidable even to the Gods themselves, who dared to hurl rocks and mountains against Heaven while letting out frightful howls; the Gods were so terrified by him that, no longer believing themselves safe in Heaven, they fled to Egypt and took shelter from the monster’s pursuit by hiding there under the forms of various animals <note>This classical myth was often used by Greek and Roman writers to explain the origins of Egyptian zoomorphism—the practice of depicting gods with animal heads or as animals.</note>.

Scholars have sought to explain what ancient authors said of Typhon through moral, historical, and physical interpretations. The applications made of these theories have sometimes been quite successful; however, it has never been possible for mythologists to explain his fable in its entirety within a single system. His marriage to Echidna <note>Echidna was a monstrous half-woman, half-serpent; she and Typhon are traditionally regarded as the "parents of all monsters" in Greek mythology.</note> made him the father of various monsters worthy of their origin, such as the Gorgon, Cerberus <note>The three-headed hound guarding the entrance to the Underworld.</note>, the Lernaean Hydra, the Sphinx, the eagle that devoured the unfortunate Prometheus, the dragons guarding the Golden Fleece and the Garden of the Hesperides, etc.

# CHAPTER VII.

## *Harpocrates.*

<margin>(a) On Isis & Osiris.</margin>
<margin>(b) The City of God, book 18, chap. 5.</margin>
There is but one sentiment among all Authors regarding Harpocrates being taken as the God of Silence; it is true that in all the monuments where he is represented, his attitude is to carry his finger to his mouth, to indicate, says Plutarch (a), that those men who knew the Gods, in whose temples Harpocrates was placed, must not speak of them rashly. This attitude distinguishes him from all other Gods of Egypt, with whom he often has some connection through the symbols that accompany him. From this comes the fact that many Authors have confused him with **Horus**, and called him the son of **Isis** and **Osiris**. In all the temples of Isis and **Serapis**, one saw another idol carrying a finger to its mouth, and this idol is undoubtedly the one mentioned by St. Augustine (b) following **Varro**, who said there was a law in Egypt forbidding, under pain of death, to say that these Gods had once been men <note>This refers to Euhemerism, the ancient theory that mythological gods were actually historical kings or heroes who were deified by their people.</note>. ### EGYPTIAN AND GREEK.

So many scholars like Saumaise <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), also known as Salmasius, was a renowned French classical scholar known for his immense erudition, though often criticized for overly complex interpretations.</note> have exhausted their learning to produce commentaries that fail to satisfy sensible readers, because they feel that all the meanings presented to them are forced. We must judge in the same way nearly all the ancient authors who speak to us of the worship of the Gods of Egypt. They only speak based on the accounts of the common people, who were not in the know. Even those like Herodotus and Diodorus of Sicily <note>Two of the most famous Greek historians who traveled to Egypt and wrote extensively about its customs and religion.</note>, who had questioned the Priests and speak according to their answers, do not provide us with more clarity. The Priests misled them, just as they misled the people; it is even reported that an Egyptian Priest named Leon <note>Likely referring to Leon of Pella, who is said to have revealed to Alexander that the gods were originally mortal kings—a philosophy now known as Euhemerism.</note> behaved in this manner toward Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, who conquered Egypt in 332 BCE.</note>, who wanted to have the Religion of Egypt explained to him. He replied that the Gods the people worshiped were only ancient Kings of Egypt, mortal men like other men. Alexander believed it as he was told and, it is said, sent word of it to his mother Olympias, recommending that she throw his letter into the fire so that the people of Greece, who worshiped the same Gods, would not be informed of it, and so that the fear of these Gods instilled in them would keep them in order and subordination.

Those who had made the laws for the succession to the throne had, for all the reasons we have deduced, taken the wise precaution of preventing all these disorders by ordering that the Kings be chosen from the number of the Priests, who communicated this secret only to their children, and to others who were likewise Priests like themselves,

When this globe is joined to a cross, it is to show that gold is composed of the four elements so well combined that they do not destroy one another. When the globe is winged, it represents the gold that must be volatilized <note>To turn a solid substance into a vapor or spirit through heating; a key stage in the refining process.</note> to succeed in giving it the transmutative virtue. ## CHAPTER IX.

### Canopus.

**Mythologists** have ventured many physical, astronomical, and moral conjectures regarding the **Canopic jars**; some of them are even quite ingenious. However, one is no more enlightened after such efforts, and everyone has twisted the allegory toward whatever struck their imagination most, without anyone yet hitting the mark that the **Egyptians** intended in the invention and representations of the **God Canopus**. If they had followed my system, they would not have needed to torture their minds so much to guess what this **Pitcher God** <note>original: "Dieu cruche"; Canopus was famously represented as a jar with a human or animal head, which the author interprets as a chemical vessel.</note> could signify. They would have needed only eyes, and they would not have wasted their time in vain over-refinement. If one shows a **Canopic jar** to a **Hermetic Philosopher**, he will not hesitate to say what it is, even if he had never heard of the **Canopus of Egypt**, nor of the **hieroglyphs** with which they are covered; because

## KINGS OF EGYPT,
->AND<-

HISTORY teaches us nothing more certain regarding the first Kings of Egypt than it does about those of Greece and other Nations. Royalty was not hereditary among the Egyptians, according to Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus: a 1st-century BC Greek historian who wrote the *Bibliotheca historica*.</note>. They elected as Kings those who had made themselves distinguished, either by the invention of some useful arts, or by their benefits toward the people. The first of this kind, if we wish to believe the Arabs, was *Hanuch*; the same as *Enoch* son of *Jared*, who was also named *Idris* or *Idaris*, and whom Father Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680): a Jesuit polymath who published extensive, though often speculative, works on Egyptian antiquities.</note> says (a) is the same as Osiris, based on the testimony of Abenephi <note>Abenephi: likely referring to the 10th-century Arab author Ibn Wahshiyya, whose work on ancient scripts was known to European scholars.</note> and some other Arabs. Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> overturns the entire order of this supposed succession; and the resulting confusion creates a labyrinth of difficulties from which it is impossible to escape.

Thus began the reign of men in Egypt, which lasted, according to some, until the 180th <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used by the Greeks for dating; the 180th Olympiad occurred around 60–57 BCE.</note>, the time when Diodorus was in Egypt and when Ptolemy IX, nicknamed Dionysus <note>Ptolemy XII Auletes, who styled himself as a "New Dionysus."</note>, reigned.

Menes <note>The first Pharaoh of the First Dynasty, credited with unifying Egypt.</note> gave the Egyptians written laws, which he claimed to have promulgated by order of Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes, identified here with the Egyptian god Thoth, the patron of scribes and law.</note> as the principle and cause of their happiness. We see that Mercury appears everywhere, whether during the reign of the Gods (which authors claim lasted a little less than eight thousand years, and whose last ruler was Horus), or during the reign of men, which began with Menes. From this, one must conclude—contrary to the opinion of Father Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar famous for his attempts to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> *(a)*—that this Menes cannot be the same as Mithras and Osiris, since the latter was the father of Horus. But let us follow Diodorus. The lineage of Menes produced 52 Kings over 1,040 years. Busiris was elected next, and eight of his descendants succeeded him. The last of these eight, who was also named Busiris, built the city of Thebes, or the City of the Sun. Its perimeter was one hundred and forty <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient unit of distance; 140 stadia is roughly 16 miles or 26 kilometers.</note>; Strabo gives it eighty in length. ...one had regard only for popular practices, which are often nothing more than an unenlightened superstition.

The secret entrusted to the Priests of Egypt did not, therefore, have as its object the worship of the true God; and animal worship was related to this secret. Intimidated by the penalty of death, and knowing moreover the fatal consequences of disclosing this secret, they kept it inviolably. The people, ignorant of the true causes of this so-called animal worship, could only offer frivolous, conjectural, and fabulous reasons for it. It would have been necessary to learn them from those who had been initiated, and they did not say them.

Historians who were not among that number found themselves in the same situation as **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE who wrote extensively about Egypt.</note>. One glimpses only through the clouds of these fabulous traditions a few rays of light that the Priests and Philosophers had allowed to escape. **Horus Apollo** <note>Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs; he interpreted them as purely symbolic and allegorical rather than phonetic.</note> himself followed only popular ideas in the interpretation he gave of Egyptian hieroglyphs. It is not, therefore, to the explanations given by these Authors that we must stick; since it is well known that they were not among the initiates, and that the Priests had not revealed their secret to them.

One must examine only the simple account they give of things, and see if there is a way to find a base upon which all this might turn—an object to which both the animals taken in themselves and the ceremonies of their so-called worship might tend and relate in everything, at least in their primitive institution. the worship was not a cult of **latria** <term>latria: in theology, the supreme worship offered to God alone, distinguished from 'dulia' or the veneration of created beings</term> or a true adoration, but only relative, & ceremonies such as those in use in public festivals, or much like how one gives incense to living persons, or to the figures represented on their tombs. The Priests had, moreover, two plausible reasons for acting thus. Filled with gratitude toward the Creator for a grace so special as that of the knowledge of the **Sacerdotal Art** <note>Also known as the "Sacred Art," a synonym for alchemy used by those who believed it was a secret science revealed by God to priests.</note>, they wished not only to offer Him particular thanksgivings for it; but they also wished to engage the people to join theirs to it, since they profited from this grace, though without knowing it, through the advantages they drew from the productions of the **Hermetic Art** <term>Hermetic Art: The practice of alchemy, traditionally attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</term>. In consequence, there was presented to this people, who are guided hardly at all except by the senses, the most useful & necessary animal, to engage them to think of the Creator & to have recourse to Him, by giving them occasion to reflect upon His benefits. They could not see God. Occupied entirely with earthly things, they needed a sensible object which recalled Him to them constantly, & particularly at certain times—that is to say, on the days of festivals & pageantry instituted for that purpose. Just as the **Bull** was the symbol of the **Philosophical chaos** <term>Philosophical chaos: Also known as the "First Matter," this refers to the raw, unrefined substance used at the beginning of the alchemical Great Work.</term>, so too the other animals signified the various qualities of the matter—such as its fixity, its volatility, its **ponticity** <term>Ponticity: An archaic chemical term referring to a sharp, astringent, or acidic quality of a substance.</term>, its dissolving and devouring power, its varied colors following the different stages of the work, and its properties relative to the elements and the nature of these animals. The common people, having seen them sculpted or painted alongside **Osiris**, **Apis**, **Isis**, **Typhon**, **Horus**, etc., began at first to hold only a certain respect for them relative to the presumed Gods near whom they saw them. This respect gradually strengthened; superstition played its part, and it was believed that they deserved a particular cult, just as **Apis** had his own. They saw no more difficulty, and found no more extravagance, in worshipping a **Ram** than in offering cult to an **Ox**; the **Lion** was worth as much as the Ram, so a cult was decreed for him, and so on for the others, according to how the people were affected. Superstitions are hatched in secret; they take root to the point that it is almost impossible to destroy them. The Priests are often only informed of them when the remedy would be capable of aggravating the evil. Progress always follows its course, growing stronger and stronger. The successors of **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy and the "Hermetic" arts is attributed.</note> could indeed have disabused the people of Egypt of these errors; they undoubtedly did so: we have proof of this in the response that the High Priest gave to **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great.</note>, in the instructions they gave to the Greeks and the...

### *Of the Dog and the Wolf.*

This animal was consecrated to Mercury because of its fidelity, its vigilance, and its industriousness. It was even the hieroglyphic character of this God; this is why he was represented with a dog’s head, and was called *Anubis*, which led Virgil to say:

# CHAPTER III.

## *Of the Cat or Aelurus <note>The word "Aelurus" is derived from the Greek "ailouros," meaning cat.</note>.*

The Cat was held in great veneration among the Egyptians, because it was consecrated to Isis. This animal was commonly represented on the top of the sistrum <term>Sistrum: A sacred musical rattle used in ancient Egyptian ceremonies, often featuring feline imagery and associated with the goddess Isis or Bastet.</term>, an instrument that one often sees in the hand of this Goddess. When a Cat died, the Egyptians embalmed it, and carried it in great mourning to the city of Bubastis <note>An ancient Egyptian city (Per-Bast) dedicated to the feline goddess Bastet, who was frequently associated or identified with Isis in later periods.</note>, where Isis was particularly revered. It would be surprising if the Cat had not received the same honors as many other animals among a people who had made such a particular study of the nature of things, and the relationships they have, or appear to have, between one another. Isis being the symbol of the Moon, could they choose an animal that had more relationship with this Star, since everyone knows that the shape of the pupil of a Cat's eyes seems to follow the various changes that occur to the Moon, in its waxing or its waning? # CHAPTER IV.

## On the Lion.

THIS animal held one of the highest ranks in the worship that the Egyptians offered to animals. He is considered their King because of his strength, his courage, and his other qualities which are far superior to those of others. The throne of Horus <note>The Egyptian god of the sky and kingship, often depicted as a falcon or a child.</note> had Lions for supports. Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 2nd-century Roman author who wrote "On the Nature of Animals."</note> says that the Egyptians consecrated Lions to Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and the forge, equated here with the Egyptian Ptah.</note>, because this animal is of an ardent nature and full of fire. The idea he gives of Vulcan confirms the one we have previously provided. "They therefore consecrate them to Vulcan (for Vulcan is nothing other than a certain fiery power of the subterranean sun, shining forth in lightning) because they are of a violently ignited nature; and thus, due to the intensity of their internal heat, they look upon external fire with great difficulty" <note>original: "Eos ideo Vulcano consecrant, (est autem Vulcanus nihil aliud, nisi ignea quædam solis subterranei virtus, & fulgure elucescens) quod sint naturæ vehementer ignitæ, atque ideo exteriorem ignem, ob interioris vehementiam ægerrimè intuentur."</note>. This interpretation by Aelian sufficiently shows what the idea of the Egyptian Priests was in consecrating the Lion to Vulcan.

All the explanations I could give relate entirely to this, since we have said that Vulcan was the <term>Philosophical Fire: A metaphorical or secret heat used by alchemists to trigger chemical and spiritual transformations.</term>. The Lion has been taken by almost all Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to Alchemists, seekers of the "Philosopher's Stone."</note> as a symbol of the <term>Hermetic Art: The practice of alchemy, named after Hermes Trismegistus.</term>. There is hardly any animal mentioned so often in the works that treat it, and always in the sense intended by Aelian. We shall have such frequent occasion to speak of it in the following pages that it is useless to expand further on this article here.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *Of the Ichneumon and the Crocodile.*

This animal was regarded as the sworn enemy of the *Crocodile*, and being unable to defeat it by force, being only a species of *Rat* <note>The Ichneumon is the Egyptian mongoose; early naturalists often compared it to a large rat or weasel.</note>, it employed cunning. When the *Crocodile* sleeps, the *Ichneumon* insinuates itself, they say, into its gaping maw, descends into its intestines, and gnaws them. Something quite similar occurs in the operations of the work. The fixed, which at first seems like little, or rather the fire it contains seems to have no strength; for a long time it appears dominated by the vo- <note>The word completes on the next page as "volatile."</note>

<margin>(a) Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 3, Chapter 3.</margin>
The Crocodile was a natural hieroglyph of the <term>Philosophical matter <note>The raw material or "First Matter" used by alchemists to begin their work.</note></term>, composed of water and earth, since this animal is amphibious; thus, we often see it accompanying the figures of *Osiris* and *Isis*. Eusebius (a) says that the Egyptians represented the Sun in a ship as its Pilot, and this ship carried by a Crocodile, to signify, he adds, the movement of the Sun in the "moist" <note>original: "l'humide"; referring to the fluid or watery stage of the alchemical process.</note>; but rather to indicate that the matter of the *Hermetic Art* is the principle or base of gold, or the *Philosophical Sun*. The water in which the Crocodile swims is this mercury, or this matter reduced to water; the ship represents the vessel of Nature, in which the Sun, or the fiery and sulfurous principle, acts as Pilot, because it is he who guides the <term>work <note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus), the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note></term> through its action on the "moist" or the mercury. The Crocodile was also the hieroglyph of Egypt itself, and particularly of Lower Egypt, because that country is marshy.

Nothing, among the hieroglyphs of the Egyptians, is more frequent than the Cynocephalus <note>From the Greek *kyno* (dog) and *kephalē* (head); this refers to the baboon, which was sacred to the Egyptians.</note>, because it was specifically the figure of Anubis or Mercury; for this animal has a body almost similar to that of a man, and a head like that of a dog. St. Augustine (a) makes mention of it, and Thomas of Valois <note>Thomas Waleys, a 14th-century Dominican theologian known for his commentaries.</note> says, in book 3, chapters 12 and 16, that St. Augustine meant to speak of Mercury or Egyptian Hermes by the Cynocephalus. Isidore (b) says that Hermes had a dog's head. Virgil, Ovid, Propertius, Prudentius, and Ammianus all give him the epithet of "barker" <note>original: "abboyeur"; likely referring to the Latin *latrator*, a common Roman literary description of the god Anubis.</note>. The Egyptians had noticed such a connection between the Cynocephalus and the Sun and the Moon, that they often employed it as a symbol of these two celestial bodies, if we are to believe Horapollo <note>An author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs, likely written in the 5th century.</note>. This animal urinated once every hour of the day and the night during the times of the equinoxes (c). It became sad and melancholy during the first two or three days of the Moon, because then, not appearing to our eyes, the animal mourned for it as if the Moon had been stolen from us. ## C H A P T E R VIII.

### Of the Ram.

The nature of the Ram, which was regarded as hot and moist, perfectly matching that of Philosophical mercury <note>In alchemy, a symbolic substance representing the fluid, transformative principle of matter, distinct from common quicksilver.</note>, the Egyptians did not forget to include this animal among their principal hieroglyphs. They subsequently spread the fable of the flight of the Gods into Egypt, where they said that Jupiter hid himself under the form of a Ram; and having consequently represented him with the head of this animal, they gave him the name Amun or Ammon.

->"And the leader of the flock," he said, "becomes Jupiter; whence even now Libyan Ammon is fashioned with curved horns." <note>original: "Duxque gregis, dixit, fit Jupiter, unde recurvis Nunc quoque formatus Lybis est, cum cornibus Ammon."</note><-

Bacchus, it is said, being in Libya with his army, found himself extremely pressed by thirst, and invoked Jupiter for help against such a pressing evil. Jupiter appeared to him in the form of a **Ram**, and led him through the deserts to a fountain where he quenched his thirst, and where, in memory of this event, a Temple was built in honor of Jupiter, under the name of **Jupiter Ammon**, and this God was represented with a Ram's head. What confirms my opinion is that this animal was one of the symbols of Mercury (a). The Ram appears to Bacchus in Libya because "Libya" signifies a stone from which water flows—from the Greek *lips* <note>original: "λιψ"</note>, coming from *leibo* <note>original: "λειβω"</note>, meaning "I distill" <note>The author is using alchemical etymology to link the geography of Libya to the chemical process of distillation.</note>; mercury, whose nature is hot and moist, is formed only by the dissolution of the Philosophical matter into water.

# CHAPTER XI.
## Of the Lotus & the Egyptian Bean.

The **Lotus** is a species of lily that grows in abundance after the flooding of the **Nile** $(a)$. After cutting it, the Egyptians would dry it in the Sun, and from a part of this plant, which resembles a poppy, they made bread.

<margin>(a)</margin> Moreover, they devised other things for the ease of their livelihood. Indeed, when the river is full and has flooded the fields, there arises in the water itself a great abundance of lilies, which the Egyptians call the lotus. . . 
<column-break/>

The design of their creators was not to make knowledge of them public; and by engraving them on their monuments to preserve them for posterity, they acted like the <term>Hermetic Philosophers</term> <note>Followers of the "Hermetic" tradition (based on the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus), who often wrote in alchemical or symbolic codes to hide secrets from the uninitiated.</note>, who write, in a way, only to be understood by those who are familiar with their science, or to provide some rays of light so absorbed, so to speak, in such great obscurity that even the most clear-sighted eyes are only struck by them after long research and deep meditation.

The majority of **Egyptian antiquities** are therefore of a nature that we cannot flatter ourselves with clarifying them perfectly. All the explanations that one might attempt to give to relate them to history will be reduced to conjectures, because everything is permeated by the mystery that reigned in that country; and because in order to base one's reasoning on the sequence of facts, one finds that the first link of the chain that binds them leads to **fables**. It is therefore to these fables that one must have recourse; and by viewing them as such, make every effort to penetrate their true meaning. When one finds a system that develops them naturally, it must be taken as a guide. All those that have been followed until now are recognized as insufficient by all the authors who have written on **Antiquities**. One finds obstacles at every step that cannot be overcome. The design of their founders was not to make knowledge of them public; and in engraving them upon their monuments to preserve them for posterity, they acted like the **Hermetic Philosophers** <note>Practitioners of a tradition of esoteric wisdom and alchemy attributed to Hermes Trismegistus; the author suggests they used symbolic language to hide truths from the uninitiated.</note>, who write in such a way as to be understood only by those who are familiar with their science, or to provide certain sparks of light absorbed, so to speak, in an obscurity so great that even the most clear-sighted eyes are only struck by them after long research and profound meditation.

Most **Egyptian antiquities** are therefore of such a nature that we cannot hope to clarify them perfectly. All the explanations that one might attempt to give in order to reduce them to history will be reduced to **conjectures**, because everything is affected by the **mystery** <note>Referring to the "Ancient Mysteries," secret religious rites and teachings of civilizations like Egypt and Greece.</note> that reigned in that country; and because, to base one's reasoning on the sequence of facts, one finds that the first link in the chain that binds them leads back to **fables**. It is therefore to these fables that one must have recourse; and by viewing them as such, make every effort to penetrate their true meaning. When one finds a system that develops them naturally, one must take it as a guide. All those that have been followed until now are recognized as insufficient by all the authors who have written on Antiquities. One finds there at every step obstacles that cannot be overcome. They are therefore not the true **thread of Ariadne** <note>original: "filets d’Ariadne"; a reference to the mythical thread used to navigate the Labyrinth. ## *Of the Egyptian Colonies.*

It is in the ancient Authors who drew their knowledge from Egypt that one should seek its interpretation; but to understand most of them, one would also need the help of an *Oedipus* <note>A reference to the mythological hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; here, it implies a reader capable of deciphering profound mysteries.</note>, because they wrote allegorically like their masters.

According to *Bochart* <note>original: "Bochard"; Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a French Protestant scholar who sought to trace all pagan mythology to Phoenician and Biblical roots.</note>, *Mercury* <note>The Roman name for the Greek Hermes, often identified with the Egyptian Thoth.</note> is the same as *Canaan* <note>The grandson of Noah.</note>, and according to *Mr. Huet* <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a scholar and bishop who famously argued in his *Demonstratio Evangelica* that most pagan gods were distorted versions of Moses.</note>, he is the same as *Moses*. The most ancient Authors do not even agree among themselves; and besides the contradictions found there, how many baseless assertions do we see, to say nothing more. As for the parallels with which the books of some modern scholars are filled, I would ask if one is permitted to say that *Nadir Shah* <note>original: "Thamas-Kouli-Cham"; a reference to the Persian ruler Nader Shah (1688–1747), often called the Napoleon of Persia.</note> is the same as *Tamerlane* <note>The 14th-century Turco-Mongol conqueror.</note> because one finds much resemblance in the temperament and actions of these two Princes?

# FABLES

...but because they copied the Egyptians, who were the first inventors of <term>Fables</term> <note>In the 18th century, "fables" referred to the whole body of mythology and religious allegories, not just moral stories for children.</note>, and because in drawing a parallel between the ancient Fables of Greece and those of Egypt, one easily notices that they all sprang from the same source. They resemble a traveler who dresses himself in each country he visits, following the fashion that is in use there. The Egyptian works which could have given us some idea of their way of thinking—those of <term>Hermes</term> <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure often identified with the Egyptian god Thoth, the patron of writing and wisdom.</note> and other Philosophers—have been lost to us over time, and we shall forever mourn over the sad ashes of the <term>Library of Alexandria</term> <note>The destruction of this Great Library resulted in the loss of thousands of scrolls containing the collective knowledge of the ancient world.</note>. # BOOK II.

### *On the allegories that have a more tangible relationship to the Hermetic Art.*

<margin>(a) In *Euterpe*, chapter 50. <note>This refers to the second book of Herodotus's *Histories*, titled "Euterpe," which is dedicated to the history and customs of Egypt.</note></margin>
Never was a country more fertile in fables than Greece. Those it had received from Egypt were not enough for it; it invented an infinite number more. The Egyptians properly recognized as Gods only Osiris, Isis, and Horus, but they multiplied their names, and were thereby led to multiply historical fictions as well. From this came twelve principal Gods: Jupiter, Neptune, Mars, Mercury, Vulcan, Apollo, Juno, Vesta, Ceres, Venus, Diana, and Minerva—six male and six female. Only these twelve, regarded as the Great Gods, were represented by golden statues. Later, others were imagined, to whom the name of "demi-gods" was given; these were not known in the time of Herodotus, or at least he makes no mention of them under that title. Their figures were sculpted in wood, or stone, or clay. The same Herodotus says (a) that the Egyptians were the first to establish these twelve names, and that the Greeks received them from them.

This Poet gave this fiction an air of history, which has caused it to be regarded as such even by our modern Mythologists, despite the impossibility they find in reconciling its circumstances. They preferred to fail in their explanations rather than see the hidden and mysterious sense it presents; a sense which the Author himself manifested quite visibly by citing, in the course of this fiction, several others of his works—namely, a *Treatise on Little Stones* <note>Likely the *Lithica*, a poem on the magical and medicinal properties of gems attributed to Orpheus.</note>, and another on *Mercury’s Cave* as the source of all blessings. ...rocks <note>The "wandering rocks" or *Planctae*, often confused with the *Symplegades*, which were said to clash together, crushing ships.</note> could not, in truth, be found in the location marked in Homer; but I would have thought it more appropriate to seek the means to reconcile Abbé Banier with Homer, rather than accusing this Poet of error to elude the difficulties that this passage gave rise to. It is easy to get oneself out of trouble when one has recourse to such resources. Homer undoubtedly had his reasons for placing those wandering rocks there; for most of the errors that one finds in this Poet, and in the other inventors of fables, seem to be placed there with affectation, as if to indicate to posterity that these are pure fictions they are delivering, and not true histories. The places that the Argonauts are made to traverse, the locations where they are made to land, are so distant from the route they should and could have taken; there is even such a manifest impossibility that they followed the one of which Orpheus speaks, that one sees clearly that the intention of this Poet was only to tell a fable.

The difficulties which present themselves in crowds to a Mythologist who wishes to find a true history in this fiction have not discouraged the majority of Scholars. Jason had Aeson for a father, Cretheus for a grandfather, Aeolus for a great-grandfather, and Jupiter <note>Original: *Jupiter*; the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods, Zeus.</note> for a great-great-grandfather. His mother was Polymede, daughter of Autolycus; others say it was Alcimede. This variation is equally suitable for the core of the story, according to my system <note>The author frequently refers to his "system," which involves interpreting these myths through an alchemical lens, where names and genealogies represent specific materials or stages in the "Great Work."</note>.

Tyro, the daughter of Salmoneus, was raised by Cretheus (her father’s brother); she pleased Neptune and by him had Neleus and Pelias. She nevertheless subsequently married her uncle Cretheus, with whom she had three sons: Aeson, Pheres, and Amythaon. Cretheus built the city of Iolcus, making it the capital of his states, and upon his death left the crown to Aeson. Pelias—to whom Cretheus had given no inheritance, as he was not his son—made himself powerful through his intrigues and dethroned Aeson.

Jason, who was born during these events, caused jealousy and anxiety in Pelias, who consequently sought every means to have him killed. But Aeson and his wife, having perceived the usurper's evil designs, carried the young Jason (who was then called Diomedes) <note>According to tradition, Chiron renamed the boy Jason, which means "Healer," to reflect his studies in medicine.</note> to the cave of Chiron. Chiron was the son of Saturn and the nymph Philyra and lived on Mount Pelion; they entrusted him with Jason's education. The Centaur <note>A mythological creature with the upper body of a human and the lower body of a horse.</note> was considered the wisest and most skilled man of his time. There, Jason learned medicine and the arts useful to life.

Pelias did not doubt that Jason would soon win the favor of the People and the Nobility. He became jealous, and seeking only a plausible pretext to rid himself of him, he proposed the conquest of the Golden Fleece, persuaded that Jason would not refuse such a favorable opportunity to acquire glory. Pelias, who knew all the risks involved, thought he would perish there. Jason himself foresaw all the dangers he would have to run. The proposal was nevertheless to his liking, and his great courage did not allow him to refuse it.

He therefore arranged everything for this purpose, and following the advice of Pallas <note>Another name for Athena, the goddess of wisdom and war, who often aided heroes in Greek mythology.</note>, he had a ship constructed, to which he fitted a mast made from a speaking oak from the forest of Dodona <note>Dodona was an ancient sanctuary where a sacred oak tree was said to deliver prophecies through the rustling of its leaves; the wood used for the Argo’s mast retained this prophetic power.</note>. This ship was named the *Ship Argo*; and authors do not agree on the motive that caused it to be so named. Apollonius, Diodorus Siculus, Servius <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil.</note>, and several others claim that this name was given to it because Argus proposed the design; and there is still much variation regarding this Argus: some take him for the same one whom Juno employed to guard Io, the son of Arestor; but Méziriac (a) insists that one should read in Apollonius of Rhodes *son of Alector*, instead of *son of Arestor*. Without entering into the details of the different opinions regarding the naming of this ship, which can be seen in several authors, I will say only that it was built from the wood of Mount Pelion, according to the most common opinion of the Ancients.

Jason was to yoke two Bulls, a gift from Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and metalworking, known as Hephaestus in Greek mythology.</note>, which had feet and horns of bronze <note>original: "airain"</note>, and which breathed whirlwinds of fire and flames from their mouths and nostrils; he had to hitch them to a plow, make them labor in the Field of Mars, and sow the teeth of the Dragon, which he had to have killed beforehand. From the sown teeth of this Dragon, armed men were destined to be born, whom he had to exterminate to the very last, and only then would the Golden Fleece be the reward for his victory.

Jason learned from his lover four ways to succeed. She gave him an ointment with which he anointed his entire body to preserve himself against the venom of the Dragon and the fire of the Bulls. The second was a sleep-inducing composition <note>A magical potion or mixture.</note> that would drowse the Dragon as soon as Jason threw it into its maw. The third was a clear water to extinguish the fire of the Bulls; the fourth, finally, was a medal upon which the Sun and the Moon were represented.

The very next day, Jason, equipped with all of this, presented himself before the Dragon and threw the enchanted composition at it; it grew drowsy, fell asleep, became bloated, and burst. Jason cut off its head and pulled out its teeth. Hardly had he finished when the Bulls came toward him, spurting a rain of fire. He protected himself from it by throwing his clear water at them. They were tamed in an instant; Jason seized them, put them under the yoke, plowed the field, and sowed the Dragon's teeth. Immediately, he saw combatants emerge from them; but, still following the good advice of Medea, he moved away...

Such is a summary of the narration by Orpheus, or, if one prefers, by Onomacritus <note>Onomacritus was a Greek poet of the 6th century BC; many "Orphic" poems are attributed to him rather than the legendary Orpheus.</note>. Father <note>original: "M. l'Abbé"</note> Banier says that the Argonaut <note>OCR "Arnogaute" corrected to "Argonaute."</note> Orpheus had written an account of this voyage in the Phoenician language. I do not see why this mythologist founds this supposition. Orpheus was not Phoenician; he accompanied Greeks, and he wrote for Greeks. Bochart <note>OCR "Brochart" refers to Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar who sought to link all ancient myths to Phoenician origins.</note> undoubtedly provided him with this idea, because he claimed to find the explanation for these fictions in the etymology of Phoenician names. But this system cannot apply to the expedition of the Argonauts, for which all the names are Greek and not Phoenician. If Onomacritus wrote his Greek poem based on the Phoenician poem of Orpheus, and he did not understand that latter language, as Father Banier claims, how could Onomacritus have followed Orpheus? If someone presented me with a Chinese poem that I did not understand, could I translate or imitate it?

The account by Apollonius of Rhodes and that of Valerius Flaccus <note>Two major epic poets: Apollonius (3rd century BC) wrote the Greek "Argonautica," and Valerius Flaccus (1st century AD) wrote the Latin version.</note> differ little from that of Orpheus; but several ancient writers have added circumstances which it is useless to report. ...this voyage, and the fables that have been made about it.

Palaephatus <note>Palaephatus was an ancient Greek writer known for "rationalizing" myths—finding mundane, historical explanations for supernatural stories.</note>, who wished to explain everything according to his own whim, imagined that under the emblem of the Golden Fleece, people intended to speak of a beautiful statue made of that metal, which the mother of Pelops had commissioned, and which Phryxus had carried away with him to Colchis. Suidas <note>The *Suda*, or Suidas, is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> believes that the Golden Fleece was a parchment book that contained the Hermetic Art <term>Hermetic Art: Another name for alchemy, the proto-scientific practice of attempting to transform base metals into gold and discover the secrets of nature.</term> or the secret of making gold. Tollius wished, according to the Abbé Banier, to revive this opinion, and was followed by all the Alchemists. It is true that Jacobus Tollius, in his treatise *Fortuita* <note>original: "Fortuita", a work of philological and alchemical speculation published in 1687.</note>, adopted this sentiment; but the Abbé Banier, in saying that all Alchemists think like him, provides a very convincing proof that he has not read the works of the Hermetic Philosophers. These philosophers regard the fable of the Golden Fleece not as Suidas and Tollius do, but as an allegory of the Great Work <term>Great Work: Known in Latin as the *Magnum Opus*, this was the alchemical term for the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term>, and of what occurs during the course of the operations of this Art. One will be convinced of this if one takes the trouble to read the works of Nicolas Flamel, Augurello, d'Espagnet, Philalethes, etc. Some authors have attempted to give this fable a purely moral meaning; but they have failed. Others, finally, forced by the evidence, have confessed that it was an allegory made to explain the secrets of Nature and the operations of the Hermetic Art; Natalis Comes <note>original: "Noel le Comte", a prominent 16th-century Italian mythographer whose works were standard textbooks for centuries.</note> is of this opinion (a) regarding this specific fiction, without, however, admitting it for others.

Let us briefly examine these different opinions; the Reader will then be able to judge which is the best founded. However different and extravagant the accounts of Authors may be—at least in appearance—regarding both the departure and the return of the Argonauts, some claim to draw a proof of the reality of this expedition from the actual existence of the places they are said to have traversed. Grave Historians have consequently adopted these accounts in whole or in part, such as Hecataeus of Miletus <note>Hecataeus was a pioneering Greek historian and geographer (c. 550 – 476 BC).</note>, Timagetes, Timaeus, etc. Even Strabo <note>Strabo was a famous Greek geographer and historian who lived during the transition from the Roman Republic to the Empire.</note>, who does not put faith in them, mentions the monuments found in the places cited by the Poets. 

But is it not known that a fiction or a novel only has charm insofar as what it puts on the stage approaches the truth? Verisimilitude <note>The quality of appearing to be true or real.</note> causes them to be taken for histories; without this quality, one would see in them only a pure fable, as puerile and insipid as Fairy Tales. 

The real existence of the locations in those countries cannot, moreover, form a proof—not even a presumption—to establish the reality of this history; since Diodorus Siculus <margin>(a)</margin> <note>Diodorus Siculus was a 1st-century BC Greek historian known for his monumental universal history, the *Bibliotheca historica*.</note> positively asserts that most of the places in Greece derived their names from the doctrine of Musaeus, Orpheus <note>Musaeus and Orpheus were legendary poets and mystics of ancient Greece, often associated with the introduction of religious rites.</note>, etc. Now, the doctrine of these Poets was that which they learned from the Priests of Egypt; and it has been seen previously that the doctrine of the Priests of Egypt was the Philosophy of Hermes, or the Sacerdotal Art <term>Sacerdotal Art: The "priestly" or "sacred" art, referring here to the secret knowledge of the Egyptian temples, which the author equates with alchemy.</term>, since called the Hermetic Art <term>Hermetic Art: A traditional term for alchemy, named after Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure who combined the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth.</term>.

But what clearly proves that the history of the Argonauts is not true is that the time, the persons, and their actions, joined with the circumstances reported about them, do not conform at all to the truth. If one pays attention to the time, it will be easy to see how much those who have tried to determine its era have been mistaken. Scholars have found such great difficulty on this subject that they have been unable to agree among themselves. 

Almost all have taken the event of the Trojan War as a fixed point, because Homer in his *Iliad* names some of these warriors, or their sons, or their grandsons as having assisted in this second expedition <note>The "second expedition" refers to the Trojan War, with the Argonautic voyage being the first.</note>. But to have a fixed pole <note>The author uses "pôle fixe" to mean an anchor or a definitive reference point.</note> with which a comparison could be made, the very era of the Trojan War would have had to be determined; which is not the case, as we shall demonstrate in the sixth book. 

These two eras being therefore as uncertain as one another, they cannot serve as reciprocal proofs; and all the reasoning our scholars do as a consequence falls apart on its own. All the erudition displayed on this subject is nothing but dust thrown before our eyes <note>An idiom meaning to deceive or dazzle someone to prevent them from seeing the truth.</note>. Whether *Castor* & *Pollux*, *Philoctetes*, *Euryalus*, *Nestor*, *Ascalaphus*, *Ialmenus* <note>Ialmenus and Ascalaphus were sons of Ares who led the Minyans during the Trojan War.</note> and some others are supposed to have been present at both expeditions, it would at most prove that they were not very far apart; but that would not determine the precise era. Some, following *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD) was a historian whose "Chronicon" attempted to align biblical and pagan history.</note>, place a distance of 96 years between these two events, while others with...

Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609) was a Dutch religious scholar and one of the founders of modern scientific chronology.</note> counts only 20; and the Abbé Banier <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741) was a French cleric known for his work "The Mythology and Fables Explained by History," which attempted to find historical truths behind myths.</note>, to split the difference, allows only about thirty-five years.

Apollodorus <note>A Greek scholar from the 2nd century BCE who wrote about the genealogy of the gods and heroes.</note> places the death of Hercules 53 years before the Trojan War (a). Herodotus counts only about 400 years from Homer to his own time, and nearly 500 from Hercules to Homer, even though he allows for only about a 160-year interval between the latter and the Siege of Troy. Hercules, according to Herodotus, would have died more than 300 years before this siege; one must therefore conclude that Hercules having been among the Argonauts, this expedition must have preceded the fall of Troy by 300 years. But according to this calculation, how could some of the Argonauts, or their sons, have been present at this latter expedition? Helen, who is said to have been its cause, would then have been a quite outdated beauty, and hardly capable of being the prize for the Judgment of Paris <note>The mythological event where the Trojan prince Paris chose Helen as his reward for naming Aphrodite the most beautiful goddess.</note>. This difficulty appeared so hard to resolve that some Ancients, to get out of the predicament, imagined that Helen, as the daughter of Jupiter, was immortal. Since all the Argonauts were the sons of some God, or descended from them, could they not have had the same privilege? Herodotus does indeed speak of this siege of Troy; but the difficulties and objections he raises to himself regarding its reality, and the answers he gives to them, prove well enough that he did not believe it was true. We shall discuss all this in the sixth book.

Another difficulty, no less hard to solve, presents itself regarding Theseus and his mother Aethra. Theseus had abducted Ariadne <note>In Greek mythology, Ariadne was the daughter of King Minos of Crete; she helped Theseus navigate the Labyrinth before he abandoned her on the island of Naxos.</note> and abandoned her on the Island of Naxos, where Bacchus <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine.</note>, having married her, had by her Thoas. Thoas became King of Lemnos and the father of Hypsipyle, who received Jason on that island; Theseus could then have been the grandfather of Hypsipyle, and Aethra her great-grandmother. How could the latter have been found as a slave of Helen during the time of the fall of Troy? It is not possible to reconcile all these facts, even if one admits, along with the Abbé Banier <note>See previous page note regarding Banier's attempts to historicize myth.</note>, only a thirty-five-year distance between these two events.

Theseus was at least thirty years old when he undertook the voyage to the Island of Crete to deliver his homeland from the tribute it paid to Minos <note>Minos demanded a periodic tribute of seven young men and seven young women from Athens to be fed to the Minotaur.</note>; since he had already performed almost all the great deeds attributed to him and had been recognized as King of Athens. Aethra, consequently, must have been at least forty-five. From this voyage of Theseus until that of the Argonauts <note>The legendary band of heroes who sailed with Jason to capture the Golden Fleece.</note>, about forty years must have elapsed; since Thoas was born of Ariadne, grew up, and even reigned on the Island of Lemnos, and had, among other children, Hypsipyle, who was reigning on that island when Jason arrived there. The Authors even say that Jason told Hypsipyle the story of Theseus as a story from the olden days.

A new difficulty: All Antiquity agrees that Theseus, at least fifty years old and already famous for a thousand noble deeds, having heard news of the beauty of Helen, resolved to kidnap her. She must have been

...barrassing <note>Completing the word "embarrassing" from the previous page's "em-".</note> for a Mythologist? But is it capable of satisfying a sensible man, who must naturally think that the Authors of these fictions undoubtedly had their reasons for introducing all these circumstances? Almost all explanations given by Mythologists either rely on nothing or are imagined to evade difficulties.

It is therefore evident that one must regard the account of the conquest of the *Golden Fleece* as an allegory. Let us examine each thing in detail. Who was *Jason*? His name, his education, and his actions announce him well enough. His name signifies *Physician* <note>original: "Médecin"</note>, from the Greek *to heal* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰᾶσθαι"</note> and *healing* <note>original: "ἴασις"</note>. He was placed under the discipline of *Chiron*, the same who also took care of the education of *Hercules* and *Achilles*—two Heroes, one of whom showed himself invincible in the *Trojan* war, and the other made to deliver the earth from the monsters that infected it. Thus *Jason* had two masters, *Chiron* and *Medea*. The first gave him the initial instructions and the theory; the second guided him in the practice through her assiduous advice. Without their help, an *Artist* <term>Artist: In alchemical literature, the "Artist" is the practitioner of the "Great Work," the process of refining base metals into gold or achieving spiritual enlightenment.</term> would never succeed, and would fall from error to error.

...barrassing for a mythologist? But is it capable of satisfying a sensible man, who must naturally think that the authors of these fictions undoubtedly had their reasons for introducing all these circumstances? Almost all the explanations given by mythologists either rest on nothing or are imagined to evade difficulties.

It is therefore evident that the account of the conquest of the Golden Fleece must be regarded as an allegory. Let us examine each thing in particular. Who was Jason? His name, his education, and his actions announce it clearly enough. His name means Physician, derived from the Greek *to heal* and *healing*. <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\pi\grave{o}\ \tau o\tilde{\upsilon}\ \iota\tilde{\alpha}\sigma\theta\alpha\iota$, & $\iota\alpha\sigma\iota\varsigma$." The author is linking the name Jason (Iasōn) to the Greek verb iasthai (to heal).</note> He was placed under the discipline of Chiron, the same who also took care of the education of Hercules and Achilles—two heroes, one of whom showed himself invincible at the Trojan War, and the other made to deliver the earth from the monsters that infested it. Thus Jason had two masters: Chiron and Medea. The first gave him his initial instructions and theory; the second guided him in practice through her constant advice. Without their help, an Artist <note>In alchemical literature, the "Artist" is the practitioner or alchemist attempting the "Great Work" of transmutation.</note> would never succeed and would fall from error into error. The detailed accounts that Bernard Trévisan and Denis Zachaire (a) provide of their own errors <note>Trévisan and Zachaire were famous alchemists who wrote about their many failed attempts and the vast sums of money they lost before allegedly discovering the secret of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> would be capable of making an Artist lose hope of reaching the end of the practice of this Art, if they did not simultaneously provide the necessary warnings to avoid them.

Jason, having taken shelter under the Ship Argo, which was falling apart from old age, was crushed and perished under its ruins. All these things clearly indicate that Orpheus was its builder and its Pilot; that is to say, this Poet declares himself to be the Author of this fiction, and that he placed the Ship among the Stars in order to better preserve its memory for posterity. <header># F A B L E S</header>

He first lands at Lemnos, and why? To make Vulcan favorable to him, it is said. What rapport and what relationship does the God of fire have with Neptune, God of the sea? If the Poet had intended for us to understand that the account he gave us was indeed that of a maritime expedition, would he have fallen into such a gross mistake? He was doubtless not ignorant that it was to the God of the waters that one must address one's vows. But it was Vulcan whom it was necessary to make favorable, because fire is absolutely required; and what fire? A fire of corruption and putrefaction. The Argonauts recognized its effects at Lemnos; there they found women who exhaled a stinking and unbearable odor. Such is the odor of the Philosophical matter <note>The primary substance used by alchemists at the start of their laboratory work.</note>, when it has fallen into putrefaction. All putrefaction being caused by humidity and internal fire acting upon it, one could not signify it better than by women, who, in the Hermetic style <note>The symbolic and coded language used by alchemists to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note>, are its ordinary symbol. Morien <note>Morienus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says (*a*) that the odor of the matter is similar to that of corpses; and some Philosophers have given the matter in this state the name *Asafoetida* <note>original: "Assa fœtida," a resin known for its strong, pungent smell, often used as a metaphor for the "blacker than black" stage of alchemy.</note>. The massacre that these women had carried out on their husbands signifies the dissolution of the fixed by the action of the volatile, commonly designated by women. Volatilization is indicated more particularly in this circumstance of the Argonauts' voyage by Thoas, father of Hypsipyle, which comes from *thoos* <note>original: "θοὸς"</note>, meaning *swift* <note>original: "celer"</note>,

All the names given to the **Harpies** express something volatile and dark, according to Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar known for his work on exotic animals and geography in the Bible.</note>: *Occipetè* <note>original: "Occipetè"; from Greek meaning "swift-flying."</note>, she who flies; *Celeno* <note>original: "Celeno"; from Greek meaning "darkness" or "the dark one."</note>, obscurity or cloud; *Aello* <note>original: "Aello"; from Greek meaning "storm-wind" or "whirlwind."</note>, tempest; from which he concluded that they signified nothing more than locusts. They were the daughters of *Neptune* and the *Earth*; that is to say, of the earth and the mercurial water <term>Mercurial water: A specialized solvent used by alchemists, often associated with the "soul" of the matter.</term> of the Philosophers. It is said the Harpies are the sisters of *Iris*, and with good reason; since *Iris* is nothing other than the colors of the rainbow, which appear on the matter after its putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: The stage where the matter turns black and "dies" before being reborn in new colors.</term>, and when it begins to volatilize.

Phoenix, King of Salmydessus <note>A city on the coast of the Black Sea, in modern-day Turkey.</note>, without informing us from whom this Phoenix descended. It would be quite difficult for Phineus to have lived until the time of the Argonauts, and even for him to have been found in Thrace; for two centuries must have elapsed, according to the calculations of Monsieur l'Abbé Banier <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741) was a French scholar who argued that myths were based on historical events (a perspective called Euhemerism).</note> himself, from the time of Agenor until the Trojan War. Consequently, according to him, Phineus would have been at least 165 years old at that time. If he is said to be the grandson of Agenor through Phoenix, this Mythologist will be no less embarrassed, since he says (a), following Hyginus (b) <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Latin mythographer of the 1st century AD.</note>, that Phoenix settled in Africa while he was searching for his sister Europa. Phineus was blind; this detail was added to signify the blackness, called *night and darkness*, since it is always night for a blind man. The Harpies only tormented him after Neptune had taken away his sight; that is to say, once the mercurial water <term>Mercurial water: A specialized alchemical solvent or "spirit" used to break down substances into their primary components.</term> had brought about putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: The stage of the alchemical process, also called the Nigredo or "Blackness," where the matter decomposes and turns black, signaling the death of the old form before rebirth.</term>. These monsters, symbols of the volatile parts, had wings and the face of a woman to signify their lightness, for according to an Ancient:

> ->What is lighter than smoke? A breeze. What than a breeze? The wind.<-
> ->What than the wind? A woman. What than a woman? Nothing.<-
> <note>original: "Quid levius fumo? flamen. Quid flamine? ventus. / Quid vento? mulier. Quid muliere? nihil."</note>

When it is said that Phineus was a soothsayer, it is because the blackness being the key to the work, it announces success to the Artist <note>In alchemical texts, "the Artist" refers to the practicing alchemist.</note>, who, knowing the theory of the rest of the operations, sees everything that will happen in the future.

Few Philosophers fail to use the allegory of the Dragon: more than sufficient proof of this will be found throughout this work. This Dragon being a fire, according to the expression of *Raymond Lully* <note>A 13th-century polymath and philosopher often associated with alchemical writings.</note>, it is not surprising that the dragon of the **Golden Fleece** was said to breathe fire from its mouth and nostrils. One can only succeed in killing it by throwing a narcotic and sleep-inducing composition into its throat; that is to say, one can only achieve the **putrefaction** <note>The stage of the "Great Work" where the matter turns black and decomposes, essential for its later transformation.</note> of the fixed matter through the help and action of the **mercurial water** <note>A symbolic term for the solvent or "living water" used to dissolve the solid substance.</note>, which seems to extinguish it by dissolving it. It is only by this means that one can pull out its teeth—that is to say, the seed of **Philosophical gold**, which must then be sown.

Each operation being but a repetition of that which preceded it regarding what manifests during the progress, it is easy to explain one when one has an understanding of the other. This one begins, therefore, like the previous one, with putrefaction; the manner of this Dragon's death and the events that accompany it are expressed in the *Testament of Arnaud de Villeneuve* (a) <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>. *D'Espagnet* <note>Jean D'Espagnet, a 17th-century French jurist and alchemist.</note>

Artemidorus of Ephesus refutes this Author, and brings as proof the fact that the Phasis <note>original: "Phasis"; the modern Rioni River in Georgia, which the Greeks believed might connect to a great northern ocean.</note> does not communicate with the Ocean at all. As if such monuments—doubtless imagined based on the accounts themselves, or cited by these Poets because they suited the circumstances they introduced into their fictions—could make possible that which is not.

Orpheus has the Argonauts travel the eastern coasts of Asia, cross the Cimmerian Bosphorus <note>The Strait of Kerch.</note>, the Maeotian Marshes <note>The Sea of Azov.</note>, then a strait—which never existed—through which they entered the Northern Ocean after nine days; from there they arrived at Peuceste Island, known to the pilot Ancaeus; then to that of Circe, then to the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note>, re-entered the Mediterranean, sailed along Sicily, and avoided Scylla and Charybdis through the help of Thetis, who was concerned for the life of Peleus, her husband. They landed in the country of the Phaeacians after being saved from the Sirens by the eloquence of Orpheus; upon leaving there, they were cast onto the Syrtes of Africa <note>The dangerous shallows off the coast of Libya.</note>, from which a Triton protected them in exchange for a tripod. Finally, they reached Cape Malea, and then Thessaly.

Apollonius of Rhodes went even further than Orpheus. The Argonauts, according to him, having remembered that Phineus <note>A blind seer and king who gave the Argonauts directions in exchange for their help in driving away the Harpies.</note> had recommended they return to Greece by a different route than the one they had taken to Colchis—and that this route had been marked out by the Priests of Thebes in Egypt—entered a great river, which failed them. They were forced to carry their vessel for twelve days until they found the sea again, along with Absyrtus, the brother of Medea, who was pursuing them and whom they disposed of by cutting him into pieces. Then the oak of Dodona <note>A famous ancient Greek oracle where the rustling leaves of sacred oak trees were interpreted as the voice of Zeus; the Argo's prow was supposedly made from its wood.</note> delivered an oracle, which predicted to Jason that he would not see his homeland again until he had submitted to the ceremony of expiation <note>A ritual purification intended to cleanse the guilt of a crime, in this case, the murder of Absyrtus.</note> for this murder. Consequently, the Argonauts took the route to Aeaea, where Circe, sister of the King of Colchis <note>original: "Cochos," likely an archaic spelling or error for Colchis.</note> and aunt of Medea, resided. She performed all the ceremonies used in expiations and then sent them on their way.

Their voyage was successful enough for some time; but they were cast onto the Syrtes of Africa <note>The dangerous shallows and sandbanks off the coast of Libya.</note>, from which they escaped only with difficulty, and under the conditions reported by Orpheus.

It is evident that these accounts are entirely false. These Authors are excused by the lack of knowledge regarding geography and navigation, which was not yet sufficiently perfected in those times. But these errors are so blatant and so obvious that Abbé Banier <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741), a French scholar who sought to explain myths as historical events "embellished" by poetry.</note>, along with many other mythologists who admit the truth of this expedition, could not help but...

This learned mythologist <note>Referring to the Abbé Banier, an 18th-century scholar known for "Euhemerism"—the practice of interpreting myths as accounts of actual historical events.</note> also admits that most of these peoples are unknown, and did not even exist in the time of Orpheus or Onomacritus <note>Onomacritus (c. 530–480 BC) was a Greek scholar who is often credited with compiling or forging the poems attributed to the legendary Orpheus.</note>. Unfortunately, Sesostris was not born until long after this alleged expedition, even if one admits the reality of this voyage at the time when this scholar fixes its date. But this difficulty was of no consequence to him. Apollonius, he says, undoubtedly possessed the history of Sesostris, and although it was later than the expedition of the Argonauts, he was able to speak by anticipation of the monuments that this Conqueror left in Colchis. I leave it to the reader to judge the solidity of this proof. The geographical errors for which these poets are criticized are only errors when viewed from a perspective that assumes a true history, but not at all in an allegory of this kind, where everything fits perfectly. The locations that would have been found naturally on the route from Colchis to Greece would not have been suitable for expressing the allegorical ideas of these poets, who, without caring much about conforming to geography, sacrificed its truth for the sake of the truth they had in view. 

In going from Greece to Colchis <note>A region on the eastern coast of the Black Sea, the destination of the Argonauts.</note>, everything was arranged as it should be; Lemnos <note>An Aegean island where the Argonauts encountered a society of women.</note> appeared first, followed by the Cyanean rocks <note>The Symplegades, or "clashing rocks," which stood at the entrance to the Black Sea.</note>, and all the rest; but Phineus <note>A blind prophet who helped the Argonauts.</note> was right to prescribe another route for the return, because the operation symbolized by this return had to be similar to the one symbolized by the voyage to Colchis, and they would not have found a Lemnos upon leaving the Phasis <note>The river in Colchis (modern Rioni) where the Golden Fleece was kept.</note>, nor any Cyanean rocks. The birds of the Island of *Aretias* <note>Also known as the Island of Mars (Ares); these birds were said to drop bronze-pointed feathers like arrows.</note>, which shot deadly feathers from afar at the *Argonauts*, never existed.

Finally, they arrive in *Colchis*; and everything that took place there are fables as extraordinary as they are difficult to explain. (ibid. p. 233.) The enchantress *Medea*, the *Dragon*, and the *Bulls* with bronze feet, the armed men who rise from the earth, the enchanted herbs, the prepared potion, the victory of *Jason*, and his departure with *Medea*; one can only say that all these fables are nothing but a pure play of the *Poets'* imagination.
(ibid. p. 235.)

Let us come to the return of the *Argonauts*. The *Poets* have imagined the murder of *Absyrtus* <note>The brother of Medea; in many versions, she killed him and scattered his limbs to slow her father’s pursuit.</note>. (ibid. p. 238.) The accounts of this return are extravagant. That of *Onomacritus* <note>A Greek priest and poet to whom the "Orphic Argonautica" was often attributed.</note> is not plausible, and that of *Apollonius* <note>Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the most famous version of the Argonaut story.</note> is even less so. (ibid. p. 240.) It is a fiction, p. 241. The *Peoples* cited by these *Authors* are either unknown, did not exist in the time of these *Poets*, or are placed at random. (p. 242.) What occurred at Lake *Tritonis* <note>A legendary lake in Libya where the Argo was said to have been carried across the desert.</note> is a tale upon which one should place little stock. (p. 244.) The history of *Jason* and that of *Medea* are, in the end, mixed with so many fables, which

## C H A P T E R  II.

### *History of the theft of the Golden Apples from the Garden of the Hesperides.*

AFTER the history of the conquest of the Golden Fleece, there is hardly any story that better suits our subject than that of the expedition of Hercules <note>A celebrated hero of Greek mythology, Hercules was tasked with Twelve Labors, the eleventh of which was to steal the golden apples from the Hesperides.</note>, to gain possession of those famous fruits known to so few people that the Authors who have spoken of them have not even agreed on their true name. The ancient Poets gave free rein to their imagination on this subject; and the Historians, who only spoke of it based on these "fathers of fables," after having searched in vain for the location of this Garden, and the name and nature of these fruits, are almost all in contradiction with one another. And how could they have said anything certain about a fact that never truly existed?

<summary>The author transitions from the Argonaut myth to the story of Hercules and the Golden Apples, arguing that efforts to find historical truth in these legends are futile as the events never occurred.</summary>
<keywords>Abbé Banier, Hercules, Golden Apples, Hesperides, myth vs. history, Euhemerism, ancient poets, Garden of the Hesperides</keywords>

--- Page 587 ---
<meta>Continuing from page 494, where the author dismissed Abbé Banier's historical interpretation of the Hesperides' apples, he now argues that most mythologists are mistaken because they ignore the Egyptian origins of Greek allegory.</meta>

<page-num>495</page-num>
<header>EGYPTIAN AND GREEK.</header>

It is pointless to engage in long discussions to favor the views of one over the other, since they are all equally in error in this regard. It is therefore with good reason that we can look upon the explanations of most <term>mythologists</term><note>Scholars who sought to explain the origins and meanings of myths, often through historical or moral lenses.</note> who have wanted to relate everything to history as hollow and chimerical ideas, however ingenious and brilliant they may be, and despite having illustrious supporters. I am doing nothing here but turning back against these mythologists the argument that one of them (a) made against <term>Michael Maier</term><note>Michael Maier (1568–1622) was a German physician and counselor to Rudolf II. He was a famous alchemist who interpreted classical myths as encoded chemical instructions for the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note>; one may judge if I am justified in doing so by the explanations we shall provide hereafter.

We should not judge the first Greek poets in the same way as those who were, so to speak, merely their imitators—whether because they only treated the same subjects, or because they worked on others, but in the style of the former. These first poets, instructed by the **Egyptians**, took the subjects of their poems from that People and disguised them in the Greek fashion, according to the genius of their language and their nation. Struck by the grandeur of the object they had in view, but which they did not wish to reveal to the common people, they applied themselves to treating it through **allegories**, whose <term>marvelous</term><note>In 18th-century literary criticism, "the marvelous" (le merveilleux) referred to the supernatural elements of a story, such as gods, magic, or monsters.</note> nature would excite admiration and surprise, often without any regard for **plausibility**; this was done so that sensible people would not mistake for a real history that which was only a fiction, and so that they would sense, at the same time, that these allegories were based upon something real.
