# FABLES

The Poets who appeared later, and who were ignorant of the perspective of the first poets, saw nothing in their works but the <term>marvelous</term><note>In 18th-century literary theory, "the marvelous" (*le merveilleux*) refers to the supernatural or fantastical elements of a story, such as gods, magic, or monsters, which were expected in epic poetry.</note>. They treated their subjects according to their own genius, and abused the privilege they had to dare anything:

> To painters and poets
> The power to dare whatever they wished has always been equal.
<note>original Latin: "Pictoribus atque Poëtis / Quidlibet audendi semper fuit æqua potestas."</note>
->Horace, *The Art of Poetry*<-

Based on this principle, when they chose subjects for their works that had already been treated, they preserved the essence, but they added or removed circumstances, or made changes according to their fancy. They applied themselves, so to speak, only to exciting admiration and surprise through the "marvelous" they spread throughout, having no other goal than to please. It is therefore not surprising that one finds in their work traits that can be explained by the objective their predecessors had set for themselves. 

But as a subject is susceptible to a thousand different <term>allegories</term><note>Stories where characters or events represent hidden meanings, typically moral, physical, or historical truths.</note>, each Poet treated it in his own way. I do not claim, therefore, that all Fables can be explained by my system, but only the ancient ones, which are based on Egyptian and Phoenician fictions; since it is known that the most ancient Greek Poets drew theirs from there, as it would be easy to prove by making a <term>concordance</term><note>A systematic comparison or cross-reference of different texts to show their points of agreement.</note>, which would clearly show that they all have the same object.

The Fables are therefore not all mere fan-

The one in question here, and almost all those of **Orpheus**, **Homer**, and the most ancient Poets, are <term>allegories</term><note>Stories where characters or events represent hidden meanings, typically moral, physical, or historical truths.</note>, which hide instructions under the veil of genealogy and the alleged actions of the Gods, Goddesses, or their descendants.

When one attempts to reduce the fable of the **Hesperides** to history, one is at a loss for how to determine anything precise. Every historian claims that he should be believed over any other, yet none provides any solid proof for his opinion. They are divided into so many different views that one does not know which to settle on. **Herodotus**, the most ancient of historians and very well-versed in all fables, makes no mention of the Hesperides, nor of many others; undoubtedly because he regarded them as fictions. Since traditions are always purer as they approach their source, he would have been better positioned than other historians to leave us something less doubtful, although he is accused of having been a bit too credulous. Shall we rely on <term>Palæphatus</term><note>An ancient Greek author (c. 4th century BCE) who attempted to provide rational, "historical" explanations for myths, often by claiming they were misunderstandings of mundane events.</note>? **Historians** place it near **Lixus**, a city of **Mauritania** on the borders of **Ethiopia**; some place it at **Tingis** <note>Modern-day Tangier, Morocco.</note>, along with **Pliny** (*a*). Malon". In Ancient Greek, the word "mēlon" (μῆλον) can mean either "apple" or "sheep/small livestock." This latter sentiment approaches the truth a bit more than the others, because it has a more immediate connection to the true sense of the allegory. But finally, since **Historians** can conclude nothing certain from this variety of opinions, they ought therefore to agree that it is a fiction. They have good reason for this, since **Historians** only speak of it following the **Poets**; and even if some historical element were found in them, it is so absorbed by what is pure fiction that it is impossible to disentangle it. The affectation observed in them to make facts seem unlikely must naturally lead one to think that they never intended to preserve for us the memory of truly historical events.

The guardian who watched over the **Golden Apples** is the natural image of the miser: hard and pitiless men who close their eyes neither day nor night, and who, consumed by their foolish passion, refuse to let others touch gold for which they themselves have no use.

**Tzetzes** <note>Joannes Tzetzes (c. 1110–1180), a Byzantine poet and grammarian who preserved much classical lore.</note>, and after him **Vossius** <margin>(*a*) On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry, Book 2, page 384.</margin>, find in this fable the **Sun**, the **Stars**, and all the luminous bodies of the firmament. The **Hesperides** represent the final hours of the day. Their **Garden** is the firmament. The **Golden Apples** are the stars. The **Dragon** is either the horizon—which, except at the equator, cuts the celestial equator at oblique angles—or the **Zodiac**, which extends obliquely from one tropic to the other. **Hercules** is the **Sun**, because his name, coming from <term>Hēras kleos</term> <note>original: "Ἥρας κλέος". Literally "the glory of Hera." In ancient allegorical etymology, Hera was often associated with the air or atmosphere (aēr), thus "the glory of the air."</note>, signifies the glory of the air. When the **Sun** appears on the horizon, it makes the stars disappear; this is **Hercules** carrying away the **Golden Apples**.

When one undertakes to explain a matter, one must ensure that the explanation accounts for all circumstances. However ingenious and brilliant it may be, it lacks foundation and solidity if even a few of these circumstances cannot be made to fit. This is precisely the case for the **Mythologists** and **Historians** regarding the fable in question here, as will be seen hereafter. It would be wrong to blame those who take the trouble to seek ways to explain fables: their motive is highly laudable; **Moralists** work to shape...

The black poplar is the form taken by *Hespera*, because she indicates the color black. <note>In alchemy, the black stage or *nigredo* is the first phase, signifying the "death" or dissolution of the matter.</note> The author of the Fable of *Hercules*’s descent to the underworld also feigned that this Hero found a poplar tree there, whose leaves were black on one side and white on the other, in order to make it understood that the color white succeeds the black. *Apollonius* designated this whiteness through *Aegle* being changed into a willow, because the leaves of this tree are downy and whitish. *Erytheis*, or the red color of the Philosophers' Stone, could hardly have been better indicated than by the elm, whose wood is yellow when it is green, and imperceptibly takes on a reddish color as it dries. This is exactly what happens in the operations of the Work, where the citrine <note>A yellow stage known as *citrinitas*, which historically occurred between the white and red stages.</note> follows the white, and the red follows the citrine, according to the testimony of *Hermes*. Finally, those who have placed *Vesta* among the number of the *Hesperides* had regard for the fiery property of the mercurial water of the Philosophers, which caused them to say: "we wash with fire, and we burn with water." Cadmus; the one who was with the cattle of **Geryon** <note>Geryon was a triple-bodied giant whose cattle were stolen by Heracles as his tenth labor.</note>, of **Cerberus**, the **Sphinx**, the **Chimera**, and so many other monsters, of which we shall speak in their proper places. All these events, however, took place in very different countries and at times very distant from one another. How could the inventors of these fictions have agreed so well, and feigned precisely the same thing in similar circumstances, if they had not had the same object in view? This reason alone should have prompted **Mythologists** <note>Scholars who study and interpret myths.</note> to reflect and determined them to also agree in their explanations. But even if they had wanted to do so, could they have succeeded? The differing sentiments among which they are divided did not allow it. They are too divided among themselves to be able to agree; they combat one another; thus, their opinions cannot sustain themselves; any state divided against itself tends toward its ruin. To know the nature of these monsters, it would have been necessary to know that of their common father. By considering **Typhon** <note>In Greek myth, the deadliest monster; in Hermetic philosophy, he often represents the "volatile" or "sulfurous" principle that must be overcome.</note> as a Prince of **Egypt**, it was not possible to regard him as the father of these monsters, whatever explanation one might imagine. They have therefore been forced to admit that all of this was nothing but fiction. It was enough to read the *Theogony* of **Hesiod** to be convinced of this. The genealogy he provides for **Typhon**, **Echidna**, and their children is not susceptible to any historical explanation, even one that is only slightly plausible.

It is not the same with a **Philosophical** explanation—

In this view, Typhon is seen as an active, violent, sulfurous, fiery, and dissolving spirit, taking the form of an impetuous and poisonous wind that destroys everything. Echidna is recognized as corrupted water mixed with a black, foul-smelling earth, depicted as a Nymph with black eyes. Prometheus was always regarded as the fiery Titan, a friend of the Ocean. He shared a common Altar with Pallas and Vulcan; because his name signifies *foreseeing, judicious* <note>original: "prévoyant, judicieux". The name Prometheus comes from the Greek "pro" (before) and "metheus" (knowledge), meaning forethought.</note>. This suits Pallas, the Goddess of Wisdom and Prudence; and indicates that the fire of Prometheus was the same as that of Vulcan <note>Vulcan, or Hephaestus, is the god of the forge and physical fire; here, the author links intellectual wisdom (Pallas) with the practical application of heat (Vulcan).</note>. As this fable forms an episode, and as it is explained elsewhere in this work, we shall say only a few words about it. This is a central axiom from the *Tabula Smaragdina* or Emerald Tablet, a foundational hermetic text.</note>; this is what caused it to be given the name of "celestial fire." Prometheus is then bound to a rock: is this not as if one were saying that this fire concentrates itself, and attaches itself to the matter which begins to coagulate into stone after the gray color, and that this is done by the operation of the **Mercury of the Philosophers**? <term>The "Mercury of the Philosophers" is not common quicksilver, but a specialized "living" solvent believed to be the essential agent in alchemical transformation.</term> The volatile part, which acts incessantly upon the igneous and fixed part, could it, so to speak, be better designated than by an Eagle, or a Vulture, and this concentrated fire better than by the liver? These birds are predatory and voracious; the liver is, so to speak, the seat of natural fire in animals. The volatile element thus acts until the **Artist** <note>In alchemical literature, "the Artist" refers to the practitioner or alchemist performing the work.</note>, of whom Hercules is the symbol, has killed this Eagle—that is to say, fixed the volatile <note>To "fix the volatile" is to stabilize a substance so it no longer evaporates or changes when subjected to heat.</note>.

These colors which follow one another are the Gods and the Metals of the Philosophers, who gave them the names of the seven Planets <note>Alchemists used "The Seven Planets" as a shorthand for the seven metals: Saturn (lead), Jupiter (tin), Mars (iron), Sol (gold), Venus (copper), Mercury (quicksilver), and Luna (silver).</note>. The first among the principal ones is black, the Lead of the Sages, or Saturn. The gray that comes after is assigned to Jupiter, and bears his name. He will imagine, if he wishes, places and peoples that never existed, and will apply himself only to pleasing his audience, while nevertheless always maintaining an exact allusion to the events being feigned—as much in the character suited to the actors as in the sequence of variations in state and color that his matter undergoes during the operations. <note>In alchemy, "operations" refer to the specific laboratory processes, such as distillation or calcination, used to transform matter.</note>

# F A B L E S

Those Authors who have claimed that Hercules did not employ violence to carry away the **Golden Apples**, but that he received them from the hand of **Atlas**, have undoubtedly not paid attention to the fact that the Fable says positively that it was necessary, to reach them, to kill that frightful **Dragon** who guarded the entrance to the Garden. But both those who are of this sentiment, and those who are of a contrary opinion, are equally right. The roles full of deception that **Pherecydes** (a) <note>Pherecydes of Athens was an ancient Greek mythographer (c. 450 BCE) who recorded many of the myths regarding Hercules.</note> makes Hercules and Atlas play on this occasion are too unworthy of them, and too poorly combined to merit being mentioned. Hercules used violence by killing the Dragon, in the sense and in the manner that we have described; and one can also say that he received the Apples from the hand of Atlas, in that this so-called King of **Mauritania** signifies nothing other than the rock into which he was changed—that is to say, the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>The "rock" refers to the "Fixed" state of the alchemical matter, often personified as Atlas holding up the heavens.</note>, from which the **Gold of the Sages** is formed, which some Philosophers have called the *fruit of the Sun* or *Golden Apples*.

But what reason could the ancient and modern Philosophers have had to invent Golden Apples? This idea must come quite naturally to a man who knows that the veins of mines extend underground much like the roots of trees. <insert>Sulphurous and mercurial substances</insert> meeting in the pores and veins of the earth and rocks coagulate to form minerals and metals, just as

They take a branch of their <term>Hermetic apple tree</term>; they put it in their water, and in a moderately warm place: it gives them flowers and fruits in its due time. Nature, aided by art, thus shortens the duration of its ordinary operations. Each kingdom has its processes, but those that Nature puts into use for one justify those of the other, because she always acts by a simple and direct path; art must imitate her, but it employs various means when it is a matter of reaching different goals.

The fable of the <term>Hesperides</term> <note>In Greek myth, the Hesperides were nymphs who guarded a garden of golden apples.</note> is proof that the <term>Hermetic Philosopher</term> must consult Nature before working, and imitate her procedures in his operations, if he wishes, like <term>Hercules</term>, to succeed in carrying off the <term>Golden Apples</term> <note>An alchemical allegory for the successful completion of the "Great Work," the creation of gold or the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. # C H A P T E R III.

## The Story of Atalanta.

The fable of Atalanta is so closely linked with that of the Garden of the Hesperides <note>A mythical garden at the edge of the world where golden apples grew, guarded by a dragon.</note> that it depends upon it absolutely, since Venus took from there the apples that she gave to Hippomenes. Ovid had undoubtedly learned from some ancient poet that Venus had gathered these apples in the *Damasean* field on the Island of Cyprus (a). The inventor of this detail alluded to the effect of these apples, since the name of the field where they are supposed to grow signifies *to conquer* or *to tame*, from the Greek <note>original: *δαμάω* (damaō)</note> *to subdue* or *to tame* <note>original Latin: *subigo, domo*</note>; a quality possessed by the Golden Apples of the <term>Philosophical garden</term> <note>In alchemical texts, "Philosophical" refers to the secrets of the Philosopher’s Stone; the "garden" is the vessel where the work matures.</note>, which is taken from the very nature of the thing, as we shall see hereafter.

Opinions have varied regarding the parents of this heroine; some, following Apollodorus, call her the daughter of Iasus, and others the daughter of Schoeneus, King of Arcadia. Some authors have even proposed another Atalanta, daughter of Maenalus, who they say was so swift of foot that no man, however vigorous he might be, could overtake her.

She was a virgin, and of a surprising beauty. She had resolved to preserve her virginity (a), because having consulted the Oracle to know if she should marry, it replied to her that she should not bind herself to a husband, but that she would nonetheless be unable to avoid it. Her beauty attracted many lovers to her, but she turned them all away by the harsh conditions she imposed on those who aspired to marry her.

She proposed that they compete with her in a footrace, on the condition that they would run unarmed; that she would follow them with a javelin, and that those she could reach before they arrived at the goal, she would pierce with this weapon; but that the first who arrived there before her would be her husband. Many attempted it, and perished there.

Hippomenes, great-grandson of the God of the Waters <note>Referring to Neptune (Poseidon), the god of the sea.</note> (b), himself struck by the known courage and the beauty of Atalanta, was not at all deterred by the misfortune of the other suitors of this valiant girl. He invoked Venus, and obtained from her three golden apples. Provided with this help, he presented himself to run with Atalanta under the same conditions as the others. Indeed, it is absolutely required in the "Work" <note>The "Work" or "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) is the traditional term for the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> that the fixed substance first be made volatile <term>volatile: a substance that easily evaporates or changes state</term> before it can, in turn, fix the volatile substance. The union of the two cannot occur before this sequence of operations; this is why the story claims that Hippomenes dropped his apples at intervals along the path.

Abbé Banier (a) <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741) was a French mythologist who famously argued that myths were merely historical events distorted by time—an approach called "euhemerism."</note> himself well understood that horns, and what is more, **golden horns** given to a Hind—which bears none of any kind—formed a circumstance that makes the history at least allegorical, and that the **feet of bronze** must have alluded to something; but he simply reported the fact of the horns without giving any explanation, however much he wished to present this fiction as a true history. For my part, if I wished to explain this fable within the system of this Scholar, I would have supposed, on the contrary, that the Author of this fiction had feigned these feet of bronze to make the fact more believable; not regarding the feet of bronze in themselves, but to suggest figuratively that this Hind was of a nature much heavier than Hinds commonly are, and consequently much less swift in the race, and easier to be caught by a man pursuing her.

Cicero, Plutarch, and many others as well, had conceived of him in a nearly similar way; but some speak only after the others, and when one goes back to the source, one sees Silenus <note>In Greek mythology, Silenus was the tutor and companion of the wine-god Bacchus. He is usually depicted as a jovial, balding drunkard, but also as a possessor of great wisdom when captured.</note> only as a true drunkard, the foster-father of the God Bacchus.

The very singularity of the adventure that delivered Silenus to Midas, and what resulted from it, can only be regarded as pure fiction. Is there any likelihood that Midas, as the greediest of men, would have squandered enough wine to fill a fountain in order to induce Silenus to drink to excess, and thus have him in his possession? Would a miser not have found a means more consistent with his greed, and was it necessary to use such a costly stratagem to obtain something so easy? The ways in which Midas treated Silenus, according to what the Abbé Banier reports, absolutely destroy even the idea of reality.

If we are to believe the same Author <note>Referring to the Abbé Banier, a prominent 18th-century mythographer who tried to explain myths as historical events.</note>, Silenus was then a very learned Philosopher, whose insights Midas employed for the establishment of Religion, and the changes he made in that of the Lydians <note>An ancient people living in western Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey).</note>. And to have a guarantor for the truth of this alleged history, he cites Herodotus *(a)*, to whom he attributes things he did not in fact say. The other explanations are so unnatural, and so far removed from the plausible, that I do not believe I should report them.

If Silenus was a Philosopher, what reason could have led to the supposition that he was the foster-father of Bacchus? Is Philosophy not incompatible with drunkenness? A man habitually addicted to this vice is in no way fit for the deep speculations required by this science. Since this alleged Philosopher was accustomed to go and sleep off his wine near the fountain where he was captured, was it necessary to take so many

Shall we believe, along with the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator who wrote explanatory notes (scholia) in the margins of classical manuscripts.</note> of Aristophanes and the Abbé Banier, that the story of Midas having donkey ears was only invented because this Prince had spies everywhere whom he questioned and listened to with great attention? Shall we say, along with this Mythologist, that he communicated his gold-making power to the Pactolus <note>A river in Lydia (modern Turkey) famous in antiquity for the gold dust found in its sands.</note> River because he forced his subjects to collect the gold that the waters of this river carried along? To gain credibility among his people, and make himself be regarded as a second Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, known for his wisdom and for establishing the city's religious laws.</note>? To conduct commerce in such a way as to become so wealthy that it was claimed he changed everything into gold?

Such are the explanations, or rather the contradictions, of this learned Mythologist, who knows how to ingeniously make use of all Authors to reach his goal. In one place, Midas reigns along the Sangarius <note>original: "Sangar"; a major river in Asia Minor.</note> River; in another, it is along the Pactolus River. There, he is a coarse and stupid man who consequently deserves the fable that he had donkey ears: here, he is a man of wit, a vast and expansive genius capable of great undertakings, worthy of being compared to Numa; and who, having found the secret of knowing everything through his spies, had thereby given cause to the fiction that he wore donkey ears.

One may recall that when the *Osiris*, *Denis* <note>Dionysus</note> or *Bacchus* of the Philosophers <note>In alchemical texts, "Philosophers" usually refers to earlier alchemists; their "Bacchus" or "Osiris" represents specific chemical substances at certain stages of the process.</note> forms, a "earth" is produced. This earth is the *Bacchus* who is said to visit *Phrygia*, because of its fiery, burning, and dry virtue; for Phrygia means *parched and arid land* <note>original Latin: "terra torrida & arida"</note>, from the Greek *to parch* or *to dry out* <note>original: "φρύγω (phrygō), torreo, arefacio"</note>. It is supposed that *Midas* reigns there; but to indicate clearly what must be understood by this alleged King, he is called the son of *Cybele* or of the Earth—the same goddess regarded as the mother of the Gods, but specifically of the Philosophico-Hermetic Gods. Thus *Bacchus*, accompanied by his *Bacchantes* and his *Satyrs*, of whom *Silenus* was the Chief (and himself a *Satyr*), leaves *Thrace* to go toward the *Pactolus* which descends from Mount *Tmolus*; it is precisely as if one were saying that the Philosophical *Bacchus*, or the sulfur, after having been dissolved and volatilized, tends toward coagulation. ...waters the **Pactolus**, in whose waters **Midas** deposited the fatal gift that had been granted to him: **Croesus** <note>The king of Lydia (reigned c. 560–546 BC) renowned for his immense wealth; he was the first to issue true gold coins.</note> would have been, without the Pactolus, nothing more than a monarch restricted in his power, and unable to incite the jealousy of **Cyrus** <note>Cyrus the Great, the founder of the Persian Empire, who defeated Croesus and conquered Lydia.</note>.

According to **Abbé Barthélemy** <note>Jean-Jacques Barthélemy (1716–1795) was a celebrated French scholar, archaeologist, and author of *The Travels of Anacharsis the Younger in Greece*.</note> (*Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres for the year 1747, up to and including the year 1748. Vol. XXI*), the Pactolus has never been more than a very mediocre river, rising from **Mount Tmolus**, flowing through the plain and even through the city of **Sardis**, and ending at the **Hermus** <note>original: "Hemus." Geographically, the Pactolus is a tributary of the Hermus River (modern Gediz) in Turkey.</note> river. **Homer**, who lived near these regions, does not mention it, nor does **Hesiod**, even though he is careful to name the rivers of Asia Minor. Long before **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) who noted that by his time, the gold in the Pactolus had run dry.</note>, the Pactolus no longer carried gold, and all subsequent centuries have found no wealth in this stream, which was so fortunate under the pens of the Poets. Although several serious historians attribute this quality to it, I do not see how Abbé Barthélemy can fix the era of the Pactolus's fertility to the eighth century before the Christian Era, under the ancestors of Croesus (who lost his Kingdom 545 years before Jesus Christ). **Lydia** could have been rich in gold independently of the Pactolus, and the treasures Cyrus found there do not prove at all that they originated from this river. No gold has ever been found on Mount Tmolus; no historian speaks of mines on this mountain. I conclude, therefore, from these reasons, that the whole story is a fable.

When the Poets tell us that everything in Midas's hands became gold, even the dishes served to him for food; we know well that this can only be understood allegorically.

It is found everywhere like the Nymphs: in the meadows, fields, woods, mountains, valleys, and gardens. Everyone sees it, and everyone despises it because of its vile appearance and because it is so common that the poor may possess it as easily as the rich, without anyone opposing them, and without spending money to acquire it.

# CHAPTER VI.

## Of the Golden Age.

**E**verything is confusion, everything is difficulty, and everything presents a labyrinth to Mythologists, from which they cannot extricate themselves when it comes to relating what Authors have transmitted to us about the fabulous ages to history. There is not a single one who does not attribute the Golden Age to the reign of Saturn <note>In Roman mythology, Saturn was the god of agriculture and time; his reign was remembered as a lost paradise of abundance and equality.</note>; but when it comes to determining both the place where this God reigned, the era of this reign, and the reasons that could have led to it being named the *Golden Age*, they no longer know how to proceed. It would have been much simpler to admit that all these alleged histories are nothing but fictions; but people wish to find reality in them, as if it were of great interest today to justify the excessive credulity of most of the Ancients. If we had contemporary authors as guarantors, or those who at least worked from reliable records <note>original: "monumens assurés"</note> and whose authenticity was well-proven, we might believe them. However, it is generally agreed that all these stories come down to us from the Poets, who imitated Egyptian fictions. It is well known that these Poets drew almost everything from their own imaginations, and that Historians only spoke of those times by following their lead. **Herodotus**, the earliest historian known to us, wrote more than four hundred years after **Homer**; and Homer himself lived long after **Orpheus**, **Linus**, and others. For Monsieur the Abbé Banier <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741), a French priest and scholar who argued that myths were actually distorted historical facts.</note>, they are a source of felicity. But finally, what reasons could the Ancients have had for attributing the life of a Golden Age to the reign of Saturn? Never was a reign sullied by more vices; wars, carnage, and crimes of all kinds flooded the earth during all that time. Saturn <note>In mythology, the Titan who ruled during the Golden Age until overthrown by his son Jupiter.</note> only ascended the throne by driving out his father, after having mutilated him. What did Jupiter do more than Saturn to deserve that his reign not be given the name of the Golden Age? Jupiter, in truth, treated him in precisely the same manner that Saturn had treated his own father. Jupiter was an adulterer, a murderer, an incestuous man, etc. But was Saturn worth any more? Had he not also married his sister Rhea? Did he not have Philyra <note>A nymph whom Saturn sought to hide his affair from his wife; she later gave birth to the centaur Chiron.</note> as a concubine, not counting the others? Did one ever see a King more inhuman than he who devours his own children? It is true that he did not devour Jupiter; but he intended to do so in good faith, and we should not give him credit for the failure; he was presented with a pebble; he swallowed it, and being unable to digest it, he brought it back up. This stone, according to Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet whose work "Theogony" describes the origins of the gods.</note>, was placed on Mount Helicon, to serve—

### CHAPTER VII.

->Of Showers of Gold.<-

The Poets have often spoken of showers of gold, & some Pagan Authors had the weakness to report as true, that a shower of gold fell at Rhodes, when the Sun <note>Helios/Apollo</note> lay there with Venus <note>Aphrodite</note>. One might forgive the Poets for this; but that Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and philosopher (c. 64 BC – 24 AD).</note> should tell us (*b*) that it rained gold at Rhodes when Minerva <note>Athena</note> was born from the brain of Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>—that we cannot permit him. Several Authors assure us, in truth, that at such or such a time, it rained stones, blood, or some liquid that resembled it, or insects. Many people even today protest they have seen it rain small frogs, that they fell in abundance on their hats mixed with a rainstorm; that they had seen such a great quantity of them that the earth was almost covered with them. Without entering into the investigation of the physical causes of such phenomena, & without

One can indeed call a *shower of gold* a rain that would produce gold, or a matter suitable for making it, just as the common people say quite often that it "rains wine" when a rain comes at the time it is desired, either to soften the grapes or to make them grow. This is precisely what happens through the circulation of the <term>Philosophical matter</term> <note>The substance undergoing alchemical transformation, often referred to as the "materia prima."</note> in the vessel where it is enclosed. It dissolves, and having risen as vapors to the top of the vessel, it condenses there and falls back as rain onto the portion remaining at the bottom. It is for this reason that the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>A term used by alchemists to refer to themselves: the "Philosophers of Nature."</note> have sometimes given the name "cloud water" to their <term>mercurial water</term> <note>The liquid solvent used in the Great Work, symbolized by Mercury.</note>. A monster, named Erichthonius, because this very name designates the thing: that is to say, "contention" and "earth" <note>original: "la contestation & la terre". It is therefore the seed of Vulcan that produces Erichthonius. And if it is said that Aglaurus was charged by Minerva with caring for him, without being permitted to look at what the basket contained; one feels clearly that a condition such as that, which rendered the thing impossible, could only have been invented for the sake of an allegory, just like her metamorphosis into a rock. The explanation of this fable will be very easy for anyone who wishes to recall those we have given of the other rains of gold. One easily understands that Danaë and the tower represent the matter and the brass <note>original: "airain". In alchemical allegory, this refers to the base metal or the metallic body before transformation.</note> of the Philosophers <note>In this context, the "Philosophers" are the alchemists, who called themselves the "Philosophers by Fire."</note> which they call *copper*, *latten*, or *brass*; that the rain of gold is the drops of golden water, or the aurific <note>Gold-making.</note> dew that rises during circulation, and falls back onto the earth, which is at the bottom of the vessel. One might even say, along with the mythologists, that Jupiter is taken for the air; but here it must be understood as the gray color called Jupiter, because the rain of gold manifests itself during the time when the matter passes from the color black to gray. Perseus is the fruit born from this circulation. I do not quite see on what basis the Abbé Banier <note>Antoine Banier (1673–1741), a French mythographer known for his historical interpretations of myths.</note> derives the etymology of Perseus from the Hebrew word *Paras*; it is true that it signifies *Horseman*; and that Perseus rode a horse. But why would the Greeks have gone looking in the Hebrew language for names that the Greek language provided them in abundance? From the drops of Medusa's blood was born Chrysaor, and from him, Geryon. This is as if one were saying that from the red water of the Philosophers—which Pythagoras calls *blood (a)*, along with many other Adepts, and Raymond Lully <note>A 13th-century polymath and philosopher to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> with

From Ripley’s Red Wine <note>original: "Riplée vin rouge". This refers to the "Red Wine" or "Blood" described by George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist; it symbolizes the soul of the gold or the transformative agent.</note>, gold is born, or the philosophical sulfur <note>In alchemy, "philosophical sulfur" represents the active, masculine principle of matter, associated with heat and fixity.</note>. It is known, moreover, that Chrysaor comes from the Greek word for gold <note>original: "χρυσὸς" (chrysos); the text also provides the Latin "aurum".</note>. This gold, dissolved in its own blood-red water, produces the elixir or Geryon, with three bodies or three heads, because it is composed of the exact combination of the three principles: sulfur, salt, and mercury <note>The "Tria Prima" or three primes. Alchemists believed these three substances were the base of all matter; Geryon's three heads represent their perfect union in the final Stone.</note>. I will explain this fable at greater length in the chapter on Perseus. I could have included several others in this second book; but by these examples, one may judge the rest. I did not intend to produce an entire Mythology; it is enough to prove my system <note>The author's "system" is the Hermetic or alchemical interpretation of ancient myths, suggesting they are secret chemical recipes rather than moral or historical tales.</note> by explaining the principal and most ancient ones. I will, moreover, have the opportunity to review a great number of them in the following book, which will deal with the genealogy of the Gods.

->**THE KING’S PRIVILEGE.**<-

LOUIS, by the grace of God, King of France and of Navarre: To our beloved and faithful Counselors, the members of our Courts of Parliament, Masters of Ordinary Requests of our Household, Grand Council, Provost of Paris, Bailiffs, Seneschals, their Civil Lieutenants, and our other Justices whom it may concern; GREETINGS. Our beloved Sieur <note>A title of respect, similar to 'Sir' or 'Mister'</note> Jean-Baptiste-Claude BAUCHE, Bookseller in Paris, has informed us that he desires to print and give to the Public several Works entitled: *Methodical Enumeration of the Plants of the Coast and Country of Nice by Carlo Allioni* <note>original Latin: 'Caroli Allionii enumeratio Methodica stirpium Littoris & agri Nicæensis'</note>; *EGYPTIAN AND GREEK Fables, and the Mytho-Hermetic Dictionary, by Dom Pernety*; *the Topography of the Universe, by the Abbé Expilly*; should it please us to grant him our Letters of privilege necessary for this: FOR THESE REASONS, wishing to treat the Petitioner favorably, We have permitted and do permit him by these Presents to have the said Works printed as many times as he sees fit, and to sell them and have them sold and distributed throughout our Kingdom for the duration of six consecutive years, counting from the date of these Presents. We forbid all Printers, Booksellers, and other persons of whatever quality and condition they may be, from introducing any foreign printing of them into any place under our authority; as well as from printing or having printed, selling, having sold, distributing, or counterfeiting the said Works, or making any extract from them under any pretext whatsoever, whether of addition, correction, change, or others, without the express written permission of the said Petitioner, or those who hold rights from him, under penalty of confiscation of the counterfeit Copies, and a fine of 3000 <term>livres</term> <note>The 'livre' was the currency of France until 1795; 3000 was a substantial sum, often exceeding the annual income of a skilled worker</note> against each offender, of which one third goes to Us, one third to the <term>Hôtel-Dieu of Paris</term> <note>The oldest and primary hospital in Paris, often a beneficiary of legal fines</note>, and the other third to the said Petitioner, or to the person holding rights from him, along with all costs, damages, and interests; on the condition that these Presents shall be recorded in full on the Register of the Guild of Printers and Booksellers of Paris within three months of the

date of these presents, provided that the printing of the said Works shall be carried out within our Kingdom, and not elsewhere, on good paper and with beautiful type characters, in accordance with the printed sheet attached as a model under the <term>Counter-seal</term> <note>A secondary seal applied to the back of a document to ensure its authenticity and prevent tampering.</note> of these Presents; that the Petitioner shall conform in all things to the Regulations of the <term>Book Trade</term> <note>The "Librairie" referred to the organized guild of booksellers and printers who were subject to strict royal censorship and trade laws.</note>, and notably to the regulation of April 10, 1725; that before offering them for sale, the Manuscripts that served as the copy for the printing of said Works shall be returned in the same condition in which the Approval was granted, into the hands of our very dear and faithful Knight, Chancellor of France, the Sieur de Lamoignon; and that two copies of each shall then be delivered to our public Library, one to that of our Castle of the Louvre, and one to that of our very dear and faithful Knight, Chancellor of France, the Sieur de Lamoignon; the whole upon pain of nullity of these Presents. We command and enjoin you to allow the said Petitioner and his successors to enjoy the contents of these Presents fully and peacefully, without permitting any trouble or hindrance to be caused to them. We will that the Copy of these Presents, which shall be printed in full at the beginning or the end of the said Work, be held as duly notified; and that the copies collated by one of our beloved and faithful Counselor-Secretaries be given the same credit as the Original. We command the first of our Ushers or Sergeants requested for this purpose to perform all necessary acts for the execution of these presents, without asking for other permission, and notwithstanding any <term>hue and cry</term> <note>original: "clameur de Haro," an ancient legal protest used to immediately halt an action</note>, <term>Norman charter</term> <note>A set of regional privileges for Normandy that often provided exemptions from royal edicts</note>, or Letters to the contrary. FOR such is our pleasure. GIVEN at Versailles on the 24th day of the month of October, in the year of grace 1757, and of our Reign the forty-third. By the King in his Council.

->LE BEGUE.<-

->Registered on the 14th Register of the Royal Chamber of Booksellers and<-
->Printers of Paris, No. 244. fol. 218. in accordance with the ancient<-
->Regulations confirmed by that of February 28, 1723. At Paris, October 7,<-
->1757. P. G. LE MERCIER, Syndic.<-
